**Lesson 39: Exodus: the burning bush — I AM sends Moses**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Moses was drawn out of the Nile and raised in Pharaoh’s house. Forty years later he killed an Egyptian, fled, and spent another forty years tending sheep in the desert. That is where God met him, in a bush that “was on fire” but “did not burn up” (3:2).

Before God gave Moses a job, he told Moses who he was dealing with: “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground” (3:5). Then God showed his heart: “I have indeed seen the misery of my people … So I have come down to rescue them” (3:7–8).

Moses asked, “Who am I?” (3:11). God didn’t answer with a pep talk. He said, “I will be with you” (3:12). Jean Wilund of Revive Our Hearts puts it well: “It didn’t matter who Moses was. He didn’t need to believe in himself and what he could do. He needed to believe in who God is.” She also quotes an old saying: “Any old bush will do as long as God is in the bush.”

Then God gave his name: “I am who I am” (3:14). John Piper explains that “the name Yahweh and the name I AM are built out of the same Hebrew word,” and that “God aims to be known not as a generic deity, but as a specific person with a name that carries his unique character and mission.” Piper warns against believing in God the way we believe in hydrogen, true but making no difference. He pictures God asking on judgment day, “Why did you treat me as though I were like hydrogen?” The God who said “I AM” is the God who leads your home.

**Exodus 3:1–15 (NIV)**
1 Now Moses was tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. 2 There the angel of the Lord appeared to him in flames of fire from within a bush. Moses saw that though the bush was on fire it did not burn up. 3 So Moses thought, “I will go over and see this strange sight—why the bush does not burn up.” 4 When the Lord saw that he had gone over to look, God called to him from within the bush, “Moses! Moses!” And Moses said, “Here I am.” 5 “Do not come any closer,” God said. “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” 6 Then he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.” At this, Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God. 7 The Lord said, “I have indeed seen the misery of my people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their slave drivers, and I am concerned about their suffering. 8 So I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land into a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey—the home of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. 9 And now the cry of the Israelites has reached me, and I have seen the way the Egyptians are oppressing them. 10 So now, go. I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people the Israelites out of Egypt.” 11 But Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” 12 And God said, “I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.” 13 Moses said to God, “Suppose I go to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ Then what shall I tell them?” 14 God said to Moses, “I am who I am. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I am has sent me to you.’” 15 God also said to Moses, “Say to the Israelites, ‘The Lord, the God of your fathers—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob—has sent me to you.’ “This is my name forever, the name you shall call me from generation to generation.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 3:7.** NIV: “I am concerned about their suffering.” LSB: “I know their sufferings.” The Hebrew verb is “know.” It means more than awareness; it is close, personal knowing. God was not watching from a distance.
- **Exod 3:12.** NIV: “you will worship God on this mountain.” LSB: “you shall serve God at this mountain.” The Hebrew word can mean either serve or worship. It is the same word used for Israel’s forced labor for Pharaoh. God was moving his people from slavery to Pharaoh to service of himself.
- **Exod 3:14.** NIV: “I am who I am.” LSB: “I AM WHO I AM.” The NIV prints the words in small capitals, so both versions signal that this is God’s name. The Hebrew can also be read “I will be what I will be,” which the NIV gives in a footnote.
- **Exod 3:15.** NIV: “The Lord.” LSB: “Yahweh.” The name Yahweh comes from the same Hebrew verb, “to be,” as “I AM.” The LSB spells it out so you can see God connecting his name to what he just said.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s sermon [“‘I Am Who I Am’”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-am-who-i-am) opens his series on the names of God and lists seven things the name teaches. Jean Wilund’s short article [“Ask the Best Questions When Life Is Too Hard”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/blog/ask-best-questions-when-life-too-hard/) follows Moses from “Who am I?” to “Show me your glory.” BibleProject’s [Exodus 1–18 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-1-18/) shows where the burning bush fits.

**Reflection question:** Where are you asking “Who am I?” about something God has put in front of you, and how would remembering “I will be with you” change the way you lead as a man, husband, and father this week?

**Lesson 40: Exodus: Passover — saved by the blood**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God sent Moses with his name, I AM. Pharaoh refused again and again through nine plagues. Today comes the last one, and with it the clearest picture of the gospel in the Old Testament.

God told each man to “take a lamb for his family, one for each household” (12:3), and to put its blood on the doorframes. “When I see the blood, I will pass over you” (12:13). Skip Heitzig, writing in Billy Graham’s *Decision* magazine, says, “The basis for a relationship with God will be the blood of an innocent sacrifice.” He describes the scene in a home: the family cared for the lamb, “But then, on the 14th day of that month, the father would kill it, explaining to his kids that it was the substitute for their family.”

Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth points out that the Israelites were not better than the Egyptians: “There’s no salvation without judgment. But wherever there is judgment, there is salvation offered. The only difference was the lamb, the blood of the lamb.” Heitzig agrees: “Blood was a sign of their faith. When God saw it, He would pass over that home. They would be saved, through faith, by the shed blood.”

Paul says, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7), and Jesus gave the Lord’s Supper at a Passover meal. Heitzig traces the line: “God’s mercy extended from one person to a family, from one family to an entire nation, and ultimately, from one nation to the whole world.” Israel kept this night every year so their children would never forget (12:42). Every time your family takes the Lord’s Supper, you have the same chance to explain what the Lamb did for them.

**Exodus 12:1–13 (NIV)**
1 The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in Egypt, 2 “This month is to be for you the first month, the first month of your year. 3 Tell the whole community of Israel that on the tenth day of this month each man is to take a lamb for his family, one for each household. 4 If any household is too small for a whole lamb, they must share one with their nearest neighbor, having taken into account the number of people there are. You are to determine the amount of lamb needed in accordance with what each person will eat. 5 The animals you choose must be year-old males without defect, and you may take them from the sheep or the goats. 6 Take care of them until the fourteenth day of the month, when all the members of the community of Israel must slaughter them at twilight. 7 Then they are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs. 8 That same night they are to eat the meat roasted over the fire, along with bitter herbs, and bread made without yeast. 9 Do not eat the meat raw or boiled in water, but roast it over a fire—with the head, legs and internal organs. 10 Do not leave any of it till morning; if some is left till morning, you must burn it. 11 This is how you are to eat it: with your cloak tucked into your belt, your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. Eat it in haste; it is the Lord’s Passover. 12 “On that same night I will pass through Egypt and strike down every firstborn of both people and animals, and I will bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. I am the Lord. 13 The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are, and when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No destructive plague will touch you when I strike Egypt.

**Exodus 12:29–42 (NIV)**
29 At midnight the Lord struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner, who was in the dungeon, and the firstborn of all the livestock as well. 30 Pharaoh and all his officials and all the Egyptians got up during the night, and there was loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead. 31 During the night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Up! Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the Lord as you have requested. 32 Take your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.” 33 The Egyptians urged the people to hurry and leave the country. “For otherwise,” they said, “we will all die!” 34 So the people took their dough before the yeast was added, and carried it on their shoulders in kneading troughs wrapped in clothing. 35 The Israelites did as Moses instructed and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold and for clothing. 36 The Lord had made the Egyptians favorably disposed toward the people, and they gave them what they asked for; so they plundered the Egyptians. 37 The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Sukkoth. There were about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. 38 Many other people went up with them, and also large droves of livestock, both flocks and herds. 39 With the dough the Israelites had brought from Egypt, they baked loaves of unleavened bread. The dough was without yeast because they had been driven out of Egypt and did not have time to prepare food for themselves. 40 Now the length of time the Israelite people lived in Egypt was 430 years. 41 At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the Lord’s divisions left Egypt. 42 Because the Lord kept vigil that night to bring them out of Egypt, on this night all the Israelites are to keep vigil to honor the Lord for the generations to come.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 12:3.** NIV: “each man is to take a lamb for his family, one for each household.” LSB: “according to their fathers’ households, a lamb for each household.” The Hebrew speaks of the “father’s house.” The LSB keeps that wording, which shows that each father was responsible to put his household under the blood.
- **Exod 12:5.** NIV: “without defect.” LSB: “without blemish.” Same meaning. The LSB’s wording matches the familiar phrase in 1 Peter 1:19, where Christ is “a lamb without blemish.”
- **Exod 12:31.** NIV: “worship the Lord.” LSB: “serve Yahweh.” This is the same Hebrew word you saw at the burning bush (3:12): it means both serve and worship. Israel was freed from serving Pharaoh to serve God.
- **Exod 12:38.** NIV: “Many other people went up with them.” LSB: “A foreign multitude also went up with them.” The Hebrew means a mixed crowd, people who were not Israelites. Even at the Exodus, outsiders found shelter with God’s people.

**Go deeper:** Skip Heitzig’s [“Getting Passed Over”](https://billygraham.org/decision-magazine/articles/getting-passed-over) in *Decision* magazine walks through the Passover’s three truths: our sin, our Substitute, and our salvation. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“His Name Is Lamb of God”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/his-name-is-lamb-of-god/) follows the lamb from Genesis 22 through Passover to Jesus. BibleProject’s [Exodus 1–18 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-1-18/) shows how the Exodus shapes the whole Bible.

**Reflection question:** As the head of your household, how can you explain to Jordyn, Eli, and Enoch this week that Jesus is the Lamb whose blood covers your family, as a man, husband, and father who leads them to him?

You are to determine the amount of lamb needed in accordance with what each person will eat. 5 The animals you choose must be year-old males without defect, and you may take them from the sheep or the goats. 6 Take care of them until the fourteenth day of the month, when all the members of the community of Israel must slaughter them at twilight. 7 Then they are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs. 8 That same night they are to eat the meat roasted over the fire, along with bitter herbs, and bread made without yeast. 9 Do not eat the meat raw or boiled in water, but roast it over a fire—with the head, legs and internal organs. 10 Do not leave any of it till morning; if some is left till morning, you must burn it. 11 This is how you are to eat it: with your cloak tucked into your belt, your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. I am the Lord. 13 The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are, and when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No destructive plague will touch you when I strike Egypt.

29 At midnight the Lord struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner, who was in the dungeon, and the firstborn of all the livestock as well. 30 Pharaoh and all his officials and all the Egyptians got up during the night, and there was loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead. 31 During the night Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Up! Leave my people, you and the Israelites! Go, worship the Lord as you have requested. 32 Take your flocks and herds, as you have said, and go. And also bless me.” 33 The Egyptians urged the people to hurry and leave the country. “For otherwise,” they said, “we will all die!” 34 So the people took their dough before the yeast was added, and carried it on their shoulders in kneading troughs wrapped in clothing. 35 The Israelites did as Moses instructed and asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold and for clothing. 36 The Lord had made the Egyptians favorably disposed toward the people, and they gave them what they asked for; so they plundered the Egyptians. 37 The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Sukkoth. - **Exod 12:5.** NIV: “without defect.” LSB: “without blemish.” Same meaning. The LSB’s wording matches the familiar phrase in 1 Peter 1:19, where Christ is “a lamb without blemish.”
- **Exod 12:31.** NIV: “worship the Lord.” LSB: “serve Yahweh.” This is the same Hebrew word you saw at the burning bush (3:12): it means both serve and worship. Israel was freed from serving Pharaoh to serve God.

**Reflection question:** Like the Israelite mothers who helped their children remember the Passover, how can you, as a woman, wife, and mother, help your children understand this Christmas season that Jesus came to be the Lamb who saves them?

**Lesson 41: Exodus: through the sea — the Lord fights for you**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the blood of the lamb covered every Israelite home, and Pharaoh finally let the people go. Today he changes his mind. His army comes after them, and Israel is pinned between the chariots and the sea.

The people panic and blame Moses (14:11–12). Moses answers, “The Lord will fight for you; you need only to be still” (14:14). Jon Bloom of Desiring God says of that spot by the water, “They were trapped in a weak place — a place designed for them by God.” God led them there on purpose so that everyone would know he is the Lord (14:18).

Bloom explains why: “God wanted Israel to understand that he was their strength and their salvation so that he would become their song.” That is what happens in the next chapter, when Moses and the people sing. Will Graham, Billy Graham’s grandson, puts it simply: “Sometimes we fail to connect the promises of God with our reality.” Then he adds, “But God is on our side. He fights our battles for us.”

Bloom also points to the cross: “The exodus was the greatest Old Testament foreshadowing of the gospel of Jesus Christ. God delivers us all as helpless children, caught between the forces of evil and the sea of God’s wrath.” Notice that God told Moses to lead the people forward (14:15). Being still did not mean sitting down. It meant stop panicking, trust God, and walk where he opens the way.

**Exodus 14:10–31 (NIV)**
10 As Pharaoh approached, the Israelites looked up, and there were the Egyptians, marching after them. They were terrified and cried out to the Lord. 11 They said to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us to the desert to die? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt? 12 Didn’t we say to you in Egypt, ‘Leave us alone; let us serve the Egyptians’? It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the desert!” 13 Moses answered the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the deliverance the Lord will bring you today. The Egyptians you see today you will never see again. 14 The Lord will fight for you; you need only to be still.” 15 Then the Lord said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to move on. 16 Raise your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea to divide the water so that the Israelites can go through the sea on dry ground. 17 I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they will go in after them. And I will gain glory through Pharaoh and all his army, through his chariots and his horsemen. 18 The Egyptians will know that I am the Lord when I gain glory through Pharaoh, his chariots and his horsemen.” 19 Then the angel of God, who had been traveling in front of Israel’s army, withdrew and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front and stood behind them, 20 coming between the armies of Egypt and Israel. Throughout the night the cloud brought darkness to the one side and light to the other side; so neither went near the other all night long. 21 Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the Lord drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The waters were divided, 22 and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. 23 The Egyptians pursued them, and all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots and horsemen followed them into the sea. 24 During the last watch of the night the Lord looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud at the Egyptian army and threw it into confusion. 25 He jammed the wheels of their chariots so that they had difficulty driving. And the Egyptians said, “Let’s get away from the Israelites! The Lord is fighting for them against Egypt.” 26 Then the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea so that the waters may flow back over the Egyptians and their chariots and horsemen.” 27 Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea went back to its place. The Egyptians were fleeing toward it, and the Lord swept them into the sea. 28 The water flowed back and covered the chariots and horsemen—the entire army of Pharaoh that had followed the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived. 29 But the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left. 30 That day the Lord saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore. 31 And when the Israelites saw the mighty hand of the Lord displayed against the Egyptians, the people feared the Lord and put their trust in him and in Moses his servant.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 14:13.** NIV: “Stand firm and you will see the deliverance the Lord will bring you today.” LSB: “Stand by and see the salvation of Yahweh.” The Hebrew word here is the word for salvation (it sounds like the name Jesus, “Yahweh saves”). The NIV says deliverance; the LSB keeps salvation, which ties this rescue to the gospel.
- **Exod 14:14.** NIV: “you need only to be still.” LSB: “you will keep silent.” The Hebrew means to be quiet or to stop. Israel was not told to do nothing, since God told them to move on in the next verse. They were told to stop panicking and complaining and let God do the fighting.
- **Exod 14:31.** NIV: “put their trust in him.” LSB: “they believed in Yahweh.” It is the same Hebrew word used of Abraham in Genesis 15:6: he “believed” the Lord. Same meaning, but the LSB lets you hear the echo.

**Go deeper:** Jon Bloom’s [“God Does Not Need You to Be Strong”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-does-not-need-you-to-be-strong) at Desiring God explains why God puts us in weak places. [“God Will Fight for You”](https://billygraham.org.uk/p/summer-soul-refresher-god-will-fight-for-you/) from the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association applies Exodus 14:14 to the battles we face today. BibleProject’s [Exodus 1–18 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-1-18/) shows the whole rescue story.

**Reflection question:** When your family feels trapped by a hard situation, how can you, as a man, husband, and father, show Sanqueta and the kids what it looks like to stop panicking, trust that the Lord fights for you, and still lead them forward?

**Lesson 42: Exodus: Sinai and the Ten Commandments**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God carried Israel through the sea. Today, three months later, he brings them to Mount Sinai and speaks the Ten Commandments.

Look at the order. Before a single command, God says, “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery” (20:2). Chris Bruno of Desiring God puts it this way: “the work of God to redeem his people from slavery comes before his commands to his people.” God did not say, “Obey, and I will rescue you.” He rescued them first, then told them how his free people should live. In 19:4 he even says he carried them “on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.”

The first commands are about loving God, and the rest are about loving people: honoring parents, protecting life, marriage, property, and the truth. Jen Wilkin writes, “Law and grace have come to be pitted against one another as enemies, when in fact, they are friends.” Bruno adds that Israel could not keep the law in its own strength: “They needed a greater redemption through a greater redeemer than Joshua or Moses.” That Redeemer is Jesus, who kept the law perfectly for us.

Christians do not all agree on how each command applies today, especially the Sabbath. Some Reformed churches treat Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday, and many Baptists see the Sabbath fulfilled in the rest Christ gives while still setting apart the Lord’s Day for worship. Bruno writes, “Regardless of whether we think nine, ten, or zero commandments are immediately binding on us today,” it is only through Christ that we can truly love God and neighbor.

**Exodus 19:1–8 (NIV)**
1 On the first day of the third month after the Israelites left Egypt—on that very day—they came to the Desert of Sinai. 2 After they set out from Rephidim, they entered the Desert of Sinai, and Israel camped there in the desert in front of the mountain. 3 Then Moses went up to God, and the Lord called to him from the mountain and said, “This is what you are to say to the descendants of Jacob and what you are to tell the people of Israel: 4 ‘You yourselves have seen what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself. 5 Now if you obey me fully and keep my covenant, then out of all nations you will be my treasured possession. Although the whole earth is mine, 6 you will be for me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words you are to speak to the Israelites.” 7 So Moses went back and summoned the elders of the people and set before them all the words the Lord had commanded him to speak. 8 The people all responded together, “We will do everything the Lord has said.” So Moses brought their answer back to the Lord.

**Exodus 20:1–17 (NIV)**
1 And God spoke all these words: 2 “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery. 3 “You shall have no other gods before me. 4 “You shall not make for yourself an image in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath or in the waters below. 5 You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the Lord your God, am a jealous God, punishing the children for the sin of the parents to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, 6 but showing love to a thousand generations of those who love me and keep my commandments. 7 “You shall not misuse the name of the Lord your God, for the Lord will not hold anyone guiltless who misuses his name. 8 “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. 9 Six days you shall labor and do all your work, 10 but the seventh day is a sabbath to the Lord your God. On it you shall not do any work, neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your male or female servant, nor your animals, nor any foreigner residing in your towns. 11 For in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, but he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy. 12 “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the Lord your God is giving you. 13 “You shall not murder. 14 “You shall not commit adultery. 15 “You shall not steal. 16 “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor. 17 “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his male or female servant, his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 19:5.** NIV: “if you obey me fully.” LSB: “if you will indeed listen to My voice.” The Hebrew repeats the verb “listen” for emphasis. In Hebrew, to truly listen to God means to obey him, so both are right. The LSB keeps the picture of hearing his voice.
- **Exod 20:6.** NIV: “showing love.” LSB: “showing lovingkindness.” The Hebrew word is *hesed*, God’s loyal, covenant love. The LSB’s longer word tries to carry that loyalty.
- **Exod 20:7.** NIV: “You shall not misuse the name of the Lord.” LSB: “You shall not take the name of Yahweh your God in vain.” The Hebrew is literally to “lift up” or “carry” his name “to emptiness.” It covers careless cursing, but also carrying God’s name as his people while living as if it means nothing.

**Go deeper:** Chris Bruno’s [“The Heart of God’s Law”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-heart-of-gods-law) at Desiring God traces the Ten Commandments to Jesus. Jen Wilkin’s [“5 Questions about the Ten Commandments”](https://www.crossway.org/articles/5-questions-about-the-ten-commandments/) explains why law and grace are friends. BibleProject’s [Exodus 19–40 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-19-40/) shows how Sinai fits the whole story.

**Reflection question:** God rescued Israel first and then gave them his commands. As a man, husband, and father, how can you lead your home so that Jordyn, Eli, and Enoch see obedience as a grateful response to God’s rescue rather than a way to earn his love?

Chris Bruno’s [“The Heart of God’s Law”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-heart-of-gods-law) at Desiring God traces the Ten Commandments to Jesus. BibleProject’s [Exodus 19–40 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-19-40/) shows how Sinai fits the whole story.

**Lesson 43: Exodus: the golden calf, and Moses sees God's glory**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God gave the Ten Commandments. Today, while Moses is still on the mountain, the people break the first two. They melt their gold, Aaron shapes a calf, and they say, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt” (32:4).

God tells Moses he will destroy them, and Moses pleads for them (32:11–13). David Mathis of Desiring God says the big question hanging over these chapters is this: “Moses knew a powerful God who had delivered his people, but would he also forgive them?” God relents (32:14). Then Moses keeps asking for more: that God’s presence would go with them, and finally, “Now show me your glory” (33:18).

God answers by showing Moses his goodness and proclaiming his name (33:19). Mathis reminds us that in this story we are not only like Moses, but like the people: “They are ‘stiff-necked.’ Rebellious. Deserving of divine justice. Desperate for mercy and grace.” Then he points to Jesus: “But in Christ, we have one far greater than Moses who intercedes for us, leveraging his own perfect favor with God on our behalf.”

Moses could only see God’s back. In Christ we see God’s glory in Jesus’ face (2 Cor 4:6). Mathis says, “What was unique in ancient Israel — speaking to God ‘as a man speaks to his friend’ — is offered to all who are in Christ.” A father who prays for his family stands in a small way where Moses stood, asking God to go with the people he leads.

**Exodus 32:1–14 (NIV)**
1 When the people saw that Moses was so long in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and said, “Come, make us gods who will go before us. As for this fellow Moses who brought us up out of Egypt, we don’t know what has happened to him.” 2 Aaron answered them, “Take off the gold earrings that your wives, your sons and your daughters are wearing, and bring them to me.” 3 So all the people took off their earrings and brought them to Aaron. 4 He took what they handed him and made it into an idol cast in the shape of a calf, fashioning it with a tool. Then they said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.” 5 When Aaron saw this, he built an altar in front of the calf and announced, “Tomorrow there will be a festival to the Lord.” 6 So the next day the people rose early and sacrificed burnt offerings and presented fellowship offerings. Afterward they sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry. 7 Then the Lord said to Moses, “Go down, because your people, whom you brought up out of Egypt, have become corrupt. 8 They have been quick to turn away from what I commanded them and have made themselves an idol cast in the shape of a calf. They have bowed down to it and sacrificed to it and have said, ‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.’ 9 “I have seen these people,” the Lord said to Moses, “and they are a stiff-necked people. 10 Now leave me alone so that my anger may burn against them and that I may destroy them. Then I will make you into a great nation.” 11 But Moses sought the favor of the Lord his God. “Lord,” he said, “why should your anger burn against your people, whom you brought out of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand? 12 Why should the Egyptians say, ‘It was with evil intent that he brought them out, to kill them in the mountains and to wipe them off the face of the earth’? Turn from your fierce anger; relent and do not bring disaster on your people. 13 Remember your servants Abraham, Isaac and Israel, to whom you swore by your own self: ‘I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and I will give your descendants all this land I promised them, and it will be their inheritance forever.’” 14 Then the Lord relented and did not bring on his people the disaster he had threatened.

**Exodus 33:12–23 (NIV)**
12 Moses said to the Lord, “You have been telling me, ‘Lead these people,’ but you have not let me know whom you will send with me. You have said, ‘I know you by name and you have found favor with me.’ 13 If you are pleased with me, teach me your ways so I may know you and continue to find favor with you. Remember that this nation is your people.” 14 The Lord replied, “My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.” 15 Then Moses said to him, “If your Presence does not go with us, do not send us up from here. 16 How will anyone know that you are pleased with me and with your people unless you go with us? What else will distinguish me and your people from all the other people on the face of the earth?” 17 And the Lord said to Moses, “I will do the very thing you have asked, because I am pleased with you and I know you by name.” 18 Then Moses said, “Now show me your glory.” 19 And the Lord said, “I will cause all my goodness to pass in front of you, and I will proclaim my name, the Lord, in your presence. I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. 20 But,” he said, “you cannot see my face, for no one may see me and live.” 21 Then the Lord said, “There is a place near me where you may stand on a rock. 22 When my glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft in the rock and cover you with my hand until I have passed by. 23 Then I will remove my hand and you will see my back; but my face must not be seen.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 32:11.** NIV: “Moses sought the favor of the Lord.” LSB: “Moses entreated the favor of Yahweh.” The Hebrew pictures softening someone’s face by pleading. Both mean Moses begged God for mercy; the LSB’s “entreated” sounds more like earnest prayer.
- **Exod 33:13.** NIV: “If you are pleased with me.” LSB: “if I have found favor in Your sight.” The LSB keeps the Hebrew phrase “found favor,” the same words used of Noah in Genesis 6:8. Moses is not claiming to deserve anything; he is leaning on grace God already showed him.
- **Exod 33:19.** NIV: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.” LSB: “I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and I will show compassion on whom I will show compassion.” The first Hebrew verb means to show grace or favor. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:15 to show that salvation rests on God’s free mercy, not on what we earn.

**Go deeper:** David Mathis’s [“Talking Back to God”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/talking-back-to-god) at Desiring God walks through Moses’s prayers in Exodus 32–33. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Down from the Mountain”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/down-mountain/) at Revive Our Hearts looks at the golden calf through Joshua’s eyes. BibleProject’s [Exodus 19–40 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-19-40/) shows how this failure fits the story.

**Reflection question:** Moses stood between God and the people he led and prayed for them by name. As a man, husband, and father, when will you set aside time this week to pray for Sanqueta, Jordyn, Eli, and Enoch the way Moses prayed for Israel?

**Lesson 44: Exodus: the tabernacle — God dwells with his people**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Israel built a golden calf, and Moses begged God not to leave them. Today we see God’s answer. The people finish the tabernacle, Moses sets it up exactly as God commanded, and then “the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle” (40:34).

This was the point of the whole Exodus. God did not rescue Israel only to get them out of Egypt. He rescued them so he could live among them. The tent sat in the middle of the camp, and the cloud over it by day and fire by night told every family that God was with them on every step of the journey (40:38).

John Piper connects this to Christmas. John says Jesus “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and Piper explains, “The word for ‘dwelt’ is the word for ‘set up a tent’ in Greek.” Then he says, “I think what pitching a tent with us implies is that God wants to be on familiar terms with us. He wants to be close. He wants a lot of interaction.” He puts it in plain terms: “But if you pitch a tent in my backyard, you will probably use my bathroom and eat often at my table.”

Piper preached that on Christmas Eve, and it fits this week. “God came to live in a tent so we can watch him more closely. God wants to be seen and known in his Son.” Moses could not even enter the tent when the glory came down (40:35). In Jesus, God came close enough to touch, and through him your family can draw near.

**Exodus 40:1–17 (NIV)**
1 Then the Lord said to Moses: 2 “Set up the tabernacle, the tent of meeting, on the first day of the first month. 3 Place the ark of the covenant law in it and shield the ark with the curtain. 4 Bring in the table and set out what belongs on it. Then bring in the lampstand and set up its lamps. 5 Place the gold altar of incense in front of the ark of the covenant law and put the curtain at the entrance to the tabernacle. 6 “Place the altar of burnt offering in front of the entrance to the tabernacle, the tent of meeting; 7 place the basin between the tent of meeting and the altar and put water in it. 8 Set up the courtyard around it and put the curtain at the entrance to the courtyard. 9 “Take the anointing oil and anoint the tabernacle and everything in it; consecrate it and all its furnishings, and it will be holy. 10 Then anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils; consecrate the altar, and it will be most holy. 11 Anoint the basin and its stand and consecrate them. 12 “Bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance to the tent of meeting and wash them with water. 13 Then dress Aaron in the sacred garments, anoint him and consecrate him so he may serve me as priest. 14 Bring his sons and dress them in tunics. 15 Anoint them just as you anointed their father, so they may serve me as priests. Their anointing will be to a priesthood that will continue throughout their generations.” 16 Moses did everything just as the Lord commanded him. 17 So the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month in the second year.

**Exodus 40:34–38 (NIV)**
34 Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. 35 Moses could not enter the tent of meeting because the cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle. 36 In all the travels of the Israelites, whenever the cloud lifted from above the tabernacle, they would set out; 37 but if the cloud did not lift, they did not set out—until the day it lifted. 38 So the cloud of the Lord was over the tabernacle by day, and fire was in the cloud by night, in the sight of all the Israelites during all their travels.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 40:3.** NIV: “the ark of the covenant law… shield the ark with the curtain.” LSB: “the ark of the testimony… screen the ark with the veil.” The Hebrew calls the tablets of the law God’s “testimony,” his witness to the covenant. “Veil” is the older word for the curtain that guarded the Most Holy Place, the same curtain that was torn in two when Jesus died (Matt 27:51).
- **Exod 40:35.** NIV: “the cloud had settled on it.” LSB: “the cloud had dwelt on it.” The Hebrew verb means to dwell or live. The word for tabernacle comes from the same root, so the tabernacle is literally God’s “dwelling place.” The LSB lets you hear that God came to live there.
- **Exod 40:38.** NIV: “all the Israelites.” LSB: “all the house of Israel.” The Hebrew says “house,” picturing Israel as one family under God’s care.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s Christmas Eve sermon [“The Word Became Flesh”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-word-became-flesh) at Desiring God explains how Jesus “pitched his tent” with us. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“The Blueprints”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/seeking-him/the-blueprints/) at Revive Our Hearts is a short word on obeying God’s pattern. BibleProject’s [Exodus 19–40 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-19-40/) shows how the tabernacle points to Jesus.

**Reflection question:** God put his tent in the center of Israel’s camp. As a man, husband, and father, what is one way you can put God’s presence at the center of your home this Christmas week, so the kids see that he is with you every day and not just on Sundays?

**Lesson 45: Leviticus: sacrifice and the Day of Atonement**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God’s glory filled the tabernacle, so full that Moses could not go in. Leviticus answers the obvious question: how can sinful people live near a holy God? The answer is sacrifice.

In chapter 1 a man brings an animal from his own herd, lays his hand on its head, and “it will be accepted on your behalf to make atonement for you” (1:4). The animal dies in his place. In chapter 16, once a year, the high priest goes behind the curtain with blood, first for his own sins and then for the people’s (16:6, 15–16). Two goats are chosen; one is sacrificed and one, the scapegoat, will carry the people’s sins away into the wilderness (16:8–10).

Jon Bloom of Desiring God writes, “Today is Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. It is perhaps the holiest day in the Jewish year.” Many Jewish people still fast and pray on that day. But Bloom says, “Yom Kippur was both provisional and a pointer.” It could never finish the job, so it had to be repeated every year.

Bloom explains what Israel missed when Jesus came: “Israel was looking for a Messiah who would deliver them from their enemies. He came. But many did not realize that the primary enemy the Messiah came to conquer in this age was sin, the thing that made man the enemy of God.” Jesus is both the priest and the sacrifice. He went into God’s presence once for all with his own blood (Heb 9:12), and the curtain tore open so we can come in.

**Leviticus 1:1–9 (NIV)**
1 The Lord called to Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting. He said, 2 “Speak to the Israelites and say to them: ‘When anyone among you brings an offering to the Lord, bring as your offering an animal from either the herd or the flock. 3 “‘If the offering is a burnt offering from the herd, you are to offer a male without defect. **Lesson 46: Leviticus: be holy, for I am holy**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God made a way for sinners to come near him through sacrifice. Today he tells the people he rescued what kind of people they are now: “be holy, because I am holy” (11:45). Peter repeats it to Christians in 1 Peter 1:16.

Jon Bloom of Desiring God admits, “For many Christians, holiness has largely negative connotations.” People “think of holiness primarily in terms of denial, as sort of a sterile existence.” But look at chapter 19. Holiness is very practical. It means honoring your parents (19:3), leaving part of the harvest for the poor (19:9–10), paying your workers on time (19:13), not cursing the deaf or tripping the blind (19:14), refusing to gossip or hold a grudge, and loving your neighbor as yourself (19:16–18).

Bloom says, “Holiness is fundamentally an affection issue, not a behavioral issue.” Jesus said the whole law hangs on loving God and loving your neighbor (Matt 22:37–40), and verse 18 is where that second command comes from. Bloom sums it up: “Holiness looks most like the delight of true love.”

Notice how often God repeats, “I am the Lord” in this chapter. Every command is tied to who he is. Bloom puts the goal plainly: “In other words, you’ve been most holy when you’ve been most happy in God.” A holy man is not a grim man. He is a man so glad in God that he treats people the way God treats them.

**Leviticus 11:44–45 (NIV)**
44 I am the Lord your God; consecrate yourselves and be holy, because I am holy. Do not make yourselves unclean by any creature that moves along the ground. 45 I am the Lord, who brought you up out of Egypt to be your God; therefore be holy, because I am holy.

**Leviticus 19:1–18 (NIV)**
1 The Lord said to Moses, 2 “Speak to the entire assembly of Israel and say to them: ‘Be holy because I, the Lord your God, am holy. 3 “‘Each of you must respect your mother and father, and you must observe my Sabbaths. I am the Lord your God. 4 “‘Do not turn to idols or make metal gods for yourselves. I am the Lord your God. 5 “‘When you sacrifice a fellowship offering to the Lord, sacrifice it in such a way that it will be accepted on your behalf. 6 It shall be eaten on the day you sacrifice it or on the next day; anything left over until the third day must be burned up. 7 If any of it is eaten on the third day, it is impure and will not be accepted. 8 Whoever eats it will be held responsible because they have desecrated what is holy to the Lord; they must be cut off from their people. 9 “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. 10 Do not go over your vineyard a second time or pick up the grapes that have fallen. Leave them for the poor and the foreigner. I am the Lord your God. 11 “‘Do not steal. “‘Do not lie. “‘Do not deceive one another. 12 “‘Do not swear falsely by my name and so profane the name of your God. I am the Lord. 13 “‘Do not defraud or rob your neighbor. “‘Do not hold back the wages of a hired worker overnight. 14 “‘Do not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block in front of the blind, but fear your God. I am the Lord. 15 “‘Do not pervert justice; do not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the great, but judge your neighbor fairly. 16 “‘Do not go about spreading slander among your people. “‘Do not do anything that endangers your neighbor’s life. I am the Lord. 17 “‘Do not hate a fellow Israelite in your heart. Rebuke your neighbor frankly so you will not share in their guilt. 18 “‘Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against anyone among your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the Lord.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Lev 11:44.** NIV: “consecrate yourselves and be holy.” LSB: “set yourselves apart as holy and be holy.” Both translate the same Hebrew root twice. To be holy means to be set apart for God, different from the world around you because you belong to him.
- **Lev 19:3.** NIV: “respect your mother and father.” LSB: “fear his mother and his father.” The Hebrew word is the same one used for fearing God in verse 14. It means deep reverence, not terror. Notice that the mother is named first here, the reverse of the fifth commandment.
- **Lev 19:17.** NIV: “Do not hate a fellow Israelite in your heart.” LSB: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart.” The Hebrew says “brother.” God’s people are one family, and holiness shows up in how we treat each other.

**Go deeper:** Jon Bloom’s [“Holiness Will Make You Unbelievably Happy”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/holiness-will-make-you-unbelievably-happy) at Desiring God shows why holiness is joy, not gloom. The Gospel Coalition’s [“20 Quotes from Jen Wilkin’s New Book on Imaging God”](https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/20-quotes-from-jen-wilkin-imaging-god/) includes her plain words on holiness. BibleProject’s [Leviticus overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/leviticus/) explains why holiness matters in the whole book.

**Reflection question:** Leviticus 19 ties holiness to ordinary things like paying workers, honoring parents, and refusing to hold a grudge. As a man, husband, and father, which one of these does God want to make more visible in you at work or at home this week?

**Lesson 47: Leviticus: the appointed feasts of the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God called his people to be holy. Today he gives them a calendar. Leviticus 23 lists the Lord’s appointed times: the weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, and the Feast of Weeks fifty days later.

Jay Sklar, writing for Desiring God, says starting the year with Passover meant “the Israelites would begin each year with the reminder that their God was above all a redeeming God. To put it differently: This was their Easter.” Firstfruits came next. Before anyone ate from the new harvest, the first sheaf went to the Lord (23:10–14). Sklar writes, “Lavish provision from God called for lavish praise to God, a tangible proclamation that he was the King worthy of their very best.” That way, “the law protected them from taking the Lord’s provision for granted.” He sums it up with a saying from fundraisers: “Thank before you bank.”

Look at how these line up with Jesus. He died at Passover as “our Passover lamb” (1 Cor 5:7). He rose on the day after the Sabbath, the day the firstfruits were waved before the Lord (23:11), and Paul calls him “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Cor 15:20). Fifty days later, at the Feast of Weeks, which the Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came and three thousand people were saved (Acts 2).

Different churches mark time differently. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and Lutheran churches follow a full church year, while many Baptist churches keep a simpler rhythm centered on the Lord’s Day, Christmas, and Easter. Either way, the point of Leviticus 23 is the same: build your family’s calendar around remembering what God has done.

**Leviticus 23:1–22 (NIV)**
1 The Lord said to Moses, 2 “Speak to the Israelites and say to them: ‘These are my appointed festivals, the appointed festivals of the Lord, which you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies. 3 “‘There are six days when you may work, but the seventh day is a day of sabbath rest, a day of sacred assembly. You are not to do any work; wherever you live, it is a sabbath to the Lord. 4 “‘These are the Lord’s appointed festivals, the sacred assemblies you are to proclaim at their appointed times: 5 The Lord’s Passover begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month. 6 On the fifteenth day of that month the Lord’s Festival of Unleavened Bread begins; for seven days you must eat bread made without yeast. 7 On the first day hold a sacred assembly and do no regular work. 8 For seven days present a food offering to the Lord. And on the seventh day hold a sacred assembly and do no regular work.’” 9 The Lord said to Moses, 10 “Speak to the Israelites and say to them: ‘When you enter the land I am going to give you and you reap its harvest, bring to the priest a sheaf of the first grain you harvest. 11 He is to wave the sheaf before the Lord so it will be accepted on your behalf; the priest is to wave it on the day after the Sabbath. 12 On the day you wave the sheaf, you must sacrifice as a burnt offering to the Lord a lamb a year old without defect, 13 together with its grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of the finest flour mixed with olive oil—a food offering presented to the Lord, a pleasing aroma—and its drink offering of a quarter of a hin of wine. 14 You must not eat any bread, or roasted or new grain, until the very day you bring this offering to your God. This is to be a lasting ordinance for the generations to come, wherever you live. 15 “‘From the day after the Sabbath, the day you brought the sheaf of the wave offering, count off seven full weeks. 16 Count off fifty days up to the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the Lord. 17 From wherever you live, bring two loaves made of two-tenths of an ephah of the finest flour, baked with yeast, as a wave offering of firstfruits to the Lord. 18 Present with this bread seven male lambs, each a year old and without defect, one young bull and two rams. They will be a burnt offering to the Lord, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings—a food offering, an aroma pleasing to the Lord. 19 Then sacrifice one male goat for a sin offering and two lambs, each a year old, for a fellowship offering. 20 The priest is to wave the two lambs before the Lord as a wave offering, together with the bread of the firstfruits. They are a sacred offering to the Lord for the priest. 21 On that same day you are to proclaim a sacred assembly and do no regular work. This is to be a lasting ordinance for the generations to come, wherever you live. 22 “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner residing among you. I am the Lord your God.’”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Lev 23:2.** NIV: “my appointed festivals.” LSB: “My appointed times.” The Hebrew word means a set time or appointment, the same word used for the “tent of meeting.” These were not only parties. They were dates God put on Israel’s calendar to meet with his people.
- **Lev 23:3.** NIV: “a day of sabbath rest.” LSB: “a sabbath of complete rest.” The Hebrew doubles the word, something like “a sabbath of sabbath-keeping.” The LSB tries to show that emphasis: this was rest all the way down.
- **Lev 23:22.** NIV: “Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner.” LSB: “leave them for the afflicted and the sojourner.” The Hebrew word covers both the poor and those who are pressed down by hardship. Even at harvest celebrations, God’s people had to make room for the needy. This is the law Ruth benefited from (Ruth 2).

**Lesson 47: Leviticus: the appointed feasts of the Lord**

Good morning. Yesterday God called his people to be holy. Today he gives them a calendar. Leviticus 23 lists the Lord’s appointed times: the weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, and the Feast of Weeks fifty days later.

Erin Davis of Revive Our Hearts studied these feasts closely. Before anyone ate from the new harvest, the first sheaf went to the Lord (23:10–14). Erin says, “In the Feast of Firstfruits, God revealed His heart to give His children His very best. He has given us Jesus, and then Jesus gave us His first fruits, the very best He had to offer. In His death on our behalf, Jesus held nothing back for Himself—not even His very life.”

Look at how these line up with Jesus. He died at Passover as “our Passover lamb” (1 Cor 5:7). He rose on the day after the Sabbath, the day the firstfruits were waved before the Lord (23:11), and Paul calls him “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Cor 15:20). Fifty days later, at the Feast of Weeks, also called Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came (Acts 2). Erin’s hope is that “we will peek into the empty tomb with a fresh sense of awe.”

Jay Sklar of Desiring God explains why the first sheaf went to God before the family ate: “the law protected them from taking the Lord’s provision for granted.” Dannah Gresh, introducing Erin’s teaching, says it honestly: “At times, I think we’re all tempted to give God the leftovers of our lives rather than our best.”

**Leviticus 23:1–22 (NIV)**
1 The Lord said to Moses, 2 “Speak to the Israelites and say to them: ‘These are my appointed festivals, the appointed festivals of the Lord, which you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies. 3 “‘There are six days when you may work, but the seventh day is a day of sabbath rest, a day of sacred assembly. You are not to do any work; wherever you live, it is a sabbath to the Lord. 4 “‘These are the Lord’s appointed festivals, the sacred assemblies you are to proclaim at their appointed times: 5 The Lord’s Passover begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month. 6 On the fifteenth day of that month the Lord’s Festival of Unleavened Bread begins; for seven days you must eat bread made without yeast. 7 On the first day hold a sacred assembly and do no regular work. 8 For seven days present a food offering to the Lord. And on the seventh day hold a sacred assembly and do no regular work.’” 9 The Lord said to Moses, 10 “Speak to the Israelites and say to them: ‘When you enter the land I am going to give you and you reap its harvest, bring to the priest a sheaf of the first grain you harvest. 11 He is to wave the sheaf before the Lord so it will be accepted on your behalf; the priest is to wave it on the day after the Sabbath. 12 On the day you wave the sheaf, you must sacrifice as a burnt offering to the Lord a lamb a year old without defect, 13 together with its grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of the finest flour mixed with olive oil—a food offering presented to the Lord, a pleasing aroma—and its drink offering of a quarter of a hin of wine. 14 You must not eat any bread, or roasted or new grain, until the very day you bring this offering to your God. This is to be a lasting ordinance for the generations to come, wherever you live. 15 “‘From the day after the Sabbath, the day you brought the sheaf of the wave offering, count off seven full weeks. 16 Count off fifty days up to the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the Lord. 17 From wherever you live, bring two loaves made of two-tenths of an ephah of the finest flour, baked with yeast, as a wave offering of firstfruits to the Lord. 18 Present with this bread seven male lambs, each a year old and without defect, one young bull and two rams. They will be a burnt offering to the Lord, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings—a food offering, an aroma pleasing to the Lord. 19 Then sacrifice one male goat for a sin offering and two lambs, each a year old, for a fellowship offering. 20 The priest is to wave the two lambs before the Lord as a wave offering, together with the bread of the firstfruits. They are a sacred offering to the Lord for the priest. 21 On that same day you are to proclaim a sacred assembly and do no regular work. This is to be a lasting ordinance for the generations to come, wherever you live. 22 “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner residing among you. I am the Lord your God.’”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Lev 23:2.** NIV: “my appointed festivals.” LSB: “My appointed times.” The Hebrew word means a set time or appointment, the same word used for the “tent of meeting.” These were not only parties. They were dates God put on Israel’s calendar to meet with his people.
- **Lev 23:3.** NIV: “a day of sabbath rest.” LSB: “a sabbath of complete rest.” The Hebrew doubles the word, something like “a sabbath of sabbath-keeping.” The LSB tries to show that emphasis: this was rest all the way down.
- **Lev 23:22.** NIV: “Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner.” LSB: “leave them for the afflicted and the sojourner.” The Hebrew word covers both the poor and those who are pressed down by hardship. Even at harvest celebrations, God’s people had to make room for the needy. This is the law Ruth benefited from (Ruth 2).

**Go deeper:** Erin Davis’s [“The Feast of Firstfruits”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/feast-firstfruits/) at Revive Our Hearts is part of her *7 Feasts* study. Jay Sklar’s [“Israel’s Calendar Was a Classroom”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/israels-calendar-was-a-classroom) at Desiring God walks through each feast. BibleProject’s [Leviticus overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/leviticus/) shows how the feasts fit the whole book.

**Reflection question:** In a busy Christmas week, what is one way you, as a woman, wife, and mother, can give God the first part of your day or your plans instead of the leftovers, and help your children see you do it?

**Lesson 48: Leviticus: Jubilee, rest, and covenant blessing**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we saw Israel’s calendar of feasts. Today God adds two bigger rhythms. Every seventh year the land rested, and after seven of those cycles, in the fiftieth year, came the Jubilee (25:8–12).

In the Jubilee, debts were cancelled, Israelites who had sold themselves into service went free, and family land went back to the family that first received it (25:10, 13). God gives the reason: “the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers” (25:23). BibleProject notes that this “would have effectively prevented cycles of intergenerational poverty.” Their podcast adds, “Since it occurred usually only once a lifetime, an impoverished Israelite would spend most of his life anticipating this event of restoration. So when we get to Jesus and the Jesus movement, it was a jubilee movement.” Jesus began his ministry by reading Isaiah 61 about “the year of the Lord’s favor” and saying, “Today this scripture is fulfilled” (Luke 4:19, 21).

Chapter 26 ends with God’s covenant blessing: rain, harvest, peace, and best of all, “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be my people” (26:12). Pastor Kevin DeYoung, speaking on Revive Our Hearts, says, “The covenant promise all throughout the Bible is that you don’t have to be alienated from God. You don’t have to be strangers to God. You can be forgiven of God. You can be close with God. You can be loved by God.”

Notice verse 13: “I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk with heads held high.” A man freed by God does not need to walk bent over by shame or debt. DeYoung says God’s closeness is so real that he will wipe away our tears, and asks, “How close do you have to be to someone to wipe a tear from their eyes?” At Christmas we celebrate that God came that close in Jesus.

**Leviticus 25:8–24 (NIV)**
8 “‘Count off seven sabbath years—seven times seven years—so that the seven sabbath years amount to a period of forty-nine years. 9 Then have the trumpet sounded everywhere on the tenth day of the seventh month; on the Day of Atonement sound the trumpet throughout your land. 10 Consecrate the fiftieth year and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you; each of you is to return to your family property and to your own clan. 11 The fiftieth year shall be a jubilee for you; do not sow and do not reap what grows of itself or harvest the untended vines. 12 For it is a jubilee and is to be holy for you; eat only what is taken directly from the fields. 13 “‘In this Year of Jubilee everyone is to return to their own property. 14 “‘If you sell land to any of your own people or buy land from them, do not take advantage of each other. 15 You are to buy from your own people on the basis of the number of years since the Jubilee. And they are to sell to you on the basis of the number of years left for harvesting crops. 16 When the years are many, you are to increase the price, and when the years are few, you are to decrease the price, because what is really being sold to you is the number of crops. 17 Do not take advantage of each other, but fear your God. I am the Lord your God. 18 “‘Follow my decrees and be careful to obey my laws, and you will live safely in the land. 19 Then the land will yield its fruit, and you will eat your fill and live there in safety. 20 You may ask, “What will we eat in the seventh year if we do not plant or harvest our crops?” 21 I will send you such a blessing in the sixth year that the land will yield enough for three years. 22 While you plant during the eighth year, you will eat from the old crop and will continue to eat from it until the harvest of the ninth year comes in. 23 “‘The land must not be sold permanently, because the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers. 24 Throughout the land that you hold as a possession, you must provide for the redemption of the land.

**Leviticus 26:3–13 (NIV)**
3 “‘If you follow my decrees and are careful to obey my commands, 4 I will send you rain in its season, and the ground will yield its crops and the trees their fruit. 5 Your threshing will continue until grape harvest and the grape harvest will continue until planting, and you will eat all the food you want and live in safety in your land. 6 “‘I will grant peace in the land, and you will lie down and no one will make you afraid. I will remove wild beasts from the land, and the sword will not pass through your country. 7 You will pursue your enemies, and they will fall by the sword before you. 8 Five of you will chase a hundred, and a hundred of you will chase ten thousand, and your enemies will fall by the sword before you. 9 “‘I will look on you with favor and make you fruitful and increase your numbers, and I will keep my covenant with you. 10 You will still be eating last year’s harvest when you will have to move it out to make room for the new. 11 I will put my dwelling place among you, and I will not abhor you. 12 I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be my people. 13 I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt so that you would no longer be slaves to the Egyptians; I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk with heads held high.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Lev 25:9.** NIV: “have the trumpet sounded.” LSB: “sound a ram’s horn.” The Hebrew word is *shofar*, a horn made from a ram. The word “jubilee” itself comes from a Hebrew word for a ram’s horn, so the year was named for the sound that started it.
- **Lev 25:10.** NIV: “proclaim liberty throughout the land.” LSB: “proclaim a release through the land.” The Hebrew word means freedom or release, the same word used in Isaiah 61:1, which Jesus read in Luke 4:18. (The NIV’s wording echoes the King James words cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.)
- **Lev 26:11.** NIV: “I will not abhor you.” LSB: “My soul will not loathe you.” The Hebrew says “my soul,” meaning God himself, with all his heart. It is a strong way of saying God truly wants to be with his people.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s podcast [“Jubilee: The Radical Year of Release”](https://bibleproject.com/podcasts/jubilee-radical-year-release/) explains Leviticus 25 and Jesus’s Jubilee. Revive Our Hearts’ [“Wonder of the Word Made Flesh”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/weekend/wonder-of-the-word-made-flesh/) gathers Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, Kevin DeYoung, and Dannah Gresh on God dwelling with us. BibleProject’s [Leviticus overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/leviticus/) shows how the book ends.

**Reflection question:** God told Israel, “the land is mine.” As a man, husband, and father, how would treating your home, money, and time as God’s rather than your own change one decision you are facing for your family right now?

sources.label: John Piper, How Do I Bless My Children Before Bed? (Desiring God, Feb 21, 2020)

**Lesson 49: Numbers: the priestly blessing, and the cloud**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we saw the Jubilee, when God set his people free and promised, “I will walk among you.” Today we open the book of Numbers. Israel is still at Sinai, the tabernacle is standing, and God gives Aaron words to speak over the people: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the LORD turn his face toward you and give you peace” (6:24–26). Then we watch the cloud rest on the tent, and Israel learn to move only when God moves (9:15–23).

BibleProject says that in the Hebrew Bible, to “bless” is “to declare God’s life-presence over another.” God tells the priests, “So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I will bless them” (6:27). BibleProject also notes that this blessing is found on the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls, the oldest surviving biblical texts we have. John Piper points out that a blessing is different from a prayer. In a prayer you talk to God; in a blessing you speak directly to a person and ask the Lord to act. “In the very act of blessing, we become part of the means by which God blesses the person that we’re speaking to.” He tells fathers, “The blessing is coming from God through Daddy. That’s a very powerful moment as children come to understand what’s going on here.” Jesus himself “took them in his arms and blessed them,” and Piper says, “It’s a very Christlike thing to do: to bless children, laying our hands on our children as we speak a blessing over them.”

Then comes the cloud. “Whenever the cloud lifted from above the tent, the Israelites set out; wherever the cloud settled, the Israelites encamped” (9:17). Sometimes it stayed a night, sometimes “a month or a year” (9:22). BibleProject calls the camp “an elaborate symbol of how God’s holy presence was at the center of their existence as a people.” A man who wants God’s name on his home learns both habits: speak the Lord’s blessing over his wife and children, and wait for the Lord instead of running ahead.

**Numbers 6:22–27 (NIV)**
22 The LORD said to Moses, 23 “Tell Aaron and his sons, ‘This is how you are to bless the Israelites. Say to them: 24 “‘“The LORD bless you and keep you; 25 the LORD make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; 26 the LORD turn his face toward you and give you peace.”’ 27 “So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I will bless them.”

**Numbers 9:15–23 (NIV)**
15 On the day the tabernacle, the tent of the covenant law, was set up, the cloud covered it. From evening till morning the cloud above the tabernacle looked like fire. 16 That is how it continued to be; the cloud covered it, and at night it looked like fire. 17 Whenever the cloud lifted from above the tent, the Israelites set out; wherever the cloud settled, the Israelites encamped. 18 At the LORD’s command the Israelites set out, and at his command they encamped. As long as the cloud stayed over the tabernacle, they remained in camp. 19 When the cloud remained over the tabernacle a long time, the Israelites obeyed the LORD’s order and did not set out. 20 Sometimes the cloud was over the tabernacle only a few days; at the LORD’s command they would encamp, and then at his command they would set out. 21 Sometimes the cloud stayed only from evening till morning, and when it lifted in the morning, they set out. Whether by day or by night, whenever the cloud lifted, they set out. 22 Whether the cloud stayed over the tabernacle for two days or a month or a year, the Israelites would remain in camp and not set out; but when it lifted, they would set out. 23 At the LORD’s command they encamped, and at the LORD’s command they set out. They obeyed the LORD’s order, in accordance with his command through Moses.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Num 6:26.** NIV: “the LORD turn his face toward you.” LSB: “Yahweh lift up His face on you.” The Hebrew is closer to the LSB. God does not merely glance your way; he lifts his face, as a father looks up with favor on his child.
- **Num 6:27.** NIV: “put my name on the Israelites.” LSB: “invoke My name on the sons of Israel.” Both are true: the priests speak God’s name over the people, and that name actually rests on them.
- **Num 9:19.** NIV: “the Israelites obeyed the LORD’s order.” LSB: “the sons of Israel would keep the charge of Yahweh.” “Charge” is a duty, like a watch to be kept. Following the cloud was not a mood. It was a trust they had to keep, even when the cloud did not move for a long time.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s interview [“How Do I Bless My Children Before Bed?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-do-i-bless-my-children-before-bed) at Desiring God shows fathers how to speak Numbers 6 over their kids. BibleProject’s [Numbers guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-numbers/) explains the priestly blessing and the cloud of God’s presence at the center of the camp.

**Reflection question:** God put his name on Israel, and a father can speak that blessing over his home. As a man, husband, and father, when will you look your wife and children in the eye this week and speak the Lord’s blessing over them?

Nancy adds, “When we speak the blessing of God into the lives of other people, what we’re really doing is creating a setting, an opportunity in which God can actually bless those individuals.” You might think, “I’m not a priest.” She answers from the New Testament: “We have all been made priests to God… We can speak blessing into the lives of others. When we do, we actually become a channel, a conduit of God’s blessing into the lives of others.” Then she makes it personal: “One of the greatest gifts you can bestow on your husband, on your children, on your friends is the blessing of God.”

BibleProject says that in the Hebrew Bible, to “bless” is “to declare God’s life-presence over another.” John Piper tells parents that “the blessing is coming from God through Daddy,” and the same is true when a mother speaks God’s name over her children. Then comes the cloud: “Whenever the cloud lifted from above the tent, the Israelites set out; wherever the cloud settled, the Israelites encamped” (9:17). BibleProject calls the camp “an elaborate symbol of how God’s holy presence was at the center of their existence as a people.” A woman who wants God’s name on her home learns both habits: speak the Lord’s blessing out loud over her husband and children, and wait for the Lord instead of rushing ahead.

**Numbers 6:22–27 (NIV)**
22 The LORD said to Moses, 23 “Tell Aaron and his sons, ‘This is how you are to bless the Israelites. Say to them: 24 “‘“The LORD bless you and keep you; 25 the LORD make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; 26 the LORD turn his face toward you and give you peace.”’ 27 “So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I will bless them.”

**Numbers 9:15–23 (NIV)**
15 On the day the tabernacle, the tent of the covenant law, was set up, the cloud covered it. From evening till morning the cloud above the tabernacle looked like fire. 16 That is how it continued to be; the cloud covered it, and at night it looked like fire. 17 Whenever the cloud lifted from above the tent, the Israelites set out; wherever the cloud settled, the Israelites encamped. 18 At the LORD’s command the Israelites set out, and at his command they encamped. As long as the cloud stayed over the tabernacle, they remained in camp. 19 When the cloud remained over the tabernacle a long time, the Israelites obeyed the LORD’s order and did not set out. 20 Sometimes the cloud was over the tabernacle only a few days; at the LORD’s command they would encamp, and then at his command they would set out. 21 Sometimes the cloud stayed only from evening till morning, and when it lifted in the morning, they set out. Whether by day or by night, whenever the cloud lifted, they set out. 22 Whether the cloud stayed over the tabernacle for two days or a month or a year, the Israelites would remain in camp and not set out; but when it lifted, they would set out. 23 At the LORD’s command they encamped, and at the LORD’s command they set out. They obeyed the LORD’s order, in accordance with his command through Moses.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Num 6:26.** NIV: “the LORD turn his face toward you.” LSB: “Yahweh lift up His face on you.” The Hebrew is closer to the LSB. God does not merely glance your way; he lifts his face, as a father looks up with favor on his child.
- **Num 6:27.** NIV: “put my name on the Israelites.” LSB: “invoke My name on the sons of Israel.” Both are true: the priests speak God’s name over the people, and that name actually rests on them.
- **Num 9:19.** NIV: “the Israelites obeyed the LORD’s order.” LSB: “the sons of Israel would keep the charge of Yahweh.” “Charge” is a duty, like a watch to be kept. Following the cloud was not a mood. It was a trust they had to keep, even when the cloud did not move for a long time.

John Piper’s interview [“How Do I Bless My Children Before Bed?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-do-i-bless-my-children-before-bed) at Desiring God shows how a parent’s spoken blessing becomes one of God’s means of grace. BibleProject’s [Numbers guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-numbers/) explains the blessing and the cloud of God’s presence.

**Reflection question:** God put his name on Israel, and you can speak that blessing over your home. As a woman, wife, and mother, who in your family needs to hear you speak the Lord’s blessing over them this week?
