**Lesson 229: 1 Timothy: godliness with contentment; fight the good fight**

Good morning. Yesterday we heard that godly leadership is a noble task, and that life and doctrine must be watched together. Today Paul sets godliness with contentment against the love of money, and he calls Timothy to fight the good fight. Godliness with contentment is great gain. We brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs. This is a pastoral warning, not a sneer at provision, and not a joke about the poor. The danger is love of money, and the wandering it causes. But you, man of God, flee from all this, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made your good confession in the presence of many witnesses. In the sight of God, who gives life to everything, and of Christ Jesus, who while testifying before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, Paul charges Timothy to keep this command without spot or blame until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, which God will bring about in his own time. To the King, the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone is immortal and who lives in unapproachable light, be honor and might forever. Amen. Command those who are rich in this present world not to be arrogant nor to put their hope in wealth, which is so uncertain, but to put their hope in God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment. Command them to do good, to be rich in good deeds, and to be generous and willing to share. In this way they will lay up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the coming age, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life. John Piper, in Money: Currency for Christian Hedonism, takes 1 Timothy 6:6–19 as one movement: godliness with contentment, the trap of wanting to get rich, fleeing, fighting the good fight, and a charge to the rich to hope in God and to be rich in good deeds. In Battling the Unbelief of Covetousness, the love of money is not a small habit. It is unbelief that wanders from the faith and pierces the heart with many griefs. The alternative is not grim poverty-theater. It is contentment, generosity, and taking hold of the life that is truly life. BibleProject’s 1 Timothy guide hears the same close of the letter: fight the good fight, and do not let wealth become the hope. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “But godliness actually is a means of great gain, when accompanied by contentment.” It also has, “For the love of money is a root of all sorts of evils, and some by aspiring to it have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.” The NIV’s “godliness with contentment is great gain.” and “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” keep that same gain, and that same warning. Godliness with contentment is great gain. Fight the good fight, and take hold of the life that is truly life. As a woman, wife, and a mother, flee the trap of wanting more as if more could save you. Put your hope in God, who richly provides, and let generosity be how wealth, if you have it, is put to work for the coming age.

**1 Timothy 6:6–19 (NIV)**
6 But godliness with contentment is great gain. 7 For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. 8 But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. 9 Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. 10 For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs. 11 But you, man of God, flee from all this, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness. 12 Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made your good confession in the presence of many witnesses. 13 In the sight of God, who gives life to everything, and of Christ Jesus, who while testifying before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, I charge you 14 to keep this command without spot or blame until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, 15 which God will bring about in his own time—God, the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords, 16 who alone is immortal and who lives in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see. To him be honor and might forever. Amen. 17 Command those who are rich in this present world not to be arrogant nor to put their hope in wealth, which is so uncertain, but to put their hope in God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment. 18 Command them to do good, to be rich in good deeds, and to be generous and willing to share. 19 In this way they will lay up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the coming age, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.

**Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where has the love of money, or a restless want of more, been quietly shaping your hope? What would it look like today to practice contentment, to fight the good fight, and to be rich in one good deed?

**Lesson 230: 2 Timothy: fan into flame the gift; endure as a good soldier**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that godliness with contentment is great gain, and that we are to fight the good fight. Today Paul writes to Timothy with tears and fire: fan into flame the gift, and endure as a good soldier. He thanks God as he remembers Timothy in his prayers, night and day, recalling his tears and longing to see him. He is reminded of Timothy’s sincere faith, which first lived in his grandmother Lois and in his mother Eunice, and which now lives in Timothy also. For this reason he reminds him to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in him through the laying on of Paul’s hands. For the Spirit God gave us does not make us timid, but gives us power, love and self-discipline. So do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, or of Paul his prisoner. Rather, join with him in suffering for the gospel, by the power of God. He has saved us and called us to a holy life, not because of anything we have done but because of his own purpose and grace. This grace was given us in Christ Jesus before the beginning of time, and it has now been revealed through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has destroyed death and has brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. That is the gospel Paul was appointed to, and he is not ashamed, because he knows whom he has believed, and is convinced that Christ is able to guard what he has entrusted to him until that day. Guard the good deposit that was entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who lives in us. You then, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. The things you have heard from Paul, entrust to reliable people who will also be qualified to teach others. Join in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. A soldier does not get entangled in civilian affairs, but tries to please his commanding officer. An athlete is not crowned without competing according to the rules. The hardworking farmer should be the first to receive a share of the crops. Reflect on what Paul is saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all this. Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David. This is Paul’s gospel, for which he is suffering, even to the point of being chained like a criminal. But God’s word is not chained. Therefore he endures everything for the sake of the elect, that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory. Here is a trustworthy saying: If we died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him. If we disown him, he will also disown us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself. For 2:1–7 we stay with the text itself, and with BibleProject, alongside Piper on the trustworthy saying that follows. The gift must be fanned, the gospel must be entrusted, and Christ remains faithful even when we are weak. John Piper, in Feed the Flame of God’s Gift, stays with 2 Timothy 1: the sincere faith in a family line, the gift that must be fanned, and a Spirit of power, love, and self-discipline, not timidity. In Battling the Unbelief of Misplaced Shame, he will not let Timothy be ashamed of the testimony, or of a chained apostle. In He Cannot Deny Himself, he takes the trustworthy saying of 2:8–13: remember Jesus Christ, God’s word is not chained, and if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself. BibleProject’s 2 Timothy guide hears a last letter of courage: fan the gift, suffer as a soldier, and keep the deposit. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “For God has not given us a spirit of timidity, but of power and love and self-discipline.” It also has, “If we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.” The NIV’s “does not make us timid, but gives us power, love and self-discipline.” and “if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself” keep that same Spirit, and that same faithful Christ. Fan into flame the gift, endure as a good soldier, and trust the Christ who remains faithful. As a man, husband, and father, do not let timidity, or shame, bury what God has already given you. Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, entrust the gospel to others, and take the next hard step as one who knows whom he has believed.

**2 Timothy 1:3–14 (NIV)**
3 I thank God, whom I serve, as my ancestors did, with a clear conscience, as night and day I constantly remember you in my prayers. 4 Recalling your tears, I long to see you, so that I may be filled with joy. 5 I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, now lives in you also. 6 For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. 7 For the Spirit God gave us does not make us timid, but gives us power, love and self-discipline. 8 So do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord or of me his prisoner. Rather, join with me in suffering for the gospel, by the power of God. 9 He has saved us and called us to a holy life—not because of anything we have done but because of his own purpose and grace. This grace was given us in Christ Jesus before the beginning of time, 10 but it has now been revealed through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has destroyed death and has brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. 11 And of this gospel I was appointed a herald and an apostle and a teacher. 12 That is why I am suffering as I am. Yet this is no cause for shame, because I know whom I have believed, and am convinced that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day. 13 What you heard from me, keep as the pattern of sound teaching, with faith and love in Christ Jesus. 14 Guard the good deposit that was entrusted to you—guard it with the help of the Holy Spirit who lives in us.

**2 Timothy 2:1–13 (NIV)**
1 You then, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. 2 And the things you have heard me say in the presence of many witnesses entrust to reliable people who will also be qualified to teach others. 3 Join with me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. 4 No one serving as a soldier gets entangled in civilian affairs, but rather tries to please his commanding officer. 5 Similarly, anyone who competes as an athlete does not receive the victor’s crown except by competing according to the rules. 6 The hardworking farmer should be the first to receive a share of the crops. 7 Reflect on what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all this. 8 Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David. This is my gospel, 9 for which I am suffering even to the point of being chained like a criminal. But God’s word is not chained. 10 Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory. 11 Here is a trustworthy saying: If we died with him, we will also live with him; 12 if we endure, we will also reign with him. If we disown him, he will also disown us; 13 if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where has timidity, or shame, been covering a gift God already gave? What would it look like today to fan that gift into flame, to endure one hard thing as a good soldier, and to rest in the Christ who remains faithful?

**Lesson 231: 2 Timothy: all Scripture is God-breathed; finish the race**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard, fan into flame the gift, and endure as a good soldier. Today Paul comes to the Scriptures that can make us wise for salvation, and to a race that must be finished. Timothy knows all about Paul’s teaching, way of life, purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, persecutions, and sufferings, and the Lord rescued him from all of them. In fact, everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evildoers and impostors go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work. The Scriptures are not an accessory to the race. They are God-breathed, and they are able to make you wise for salvation. In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of his appearing and his kingdom, Paul gives this charge: Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; correct, rebuke and encourage—with great patience and careful instruction. For the time will come when people will not put up with sound doctrine. Instead, to suit their own desires, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to say what their itching ears want to hear. They will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths. But you, keep your head in all situations, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, discharge all the duties of your ministry. For Paul, the time for his departure is near. He has fought the good fight, he has finished the race, he has kept the faith. Now there is in store for him the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to him on that day—and not only to him, but also to all who have longed for his appearing. John Piper, in Building Our Lives on the Bible, and in All Scripture Is Breathed Out by God — Continue in It, and in All Scripture Is Breathed Out by God and Profitable, stays with 3:10–17: continue in what you have learned, the Scriptures make you wise for salvation, and all Scripture is God-breathed and useful, so that the servant of God may be equipped. In Preach the Word, For the Time of My Departure Has Come, and in I Have Kept the Faith, he takes 4:1–8 as a last charge and a finished race: preach the word, keep your head, endure hardship, and look to the crown the righteous Judge will give to all who have longed for his appearing. BibleProject’s 2 Timothy guide hears the letter land here: a God-breathed word, and a life that finishes the race. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness,” and, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.” The NIV’s “useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness,” and “I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” keep that same God-breathed word, and that same finished course. All Scripture is God-breathed. Preach the word, and finish the race. As a man, husband, and father, continue in what you have learned. Do not trade sound doctrine for itching ears, and do not leave the race half-run. Keep your head, endure the next hardship, and long for the appearing of the righteous Judge.

**2 Timothy 3:10–17 (NIV)**
10 You, however, know all about my teaching, my way of life, my purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, 11 persecutions, sufferings—what kinds of things happened to me in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, the persecutions I endured. Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. 12 In fact, everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, 13 while evildoers and impostors will go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. 14 But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, 15 and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

**2 Timothy 4:1–8 (NIV)**
1 In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of his appearing and his kingdom, I give you this charge: 2 Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; correct, rebuke and encourage—with great patience and careful instruction. 3 For the time will come when people will not put up with sound doctrine. Instead, to suit their own desires, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to say what their itching ears want to hear. 4 They will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths. 5 But you, keep your head in all situations, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, discharge all the duties of your ministry. 6 For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time for my departure is near. 7 I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. 8 Now there is in store for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but also to all who have longed for his appearing.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been neglecting the God-breathed Scriptures, or slowing in the race? What would it look like today to continue in what you have learned, to receive one correction from the word, and to take the next step as someone who means to finish and keep the faith?

10 You, however, know all about my teaching, my way of life, my purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, 11 persecutions, sufferings—what kinds of things happened to me in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, the persecutions I endured. Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. 12 In fact, everyone who wants to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, 13 while evildoers and impostors will go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. 14 But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, 15 and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

**Lesson 232: Titus: sound doctrine that produces sound lives**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that all Scripture is God-breathed, and that we are to finish the race. Today Paul writes to Titus about sound doctrine that produces sound lives. He left Titus in Crete to put in order what was left unfinished and to appoint elders in every town. An elder must be blameless, faithful to his wife, a man whose children believe and are not open to the charge of being wild and disobedient. Since an overseer manages God’s household, he must be blameless, not overbearing, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not pursuing dishonest gain. Instead, he must be hospitable, one who loves what is good, who is self-controlled, upright, holy and disciplined. He must hold firmly to the trustworthy message as it has been taught, so that he can encourage others by sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it. The trustworthy message is not a private hobby. It is held firmly so that a household of God can be encouraged, and so that error can be answered. You, however, must teach what is appropriate to sound doctrine. Paul then speaks, with dignity, to the ordinary rooms of the church’s life. Teach the older men to be temperate, worthy of respect, self-controlled, and sound in faith, in love and in endurance. Teach the older women to be reverent, not to be slanderers or addicted to much wine, but to teach what is good, so that they can urge the younger women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled and pure, to be busy at home, to be kind, and to be subject to their husbands, so that no one will malign the word of God. Similarly, encourage the young men to be self-controlled. In everything set them an example by doing what is good. In your teaching show integrity, seriousness and soundness of speech that cannot be condemned. Teach slaves to be subject to their masters in everything, to try to please them, not to talk back or steal, but to show that they can be fully trusted, so that in every way they will make the teaching about God our Savior attractive. This is first-century household life, told under the Lord, not as a weapon, and not as a joke. Sound doctrine is meant to make the teaching about the Savior look beautiful in actual lives. I did not use a Piper sermon whose main text is Titus 1:5–9 or 2:1–10. We stay with the text itself, and with BibleProject’s Titus guide. The letter wants a church put in order by elders who can hold the trustworthy message, and then a people whose ordinary lives, in every station, make the teaching about God our Savior attractive. Doctrine that cannot become a life is not yet the sound doctrine Paul is after. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “holding fast the faithful word which is in accordance with the teaching, so that he will be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to reprove those who contradict.” It also has, “speak the things which are proper for sound doctrine.” The NIV’s “hold firmly to the trustworthy message” and “teach what is appropriate to sound doctrine” keep that same charge: hold the word, and teach a life that fits it. Sound doctrine is meant to produce sound lives, and to make the teaching about the Savior attractive. As a man, husband, and father, hold firmly to the trustworthy message, and let it show up at home, in speech, and in self-control. Do not treat doctrine as a private stash, or ordinary faithfulness as a small thing.

**Titus 1:5–9 (NIV)**
5 The reason I left you in Crete was that you might put in order what was left unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you. 6 An elder must be blameless, faithful to his wife, a man whose children believe and are not open to the charge of being wild and disobedient. 7 Since an overseer manages God’s household, he must be blameless—not overbearing, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not pursuing dishonest gain. 8 Rather, he must be hospitable, one who loves what is good, who is self-controlled, upright, holy and disciplined. 9 He must hold firmly to the trustworthy message as it has been taught, so that he can encourage others by sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it.

**Titus 2:1–10 (NIV)**
1 You, however, must teach what is appropriate to sound doctrine. 2 Teach the older men to be temperate, worthy of respect, self-controlled, and sound in faith, in love and in endurance. 3 Likewise, teach the older women to be reverent in the way they live, not to be slanderers or addicted to much wine, but to teach what is good. 4 Then they can urge the younger women to love their husbands and children, 5 to be self-controlled and pure, to be busy at home, to be kind, and to be subject to their husbands, so that no one will malign the word of God. 6 Similarly, encourage the young men to be self-controlled. 7 In everything set them an example by doing what is good. In your teaching show integrity, seriousness 8 and soundness of speech that cannot be condemned, so that those who oppose you may be ashamed because they have nothing bad to say about us. 9 Teach slaves to be subject to their masters in everything, to try to please them, not to talk back to them, 10 and not to steal from them, but to show that they can be fully trusted, so that in every way they will make the teaching about God our Savior attractive.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where has your doctrine been sounder than your life, or your life unhooked from the trustworthy message? What would it look like today to hold the word firmly, and to make the teaching about God our Savior attractive in one ordinary place?

**Lesson 233: Titus: grace teaches us to say no, and yes to good works**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that sound doctrine is meant to produce sound lives. Today Paul names the grace that teaches us both to say no, and to say yes to good works. For the grace of God has appeared that offers salvation to all people. It teaches us to say “No” to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age, while we wait for the blessed hope—the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people that are his very own, eager to do what is good. These, then, are the things you should teach. Encourage and rebuke with all authority. Do not let anyone despise you. Grace is not a soft word that never refuses anything. It has appeared, it saves, and it trains a people to wait for Jesus and to be eager for what is good. Then, after a short stretch we are not reading as official text today, Paul tells the truth about what we once were, and about what mercy has done. At one time we too were foolish, disobedient, deceived and enslaved by all kinds of passions and pleasures. We lived in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. We say that with honesty, not as a spectacle. But when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. He saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us generously through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs having the hope of eternal life. This is a trustworthy saying. And I want you to stress these things, so that those who have trusted in God may be careful to devote themselves to doing what is good. These things are excellent and profitable for everyone. Grace says no to the old passions, and yes to good works, because mercy has already saved us. John Piper, in Our Hope: The Appearing of Jesus Christ, stays with Titus 2:11–13: grace has appeared, it trains us, and we wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of our great God and Savior. In Through the Washing of Regeneration, he takes 3:1–8, including the official stretch we have today: we were once enslaved, but God saved us not by works we had done, but by mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, so that those who have trusted in God would devote themselves to what is good. BibleProject’s Titus guide hears the same center of the letter: saving grace that trains a people for good works. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men,” and, “through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,” It also has, “so that having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.” The NIV’s grace that “offers salvation to all people.” “the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,” and being “justified by his grace” keep that same appearing of mercy, and that same hope. Grace has appeared. It teaches us to say no to ungodliness, and to devote ourselves to what is good. As a man, husband, and father, do not treat mercy as a reason to stay as you were, or good works as a way to earn what God has already given. Wait for the appearing of Jesus, and be careful today to do what is good.

**Titus 2:11–15 (NIV)**
11 For the grace of God has appeared that offers salvation to all people. 12 It teaches us to say “No” to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age, 13 while we wait for the blessed hope—the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ, 14 who gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a people that are his very own, eager to do what is good. 15 These, then, are the things you should teach. Encourage and rebuke with all authority. Do not let anyone despise you.

**Titus 3:3–8 (NIV)**
3 At one time we too were foolish, disobedient, deceived and enslaved by all kinds of passions and pleasures. We lived in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. 4 But when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, 5 he saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. He saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, 6 whom he poured out on us generously through Jesus Christ our Savior, 7 so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs having the hope of eternal life. 8 This is a trustworthy saying. And I want you to stress these things, so that those who have trusted in God may be careful to devote themselves to doing what is good. These things are excellent and profitable for everyone.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where has grace needed to teach you a clearer no, or a more careful yes to what is good? What would it look like today to wait for Jesus, and to devote yourself to one good work because you have already been saved by mercy?

lessons.title: Philemon: a runaway, a brother, and the power of forgiveness
lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 234: Philemon: a runaway, a brother, and the power of forgiveness**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness, and yes to good works. Today we read a whole short letter: Philemon, a runaway, a brother, and the power of forgiveness. Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, writes to Philemon, their dear friend and fellow worker, to Apphia, to Archippus, and to the church that meets in Philemon’s house. He thanks God for Philemon’s love and faith, and prays that this partnership in the faith may be effective in deepening their understanding of every good thing we share in Christ. Philemon’s love has given Paul great joy and encouragement, because he has refreshed the hearts of the Lord’s people. Therefore, although in Christ Paul could be bold and order him to do what he ought to do, he prefers to appeal on the basis of love. He appeals for Onesimus, who became his son while Paul was in chains. Once he was useless to Philemon, but now he has become useful both to Philemon and to Paul. Paul is sending him back, which is like sending his own heart, and he would have liked to keep him, to take Philemon’s place in helping him in chains for the gospel. But he would do nothing without consent, so that any favor would be spontaneous, not forced. Perhaps the reason Onesimus was separated for a little while was that Philemon might have him back forever, no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother, both as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord. We tell this first-century story with dignity. Paul does not make a spectacle of the runaway, and he does not treat Onesimus as a tool. He asks Philemon to welcome him as he would welcome Paul, to charge any debt to Paul’s account, and to refresh his heart in Christ. Paul even hopes to be restored to them as a guest. The letter ends in grace. Forgiveness here is public, costly, and personal: a man sent back as a brother, and a debt willingly carried. I did not use a Piper sermon whose main text is the letter to Philemon. We stay with the letter itself, and with BibleProject’s Philemon guide. The appeal is love, not mere command. Onesimus is sent back as a dear brother, and Paul is willing to have any debt charged to his own account, so that the welcome would be as if Paul himself had come. The gospel does not shrug at wrongs, and it does not leave a man in the category of useless. It makes room for a brother, and for a refreshed heart. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.” The NIV’s “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother.” and “both as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord” keep that same appeal: receive him as family, not merely as a returned worker. Welcome the person God has made a brother, and let forgiveness carry the cost. As a man, husband, and father, do not keep someone in a smaller category than the gospel has given them. If a debt must be absorbed so that a welcome can be real, consider what it would mean to charge it to your own account, as Paul did, and to refresh a heart in Christ.

**Philemon 1:1–25 (NIV)**
1 Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our dear friend and fellow worker— 2 also to Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier—and to the church that meets in your home: 3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. 4 I always thank my God as I remember you in my prayers, 5 because I hear about your love for all his holy people and your faith in the Lord Jesus. 6 I pray that your partnership with us in the faith may be effective in deepening your understanding of every good thing we share for the sake of Christ. 7 Your love has given me great joy and encouragement, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the Lord’s people. 8 Therefore, although in Christ I could be bold and order you to do what you ought to do, 9 yet I prefer to appeal to you on the basis of love. It is as none other than Paul—an old man and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus— 10 that I appeal to you for my son Onesimus, who became my son while I was in chains. 11 Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. 12 I am sending him—who is my very heart—back to you. 13 I would have liked to keep him with me so that he could take your place in helping me while I am in chains for the gospel. 14 But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that any favor you do would not seem forced but would be voluntary. 15 Perhaps the reason he was separated from you for a little while was that you might have him back forever— 16 no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother. He is very dear to me but even dearer to you, both as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord. 17 So if you consider me a partner, welcome him as you would welcome me. 18 If he has done you any wrong or owes you anything, charge it to me. 19 I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand. I will pay it back—not to mention that you owe me your very self. 20 I do wish, brother, that I may have some benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ. 21 Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. 22 And one thing more: Prepare a guest room for me, because I hope to be restored to you in answer to your prayers. 23 Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings. 24 And so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, my fellow workers. 25 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, whom have you been quietly treating as less than a brother or sister? What would it look like today to welcome that person as you would welcome a beloved friend, and to let forgiveness carry a real cost?

**Lesson 234: Philemon: a runaway, a brother, and the power of forgiveness**

Good morning. Yesterday we heard that grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness, and yes to good works. Today we read a whole short letter: Philemon, a runaway, a brother, and the power of forgiveness. Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, writes to Philemon, their dear friend and fellow worker, to Apphia, to Archippus, and to the church that meets in Philemon’s house. He thanks God for Philemon’s love and faith, and prays that this partnership in the faith may be effective in deepening their understanding of every good thing we share in Christ. Philemon’s love has given Paul great joy and encouragement, because he has refreshed the hearts of the Lord’s people. Therefore, although in Christ Paul could be bold and order him to do what he ought to do, he prefers to appeal on the basis of love. He appeals for Onesimus, who became his son while Paul was in chains. Once he was useless to Philemon, but now he has become useful both to Philemon and to Paul. Paul is sending him back, which is like sending his own heart, and he would have liked to keep him, to take Philemon’s place in helping him in chains for the gospel. But he would do nothing without consent, so that any favor would be spontaneous, not forced. Perhaps the reason Onesimus was separated for a little while was that Philemon might have him back forever, no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother, both as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord. We tell this first-century story with dignity. Paul does not make a spectacle of the runaway, and he does not treat Onesimus as a tool. He asks Philemon to welcome him as he would welcome Paul, to charge any debt to Paul’s account, and to refresh his heart in Christ. Paul even hopes to be restored to them as a guest. The letter ends in grace. Forgiveness here is public, costly, and personal: a man sent back as a brother, and a debt willingly carried. I did not use a Piper sermon whose main text is the letter to Philemon. We stay with the letter itself, and with BibleProject’s Philemon guide. The appeal is love, not mere command. Onesimus is sent back as a dear brother, and Paul is willing to have any debt charged to his own account, so that the welcome would be as if Paul himself had come. The gospel does not shrug at wrongs, and it does not leave a man in the category of useless. It makes room for a brother, and for a refreshed heart. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.” The NIV’s “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother.” and “both as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord” keep that same appeal: receive him as family, not merely as a returned worker. Welcome the person God has made a brother, and let forgiveness carry the cost. As a woman, wife, and a mother, do not keep someone in a smaller category than the gospel has given them. If a debt must be absorbed so that a welcome can be real, consider what it would mean to charge it to your own account, as Paul did, and to refresh a heart in Christ.

**Philemon 1:1–25 (NIV)**
1 Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our dear friend and fellow worker— 2 also to Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier—and to the church that meets in your home: 3 Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. 4 I always thank my God as I remember you in my prayers, 5 because I hear about your love for all his holy people and your faith in the Lord Jesus. 6 I pray that your partnership with us in the faith may be effective in deepening your understanding of every good thing we share for the sake of Christ. 7 Your love has given me great joy and encouragement, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the Lord’s people. 8 Therefore, although in Christ I could be bold and order you to do what you ought to do, 9 yet I prefer to appeal to you on the basis of love. It is as none other than Paul—an old man and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus— 10 that I appeal to you for my son Onesimus, who became my son while I was in chains. 11 Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. 12 I am sending him—who is my very heart—back to you. 13 I would have liked to keep him with me so that he could take your place in helping me while I am in chains for the gospel. 14 But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that any favor you do would not seem forced but would be voluntary. 15 Perhaps the reason he was separated from you for a little while was that you might have him back forever— 16 no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother. He is very dear to me but even dearer to you, both as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord. 17 So if you consider me a partner, welcome him as you would welcome me. 18 If he has done you any wrong or owes you anything, charge it to me. 19 I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand. I will pay it back—not to mention that you owe me your very self. 20 I do wish, brother, that I may have some benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ. 21 Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. 22 And one thing more: Prepare a guest room for me, because I hope to be restored to you in answer to your prayers. 23 Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings. 24 And so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, my fellow workers. 25 The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

**Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and a mother, whom have you been quietly treating as less than a brother or sister? What would it look like today to welcome that person as you would welcome a beloved friend, and to let forgiveness carry a real cost?

**Lesson 235: Hebrews: the Son superior to angels — pay careful attention**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we read Philemon, and saw a runaway welcomed as a brother. Today Hebrews opens with the Son, superior to angels, and with a call to pay careful attention. In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom also he made the universe. The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of his being, sustaining all things by his powerful word. After he had provided purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven. So he became as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is superior to theirs. The writer then asks, from the Scriptures, whether God ever said to an angel, You are my Son, or called the angels to worship the firstborn, or told an angel to sit at his right hand. He makes his angels winds, his servants flames of fire, but of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, will last for ever and ever. Angels are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. The Son is not one more servant in that company. He is the heir, the radiance, the one who sat down. We must pay the most careful attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. For since the message spoken through angels was binding, and every violation and disobedience received its just punishment, how shall we escape if we ignore so great a salvation? This salvation, which was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard him. God also testified to it by signs, wonders and various miracles, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will. Drifting is quiet. The danger is not only a loud refusal. It is letting so great a salvation, spoken by the Son himself, slip from our hands. John Piper, in In These Last Days, God Has Spoken by a Son, and in He Made Purification of Sins, stays with 1:1–4: the Son is the last and full speech of God, the radiance of his glory, and the one who provided purification for sins and sat down. In Jesus Christ: Infinitely Superior to Angels, the comparisons of chapter 1 are not a curiosity about angels. They are meant to show how great the Son is. In The Danger of Drifting from the Word, and in Spoken, Confirmed, Witnessed: a Great Salvation, he takes 2:1–4 as a warning that fits the glory just named: pay the most careful attention, and do not ignore so great a salvation. BibleProject’s Hebrews guide hears the letter begin here: God has spoken by his Son, so do not drift. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “who is the radiance of His glory and the exact representation of His nature,” and, “having accomplished cleansing for sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,” It also has, “we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away.” and, “how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” The NIV’s “exact representation of his being,” “provided purification for sins,” and “how shall we escape if we ignore so great a salvation?” keep that same radiance, and that same warning. God has spoken by his Son. Pay careful attention, and do not drift. As a man, husband, and father, do not treat the salvation announced by the Lord as background noise. Hold what you have heard, and let the greatness of the Son keep you from a quiet drift today.

**Hebrews 1:1–14 (NIV)**
1 In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, 2 but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom also he made the universe. 3 The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of his being, sustaining all things by his powerful word. After he had provided purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in heaven. 4 So he became as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is superior to theirs. 5 For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son; today I have become your Father”? Or again, “I will be his Father, and he will be my Son”? 6 And again, when God brings his firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.” 7 In speaking of the angels he says, “He makes his angels spirits, and his servants flames of fire.” 8 But about the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, will last for ever and ever; a scepter of justice will be the scepter of your kingdom. 9 You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has set you above your companions by anointing you with the oil of joy.” 10 He also says, “In the beginning, Lord, you laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. 11 They will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment. 12 You will roll them up like a robe; like a garment they will be changed. But you remain the same, and your years will never end.” 13 To which of the angels did God ever say, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”? 14 Are not all angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?

**Hebrews 2:1–4 (NIV)**
1 We must pay the most careful attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. 2 For since the message spoken through angels was binding, and every violation and disobedience received its just punishment, 3 how shall we escape if we ignore so great a salvation? This salvation, which was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard him. 4 God also testified to it by signs, wonders and various miracles, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been quietly drifting from what God has spoken by his Son? What would it look like today to pay the most careful attention to this great salvation, and to hold it more firmly than yesterday?

**Lesson 236: Hebrews: a great high priest who sympathizes**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the Son is superior to angels, and that we must pay careful attention so we do not drift. Today we are given a great high priest who sympathizes, and a throne of grace we may approach. Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has ascended into heaven, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to the faith we profess. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin. Let us then approach God’s throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need. The priest is not far, and the throne is not a throne of ice. It is a throne of grace, and the help is well-timed for weakness. Then, after a few verses we are not reading as official text today, the writer shows us Jesus in the days of his life on earth. He offered up prayers and petitions with fervent cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission. Son though he was, he learned obedience from what he suffered and, once made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him and was designated by God to be high priest in the order of Melchizedek. We tell the cries and the suffering with care, not as a spectacle. This is why he can sympathize. He has walked the path of obedience through suffering, and he has become the source of eternal salvation. So hold the faith, and come to the throne. John Piper, in Draw Near to the Throne of Grace with Confidence, and in A Well-Timed Help, stays with Hebrews 4:14–16: a great high priest who sympathizes, and a throne we may approach with confidence, to receive mercy and find grace in time of need. In He Is the Source of Eternal Salvation for All Who Obey Him, he takes 5:4–10, including the official verses we have today: the Son learned obedience from what he suffered, and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him. BibleProject’s Hebrews guide hears the same invitation: because of this priest, draw near. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.” It also has, “He learned obedience from the things which He suffered.” and, “He became to all those who obey Him the source of eternal salvation,” The NIV’s “approach God’s throne of grace with confidence,” “he learned obedience from what he suffered” and “the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him” keep that same sympathy, and that same source. You have a great high priest who sympathizes. Draw near to the throne of grace. As a man, husband, and father, do not stay away from God as if your weakness disqualifies you. Hold firmly to the faith you profess, and come with confidence today to receive mercy and help in the time of need.

**Hebrews 4:14–16 (NIV)**
14 Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has ascended into heaven, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to the faith we profess. 15 For we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin. 16 Let us then approach God’s throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.

**Hebrews 5:7–10 (NIV)**
7 During the days of Jesus’ life on earth, he offered up prayers and petitions with fervent cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission. 8 Son though he was, he learned obedience from what he suffered 9 and, once made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him 10 and was designated by God to be high priest in the order of Melchizedek.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been avoiding the throne of grace, as if Jesus could not sympathize? What would it look like today to come with confidence, to tell him the real weakness, and to ask for mercy and help?

**Lesson 237: Hebrews: a better covenant, and blood that cleanses the conscience**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we have a great high priest who sympathizes, and that we may approach the throne of grace. Today the writer names a better covenant, and blood that cleanses the conscience. The main point is this: we do have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who serves in the sanctuary, the true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by a mere human being. Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, so this one too has something to offer. If he were on earth, he would not be a priest, for there are already priests who offer the gifts prescribed by the law. They serve at a sanctuary that is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. But in fact the ministry Jesus has received is as superior to theirs as the covenant of which he is mediator is superior to the old one, since the new covenant is established on better promises. If there had been nothing wrong with the first covenant, no place would have been sought for another. God found fault with the people and promised a new covenant, not like the one made when he took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt. He would put his laws in their minds and write them on their hearts. He would be their God, and they would be his people. They would all know him, from the least to the greatest. For I will forgive their wickedness and will remember their sins no more. By calling this covenant new, he has made the first one obsolete, and what is obsolete and outdated will soon disappear. **Lesson 238: Hebrews: draw near; faith is confidence in what we hope for**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that Christ is the mediator of a better covenant, and that his blood cleanses the conscience. Today we are told to draw near, and we are shown what faith is. Therefore, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way opened for us through the curtain, that is, his body, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near to God with a sincere heart and with the full assurance that faith brings, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and having our bodies washed with pure water. Let us hold unswervingly to the hope we profess, for he who promised is faithful. And let us consider how we may spur one another on toward love and good deeds, not giving up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another—and all the more as you see the Day approaching. The opened way is not meant to leave us alone. Draw near, hold hope, and keep meeting. Now faith is confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see. This is what the ancients were commended for. By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible. By faith Abel brought a better offering, and by faith he still speaks, though he died. We name that death simply. By faith Enoch was taken from this life, so that he did not experience death. And without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who comes to him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him. By faith Noah, warned about things not yet seen, built an ark to save his family. By faith Abraham obeyed and went, even though he did not know where he was going. By faith he made his home in the promised land like a stranger, as did Isaac and Jacob. By faith Sarah was enabled to bear a child, because she considered him faithful who had made the promise. And so from this one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars. All these people were still living by faith when they died. They did not receive the things promised; they only saw them and welcomed them from a distance, admitting that they were foreigners and strangers on earth. People who say such things show that they are looking for a country of their own. If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return. Instead, they were longing for a better country—a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. John Piper, in Let Us Draw Near to God, and in The Fullness of Hope and the Fellowship of Love, and in Encouraging Each Other at the End of the Age, stays with 10:19–25: an opened way, a sincere heart, a hope held unswervingly, and a people who will not give up meeting together. In What Faith Knows and Hopes For, faith is confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see. In Without Faith It Is Impossible to Please God, the one who comes must believe that God exists and that he rewards those who seek him. In The Faith of Noah, Abraham, and Sarah, and in The Hope of Exiles on the Earth, he follows 11:7–16 to a people who die still living by faith, longing for a better country, a heavenly one, and to a God who is not ashamed to be called their God. BibleProject’s Hebrews guide hears the same turn: because of the priest and the opened way, draw near, and live by faith. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith,” and, “Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” It also has, “without faith it is impossible to please Him” and, “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He prepared a city for them.” The NIV’s “draw near to God with a sincere heart and with the full assurance that faith brings,” “confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see.” and the God who “has prepared a city for them” keep that same nearness, and that same country. Draw near. Faith is confidence in what we hope for, and God has prepared a city for his people. As a man, husband, and father, do not give up meeting, and do not treat the unseen promise as less real than what you can already hold. Come near with a sincere heart, encourage someone toward love and good deeds, and live today as a person looking for a better country.

19 Therefore, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, 20 by a new and living way opened for us through the curtain, that is, his body, 21 and since we have a great priest over the house of God, 22 let us draw near to God with a sincere heart and with the full assurance that faith brings, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and having our bodies washed with pure water. 23 Let us hold unswervingly to the hope we profess, for he who promised is faithful. 24 And let us consider how we may spur one another on toward love and good deeds, 25 not giving up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another—and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

**Hebrews 11:1–16 (NIV)**
1 Now faith is confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see. 2 This is what the ancients were commended for. 3 By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible. 4 By faith Abel brought God a better offering than Cain did. By faith he was commended as righteous, when God spoke well of his offerings. And by faith Abel still speaks, even though he is dead. 5 By faith Enoch was taken from this life, so that he did not experience death: “He could not be found, because God had taken him away.” For before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God. 6 And without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who comes to him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him. 7 By faith Noah, when warned about things not yet seen, in holy fear built an ark to save his family. By his faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that is in keeping with faith. 8 By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, even though he did not know where he was going. 9 By faith he made his home in the promised land like a stranger in a foreign country; he lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. 10 For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God. 11 And by faith even Sarah, who was past childbearing age, was enabled to bear children because she considered him faithful who had made the promise. 12 And so from this one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore. 13 All these people were still living by faith when they died. They did not receive the things promised; they only saw them and welcomed them from a distance, admitting that they were foreigners and strangers on earth. 14 People who say such things show that they are looking for a country of their own. 15 If they had been thinking of the country they had left, they would have had opportunity to return. 16 Instead, they were longing for a better country—a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been hanging back from God, or from the gathering of his people, or from the unseen promise? What would it look like today to draw near with a sincere heart, to encourage one person, and to take one step as someone who wants a better country?

**Lesson 239: Hebrews: run with perseverance; Jesus is the same yesterday, today, and forever**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we may draw near to God, and that faith is confidence in what we hope for. Today we are told to run with perseverance, and we are told that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily entangles. And let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us, fixing our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith. For the joy set before him he endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. We speak of the cross with reverence, not as a spectacle. The race is already marked out, and the eyes have a place to rest: Jesus, who has already sat down. Consider him who endured such opposition from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart. In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. We name that struggle simply. And have you completely forgotten this word of encouragement that addresses you as a father addresses his son? **Lesson 240: James: consider it pure joy — faith, trials, and every good gift**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we are to run with perseverance, and that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Today James says to consider it pure joy when we face trials, and he traces faith, testing, and every good gift. Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance. Let perseverance finish its work so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything. If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you. But when you ask, you must believe and not doubt, because the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind. That person should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. Such a person is double-minded and unstable in all they do. Believers in humble circumstances ought to take pride in their high position. But the rich should take pride in their humiliation—since they will pass away like a wild flower. The sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its blossom falls and its beauty is destroyed. In the same way, the rich will fade away even as they go about their business. Blessed is the one who perseveres under trial because, having stood the test, that person will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him. When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does he tempt anyone; but each person is tempted when they are dragged away by their own evil desire and enticed. Then, after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death. We speak of desire and death with care, not as a spectacle. God is not the author of the hook that pulls us toward evil. Don’t be deceived, my dear brothers and sisters. Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, who does not change like shifting shadows. He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we might be a kind of firstfruits of all he created. The Father who does not change is the Giver, not the tempter. Trials may test faith, and they can produce perseverance. They are not God enticing you toward sin. I did not use a Piper sermon whose main text is James 1:2–11. We stay with the text itself there: consider it pure joy, let perseverance finish its work, and ask God for wisdom. John Piper, in The Fullest, Longest Happiness, stays with James 1:12–18, the official close of today’s reading: the one who perseveres under trial is blessed, God tempts no one, and every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father who does not change. BibleProject’s James guide hears the letter begin here: faith is tested, wisdom is asked for, and the Father is a generous Giver. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you encounter various trials,” It also has, “Every good thing given and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shifting shadow.” The NIV’s “Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds,” and “Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, who does not change like shifting shadows.” keep that same joy under trial, and that same unchanging Giver. Consider it pure joy when faith is tested, and receive every good gift from the Father who does not change. As a man, husband, and father, do not call God the tempter, and do not waste a trial as if it could produce nothing. Ask him for wisdom, let perseverance finish its work, and thank him today for one good gift that has come down from above.

2 Consider it pure joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you face trials of many kinds, 3 because you know that the testing of your faith produces perseverance. 4 Let perseverance finish its work so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything. 5 If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you. 6 But when you ask, you must believe and not doubt, because the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind. 7 That person should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. 8 Such a person is double-minded and unstable in all they do. 9 Believers in humble circumstances ought to take pride in their high position. 10 But the rich should take pride in their humiliation—since they will pass away like a wild flower. 11 For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its blossom falls and its beauty is destroyed. In the same way, the rich will fade away even while they go about their business. 12 Blessed is the one who perseveres under trial because, having stood the test, that person will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love him. 13 When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does he tempt anyone; 14 but each person is tempted when they are dragged away by their own evil desire and enticed. 15 Then, after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death. 16 Don’t be deceived, my dear brothers and sisters. 17 Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, who does not change like shifting shadows. 18 He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we might be a kind of firstfruits of all he created.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you treated a trial only as a loss, or blamed God for a temptation, or forgotten the Giver? What would it look like today to ask for wisdom without doubting, and to receive one ordinary good gift as coming down from the Father?

**Lesson 241: James: be doers of the word; faith without works is dead**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we may consider trials as joy, and that every good gift comes down from the Father. Today James says we must be doers of the word, and that faith without deeds is dead. My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteousness that God desires. Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and the evil that is so prevalent and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save you. Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says. Anyone who listens to the word but does not do what it says is like someone who looks at his face in a mirror and, after looking at himself, goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like. But whoever looks intently into the perfect law that gives freedom, and continues in it—not forgetting what they have heard, but doing it—they will be blessed in what they do. Those who consider themselves religious and yet do not keep a tight rein on their tongues deceive themselves, and their religion is worthless. Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world. The planted word is meant to become a life: a restrained tongue, a cared-for widow, a kept heart. What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can such faith save them? Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, “Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,” but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead. But someone will say, “You have faith; I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. You believe that there is one God. Good! Even the demons believe that—and shudder. You foolish person, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is useless? Was not our father Abraham considered righteous for what he did when he offered Isaac his son on the altar? We tell Abraham’s offering simply, not as a spectacle. You see that his faith and his actions were working together, and his faith was made complete by what he did. And the scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called God’s friend. You see that a person is considered righteous by what they do and not by faith alone. In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute considered righteous for what she did when she gave lodging to the spies and sent them off in a different direction? We name Rahab with honor. Her past is not a joke, and it is not a story to be used against her. She believed, and she acted, and she is held up as righteous for what she did. As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead. John Piper, in Receive with Meekness the Implanted Word, stays with James 1:18–25, including the official call we have today: humbly accept the word planted in you, and do not merely listen. Be a doer. In Does James Contradict Paul?, he takes 2:14–26 and answers no: James is not at war with Paul. A claimed faith that will not move toward a hungry brother is dead, and a living faith is completed by what it does.
