lessons.title: Many waters cannot quench love
lessons.body:
**Lesson 271: Many waters cannot quench love**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the Song said, I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me, and Paul called us to a holy and honorable self-control. Today the poem gives love a seal and a strength. Place me like a seal over your heart, like a seal on your arm; for love is as strong as death, its jealousy unyielding as the grave. It burns like blazing fire, like a mighty flame. We hear jealousy here as covenant zeal, not as a petty mood, and we do not turn the fire into a spectacle.

Many waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away. If one were to give all the wealth of one’s house for love, it would be utterly scorned. This is not a cheap feeling that floods can wash out, and it is not a thing you can buy. The seal says, I am yours; keep me close. The waters say, this love will not be put out. In a marriage, that is a call to a faithful, costly love, the kind that remains when days are ordinary and when they are hard. The official wording is enough. We do not need to add heat to it.

I looked for a John Piper sermon on Desiring God whose main text is Song of Songs 8:6–7, and I did not find a /messages/ sermon on that range, so we stay with the text itself and with the BibleProject guide to Song of Songs. The guide helps us hear the close of the song as covenant love: sealed, strong, unquenchable, and not for sale.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Song of Songs 8:6 has, Put me like a seal over your heart, Like a seal on your arm. For love is as strong as death, Jealousy is as severe as Sheol; Its flashes are flashes of fire, The very flame of Yah. And Song of Songs 8:7 has, Many waters cannot quench love, Nor will rivers overflow it; If a man were to give all the riches of his house for love, It would be utterly despised.

Place me like a seal over your heart. Love is as strong as death. Many waters cannot quench it, and no one can buy it. That is the love this covenant is meant to hold.

**Song of Songs 8:6–7 (NIV)**
6 Place me like a seal over your heart, like a seal on your arm; for love is as strong as death, its jealousy unyielding as the grave. It burns like blazing fire, like a mighty flame. 7 Many waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away. If one were to give all the wealth of one’s house for love, it would be utterly scorned.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has love in your house been treated as a weak mood, or as something money and ease could replace? What would it look like today to keep a seal over the heart, and to practice a love the waters cannot quench?

*Scripture quotations taken from the Holy Bible, New International Version®, NIV® Copyright ©1973, 1978, 1984, 2011 by Biblica, Inc.® Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. lessons.title: Talking honestly: listen before you speak

sources.label: John Piper, Receive with Meekness the Implanted Word (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 272: Talking honestly: listen before you speak**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the Song said that many waters cannot quench love. Today the house is given a plainer wisdom: talking honestly, and listening first. My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteousness that God desires. Honest talk is not the same as fast talk. The first obedience is to hear.

Proverbs makes the same point in a sharp line: To answer before listening— that is folly and shame. We know this in a kitchen, in a car, and at the end of a long day. A reply that will not wait is often a reply that will have to be repaired. Slow speech is not weakness. It is honor. It leaves room for the truth, and it leaves less room for the anger that does not produce the righteousness God desires. We teach the anger warning simply. We do not make a game of a sharp tongue, and we do not pretend that every quick feeling is righteousness.

In *Receive with Meekness the Implanted Word*, on James 1:18–25, John Piper keeps James’s order in view: the word is to be received with meekness, and a meek hearing is quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 18:13, so that proverb is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Proverbs: answering before you listen is folly and shame. The BibleProject guide to James helps us hear this as a real household obedience, not as a slogan.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: James 1:19–20 has, Know this, my beloved brothers. But everyone must be quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger; for the anger of man does not achieve the righteousness of God. And Proverbs 18:13 has, He who responds with a word before he hears, It is folly and shame to him.

Be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to become angry. To answer before listening is folly and shame. Honest talk begins with a hearing ear.

**James 1:19–20 (NIV)**
19 My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, 20 because human anger does not produce the righteousness that God desires.

**Proverbs 18:13 (NIV)**
13 To answer before listening— that is folly and shame.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where have you answered before you heard, or let a quick anger speak first? What would it look like today to be quick to listen in your house, and slow to speak?

lessons.title: A gentle answer and careful words at home

sources.label: John Piper, Make Your Mouth a Means of Grace (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 273: A gentle answer and careful words at home**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we were told to be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry. Today the same wisdom comes home in a gentle answer, and in careful words. A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. We have watched this in a room. A hard word raises the temperature. A gentle answer can lower it. Gentleness here is not a refusal to tell the truth. It is the way the truth is spoken in a house.

Paul gives the words a holy aim: Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs, that it may benefit those who listen. Unwholesome talk is not only crude talk. It is speech that does not build, speech that does not fit the need, speech that does not benefit the one who hears. The test is not, did I get to say it? The test is, did this help? In a marriage, and with children in the room, this is everyday work. Careful words are a way of honoring the people who have to live with what we say.

In *Make Your Mouth a Means of Grace*, on Ephesians 4:29–30, John Piper shifts the question from merely clean language to love: is your mouth a means of grace, meeting a need, building up the one who hears? I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 15:1, so the gentle answer is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Proverbs: a gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The BibleProject guide to Ephesians helps us hear careful words as part of the new life in Christ, not as a thin politeness.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Ephesians 4:29 has, Let no unwholesome word proceed from your mouth, but only such a word as is good for building up what is needed, so that it will give grace to those who hear.

A gentle answer turns away wrath. Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what builds up, fits the need, and benefits the one who listens. Careful words are a gift at home.

**Proverbs 15:1 (NIV)**
1 A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

**Ephesians 4:29 (NIV)**
29 Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs, that it may benefit those who listen.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, what kind of word most often comes out of your mouth at home—a harsh word that stirs, or a word that builds? What would it look like today to give a gentle answer, and to speak only what benefits those who listen?

lessons.title: A gentle answer and careful words at home

sources.label: John Piper, Make Your Mouth a Means of Grace (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 273: A gentle answer and careful words at home**

Good morning. Yesterday we were told to be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry. Today the same wisdom comes home in a gentle answer, and in careful words. A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. We have watched this in a room. A hard word raises the temperature. A gentle answer can lower it. Gentleness here is not a refusal to tell the truth. It is the way the truth is spoken in a house.

Paul gives the words a holy aim: Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs, that it may benefit those who listen. Unwholesome talk is not only crude talk. It is speech that does not build, speech that does not fit the need, speech that does not benefit the one who hears. The test is not, did I get to say it? The test is, did this help? In a marriage, and with children in the room, this is everyday work. Careful words are a way of honoring the people who have to live with what we say.

In *Make Your Mouth a Means of Grace*, on Ephesians 4:29–30, John Piper shifts the question from merely clean language to love: is your mouth a means of grace, meeting a need, building up the one who hears? I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 15:1, so the gentle answer is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Proverbs: a gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The BibleProject guide to Ephesians helps us hear careful words as part of the new life in Christ, not as a thin politeness.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Ephesians 4:29 has, Let no unwholesome word proceed from your mouth, but only such a word as is good for building up what is needed, so that it will give grace to those who hear.

A gentle answer turns away wrath. Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what builds up, fits the need, and benefits the one who listens. Careful words are a gift at home.

1 A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

**Ephesians 4:29 (NIV)**
29 Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs, that it may benefit those who listen.

**For reflection.** As a woman, wife, and a mother, what kind of word most often comes out of your mouth at home—a harsh word that stirs, or a word that builds? What would it look like today to give a gentle answer, and to speak only what benefits those who listen?

lessons.title: Conflict without tearing down

sources.label: John Piper, Getting Right with God and Each Other (Desiring God)
John Piper, Satan Seeks a Gap Called Grudge (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 274: Conflict without tearing down**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard a gentle answer and careful words at home. Today Jesus and Paul speak to conflict that must be faced without tearing a person down. Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift. Worship is not a way to skip a rupture you already know is there. Go first. Be reconciled. Then come.

Settle matters quickly with your adversary who is taking you to court. Do it while you are still together on the way. Delay can turn a wound into a harder case. Jesus is not giving us a game, and he is not telling us to crush the other person. He is telling us to make peace while there is still a way. Truly I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the last penny. We leave that warning in his mouth, and we do not soften it into a shrug.

Paul comes close to the same fire in the house: “In your anger do not sin”: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry, and do not give the devil a foothold. Anger may come. Sin is not required. A long, kept anger is a door. We do not treat the devil as a spectacle here. We treat a grudge as a danger, and we put it down before the day is gone, as far as it is in us to do so. Conflict can be honest. It must not be used to tear a husband, a wife, or a child down.

In *Getting Right with God and Each Other*, on Matthew 5:21–26, John Piper lingers over reconciliation that will not wait until worship feels convenient: leave the gift, go first, be reconciled. Today’s official text is Matthew 5:23–26, so we stay with that call and do not take up the earlier verses as today’s official word. In *Satan Seeks a Gap Called Grudge*, on Ephesians 4:22–27, he treats a held anger as a gap the enemy looks for. We keep the official word in 4:26–27: in your anger do not sin, and do not give the devil a foothold. The BibleProject guides to Matthew and Ephesians help us hear both texts as the gospel’s ordinary work in a house, not as a license to win.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Matthew 5:23–24 has, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your offering there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother. Matthew 5:25 has, Make friends quickly with your opponent at law while you are with him on the way. Ephesians 4:26–27 has, Be angry, and yet do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and do not give the devil an opportunity.

Go first. Be reconciled. In your anger do not sin, and do not let the sun go down while you are still angry. Conflict may be real. Tearing one another down is not the way.

**Matthew 5:23–26 (NIV)**
23 “Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, 24 leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift. 25 “Settle matters quickly with your adversary who is taking you to court. Do it while you are still together on the way, or your adversary may hand you over to the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer, and you may be thrown into prison. 26 Truly I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.

**Ephesians 4:26–27 (NIV)**
26 “In your anger do not sin”: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry, 27 and do not give the devil a foothold.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, is there a gift you have been trying to bring while a brother or sister still has something against you? What would it look like today to go first, to settle matters quickly, and to put anger down before it becomes a foothold?

lessons.title: Forgiveness in the home

sources.label: John Piper, Marriage: Forgiving and Forbearing (Desiring God)
John Piper, Teaching and Admonishing One Another in All Wisdom (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 275: Forgiveness in the home**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we were told to face conflict without tearing one another down. Today the house is called to forgive. Therefore, as God’s chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. This is not a thin politeness. It is the dress of people the Lord has already forgiven.

And over all these virtues put on love, which binds them all together in perfect unity. Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, since as members of one body you were called to peace. And be thankful. Forgiveness in the home is not the only garment, but without it the others tear. Love holds them. The peace of Christ is meant to rule, not merely to visit.

Jesus makes the matter weighty: For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins. We hear this pastorally, not as a tool to crush a tender conscience that is still learning how to forgive a deep wound. Jesus is not casual about settled unforgiveness. A hard, kept refusal to forgive is serious. The same Lord who warns us is the Lord who forgave us, and who clothes us to forgive as he forgave.

In *Marriage: Forgiving and Forbearing*, on Colossians 3:12–19, and in *Teaching and Admonishing One Another in All Wisdom*, on Colossians 3:12–17, John Piper treats this clothing as the ordinary life of a forgiven people: compassion, patience, bearing with one another, and forgiving as the Lord forgave you. Today’s official text is Colossians 3:12–15, so we stay inside that range. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Matthew 6:14–15, so Jesus’ warning is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Matthew. The BibleProject guide to Colossians helps us hear forgiveness as part of the new life we put on, not as a way to pretend a wound never happened.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Colossians 3:12 has, So, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Colossians 3:13 has, bearing with one another, and graciously forgiving each other, whoever has a complaint against anyone, just as the Lord graciously forgave you, so also should you. Colossians 3:14 has, Above all these things put on love, which is the perfect bond of unity. Matthew 6:14–15 has, For if you forgive others for their transgressions, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others, then your Father will not forgive your transgressions.

Clothe yourselves with compassion and patience. Bear with each other, and forgive as the Lord forgave you. Put on love. Let the peace of Christ rule. Forgive others their sins, as those who have been forgiven.

**Colossians 3:12–15 (NIV)**
12 Therefore, as God’s chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. 13 Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. 14 And over all these virtues put on love, which binds them all together in perfect unity. 15 Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, since as members of one body you were called to peace. And be thankful.

**Matthew 6:14–15 (NIV)**
14 For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. 15 But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a grievance been easier to keep than to forgive? What would it look like today to put on compassion, to forgive as the Lord forgave you, and to let the peace of Christ rule in your heart at home?

lessons.title: Praying together as husband and wife

sources.label: John Piper, That Your Prayers May Not Be Hindered (Desiring God)
John Piper, Honor, Guard, and Cherish (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 276: Praying together as husband and wife**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we were called to forgive in the home. Today Jesus and Peter turn that same house toward prayer. Again, truly I tell you that if two of you on earth agree about anything they ask for, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven. For where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them. A husband and a wife are not a crowd. They can still be two who agree, two who gather in his name. He is not far from a quiet prayer in an ordinary room.

Peter then speaks a hard, holy word to husbands: Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers. Weaker partner is not a slur, and it is not a license to rule a wife as less. She is an heir with you of the gracious gift of life. Consideration and respect belong to that shared gift. If they are withheld, prayer in the house is not a small thing that still works the same. Peter says the prayers can be hindered.

So praying together is not only a sweet habit. It is bound to how a husband lives with his wife, and to how both of them come to the Father in the name of Jesus. Agreeing in prayer does not mean there is never a hard conversation. It means the two come, in his name, and ask.

In *That Your Prayers May Not Be Hindered* and in *Honor, Guard, and Cherish*, on 1 Peter 3:7, John Piper treats a husband’s consideration and honor as part of the life in which prayer can move freely, and a wife as a fellow heir of the grace of life. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Matthew 18:19–20, so Jesus’ promise about two who agree, and his presence where two or three gather in his name, is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Matthew. The BibleProject guide to 1 Peter helps us hear honor at home as part of the same holy life, not as a side rule.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Matthew 18:20 has, For where two or three have gathered together in My name, I am there in their midst. 1 Peter 3:7 has, You husbands in the same way, live with your wives in an understanding way, as with a weaker vessel, since she is a woman; and show her honor as a fellow heir of the grace of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.

Where two gather in his name, he is with them. Live with honor, as heirs together of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers. A marriage can become a place of agreed asking.

**Matthew 18:19–20 (NIV)**
19 “Again, truly I tell you that if two of you on earth agree about anything they ask for, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven. 20 For where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them.”

**1 Peter 3:7 (NIV)**
7 Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, what would it look like today for the two of you to gather in Jesus’ name and agree about something you ask? How might consideration and honor at home keep your prayers from being hindered?

lessons.title: Serving one another in ordinary days

sources.label: John Piper, Freed to Love (Desiring God)
John Piper, The Sovereign Sacrifice: Foreknown, Foretold, for Faith (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 277: Serving one another in ordinary days**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that a husband and a wife can pray together, and that honor at home is bound to those prayers. Today the call comes down to ordinary days. You, my brothers and sisters, were called to be free. But do not use your freedom to indulge the flesh; rather, serve one another humbly in love. Freedom is not a cover for self. Flesh here is not a spectacle. It is the old pull to use a person, or a day, for yourself. The gospel’s freedom turns us toward one another, in love, in the small work of a house.

Jesus had already made the pattern low and clear. When he had finished washing their feet, he put on his clothes and returned to his place. “Do you understand what I have done for you?” he asked them. You call me ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord,’ and rightly so, for that is what I am. Now that I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. I have set you an example that you should do as I have done for you. Very truly I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him. Now that you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.

We do not need a basin to hear the point. Ordinary service in a marriage is often unseen: a meal, a late child, a hard errand, a quiet help no one applauds. The Lord and Teacher washed feet. We are not greater than he is. The blessing is promised to those who do this, not only to those who admire it.

In *Freed to Love*, on Galatians 5:13–15, John Piper treats freedom as a call to serve one another through love, not as a chance to indulge the flesh. Today’s official text is Galatians 5:13, so we stay with that verse and do not take up the next lines as today’s official word. In *The Sovereign Sacrifice: Foreknown, Foretold, for Faith*, on John 13:12–20, he reads the foot-washing and the example Jesus sets. Today’s official text is John 13:12–17, so we stay with the washing and the call to do as he has done, and we do not take up the later verses as today’s official word. The BibleProject guides to Galatians and John help us hear humble service as the freedom and the example the gospel actually gives.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Galatians 5:13 has, For you were called to freedom, brothers; only do not turn your freedom into an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. lessons.title: The two shall become one

sources.label: John Piper, What God Has Joined Together, Let Not Man Separate, Part 1 (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 278: The two shall become one**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we were called to serve one another humbly in love, in ordinary days. Today Jesus takes us back to the beginning of the covenant itself. But at the beginning of creation God ‘made them male and female.’ ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.

This is not a thin partnership, and it is not a contract we invented. God made them male and female. A man leaves, and is united to his wife, and the two become one flesh. They are no longer two. What God has joined together is not ours to pull apart at will. We have already heard this holy joining in earlier days of this series. We hear it again here as a guard and a comfort: the marriage is God’s work, and it is to be honored as one.

Let no one separate is a serious word. It is not a dare to stay cruel, and it is not a casual threat. It is Jesus’ way of telling us that this union is not a private experiment. God has joined. We do not treat the bond as disposable.

In *What God Has Joined Together, Let Not Man Separate, Part 1*, on Mark 10:1–12, John Piper stays with Jesus’ word from the beginning: God made them male and female, the two become one flesh, and what God has joined together, no one is to separate. Today’s official text is Mark 10:6–9, so we stay inside that range and do not take up the surrounding verses as today’s official word. The BibleProject guide to Mark helps us hear this as Jesus’ own appeal to creation, not as a later rule tacked onto marriage.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Mark 10:6 has, But from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female. Mark 10:9 has, What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.

God made them male and female. The two will become one flesh, and they are no longer two. What God has joined together, let no one separate.

**Mark 10:6–9 (NIV)**
6 “But at the beginning of creation God ‘made them male and female.’ 7 ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, 8 and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. 9 Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, how would your day change if you treated your marriage as what God has joined together, and not as two lives that merely share a house? What would it look like today to honor that one flesh with faithfulness and care?

lessons.title: When marriage is hard: endurance and hope

sources.label: John Piper, A Call to Love — and to Death (Desiring God)
John Piper, Let Love Be Genuine (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 279: When marriage is hard: endurance and hope**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the two shall become one flesh, and that what God has joined together, let no one separate. Today we hear what love looks like when the days are hard. Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres.

This is not a soft poem for an easy season. Patience, kindness, and no record of wrongs are the tools of a long faithfulness. Always hopes, always perseveres is not a command to pretend a wound is fine. It is a refusal to let hardness have the last word. Marriage can be hard. The word here is endurance and hope, not despair, and not a spectacle of pain.

Paul says the same in another key: Love must be sincere. Hate what is evil; cling to what is good. Be devoted to one another in love. Honor one another above yourselves. Never be lacking in zeal, but keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord. Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer. Sincere love does not flatter. It hates what is evil, clings to what is good, stays devoted, and keeps praying when the day is heavy.

In *A Call to Love — and to Death*, on 1 Corinthians 13:4–7, John Piper treats this love as more than a feeling: it is patient and kind, it keeps no record of wrongs, and it perseveres. In *Let Love Be Genuine*, on Romans 12:9, he lingers over love that must be sincere, that hates what is evil and clings to what is good. Romans 12:10–12, the rest of today’s official range, is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Romans: be devoted, honor one another, be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer. The BibleProject guide to 1 Corinthians helps us hear love that endures as the way of Christ in a real house, not as a slogan.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 1 Corinthians 13:5 has, does not take into account a wrong suffered. 1 Corinthians 13:7 has, it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Romans 12:9 has, Let love be without hypocrisy—by abhorring what is evil, clinging to what is good. Romans 12:12 has, rejoicing in hope, persevering in affliction, being devoted to prayer.

Love is patient and kind. It keeps no record of wrongs, and it always hopes, always perseveres. Let love be sincere. Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer. When marriage is hard, this is the way of endurance and hope.

**1 Corinthians 13:4–7 (NIV)**
4 Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5 It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. 6 Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. 7 It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres.

**Romans 12:9–12 (NIV)**
9 Love must be sincere. Hate what is evil; cling to what is good. 10 Be devoted to one another in love. Honor one another above yourselves. 11 Never be lacking in zeal, but keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord. 12 Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, faithful in prayer.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a hard season made it easier to keep a record of wrongs than to be patient and kind? What would it look like today to let love be sincere, to hope, to persevere, and to stay faithful in prayer?

lessons.title: Guarding the covenant: purity and a hedge
lessons.body:
**Lesson 280: Guarding the covenant: purity and a hedge**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard love that is patient and kind, that always hopes and always perseveres, when marriage is hard. Today the covenant is guarded. I made a covenant with my eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman. Job names a watch at the first gate, the eyes. This is not a sneer at a woman, and it is not a joke. It is a holy hedge: the look is already a place where a covenant can be kept or broken.

Jesus takes the same seriousness into the heart. You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart. If your right eye causes you to stumble, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to go into hell. We hear this with care. Jesus is not commanding literal self-harm, and we do not turn his words into a graphic scene or a game. He is telling us that lust is not small, and that hell is not a metaphor we may shrug off. The eye and the hand are named because the heart uses them. The call is drastic holiness, not harm of the body.

Proverbs sets a hedge around the same covenant. My son, keep your father’s command and do not forsake your mother’s teaching. Bind them always on your heart; fasten them around your neck. That teaching is a lamp, and it keeps you from your neighbor’s wife, from the smooth talk of a wayward woman. Do not lust in your heart after her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes. A man who commits adultery has no sense; whoever does so destroys himself. We do not linger on the fire, the blows, or the fury in this chapter as a scare show. We hear the warning as a hedge: adultery destroys the one who does it, and it wounds a house. The wise path is to keep the teaching close, and to refuse the look, the lust, and the act.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Job 31:1, Matthew 5:27–30, or Proverbs 6:20–35, so today’s word is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Job, Matthew, and Proverbs. Job’s covenant with his eyes, Jesus’ word about lust in the heart, and the father’s command that keeps a son from another’s wife all say the same thing with dignity: the marriage covenant is to be guarded early, at the look and in the heart, not only after a life has already been burned.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Job 31:1 has, I have cut a covenant with my eyes; How then could I gaze at a virgin? Matthew 5:28 has, everyone who looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Proverbs 6:24–25 has, To keep you from the evil woman, From the smooth tongue of the foreign woman. Do not desire her beauty in your heart. Proverbs 6:32 has, The one who commits adultery with a woman is lacking a heart of wisdom; He who would destroy his soul does it.

Make a covenant with your eyes. Do not look lustfully, and do not treat lust as a small thing. Keep the teaching close. A man who commits adultery destroys himself. Guard the covenant. Build a hedge while it is still day.

**Job 31:1 (NIV)**
1 “I made a covenant with my eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman.

**Matthew 5:27–30 (NIV)**
27 “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ 28 But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart. 29 If your right eye causes you to stumble, gouge it out and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to be thrown into hell. 30 And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away. It is better for you to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to go into hell.

**Proverbs 6:20–35 (NIV)**
20 My son, keep your father’s command and do not forsake your mother’s teaching. 21 Bind them always on your heart; fasten them around your neck. 22 When you walk, they will guide you; when you sleep, they will watch over you; when you awake, they will speak to you. 23 For this command is a lamp, this teaching is a light, and correction and instruction are the way to life, 24 keeping you from your neighbor’s wife, from the smooth talk of a wayward woman. 25 Do not lust in your heart after her beauty or let her captivate you with her eyes. 26 For a prostitute can be had for a loaf of bread, but another man’s wife preys on your very life. 27 Can a man scoop fire into his lap without his clothes being burned? 28 Can a man walk on hot coals without his feet being scorched? 29 So is he who sleeps with another man’s wife; no one who touches her will go unpunished. 30 People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his hunger when he is starving. 31 Yet if he is caught, he must pay sevenfold, though it costs him all the wealth of his house. 32 But a man who commits adultery has no sense; whoever does so destroys himself. 33 Blows and disgrace are his lot, and his shame will never be wiped away. 34 For jealousy arouses a husband’s fury, and he will show no mercy when he takes revenge. 35 He will not accept any compensation; he will refuse a bribe, however great it is.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where does this covenant need a clearer hedge—in the eyes, in the heart, or in what you allow to come close? What would it look like today to keep the teaching near, and to refuse lust before it becomes a fire?

**For reflection.** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where does this covenant need a clearer hedge—in the eyes, in the heart, or in what you allow to come close? What would it look like today to keep the teaching near, and to refuse lust before it becomes a fire?

lessons.title: Repairing trust after hurt

sources.label: John Piper, A Broken and Contrite Heart God Will Not Despise (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 281: Repairing trust after hurt**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the covenant is to be guarded, with purity and a hedge. Today the word turns to what happens after a hurt: trust must be repaired, and forgiveness must be real. So watch yourselves. If your brother or sister sins against you, rebuke them; and if they repent, forgive them. Even if they sin against you seven times in a day and seven times come back to you saying ‘I repent,’ you must forgive them. Repair is not silence, and it is not a shrug. Jesus puts a holy rebuke in the path, then repentance, then forgiveness—again, even in one day.

This is careful work in a house. Rebuke, here, is not a chance to tear the other person down. It is telling the truth about a real wrong. Repentance is not a thin sorry meant to end the conversation. Forgiveness is required when they come back saying ‘I repent,’ even seven times. Trust may still need time to grow again. The text does not ask us to pretend nothing happened. It does ask us not to refuse forgiveness when repentance comes.

David shows the inner work that makes such repair possible: Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me. Do not cast me from your presence or take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation and grant me a willing spirit, to sustain me. Then I will teach transgressors your ways, so that sinners will turn back to you. We hear this pastorally, not as a spectacle of David’s sin. A pure heart, a steadfast spirit, and the joy of salvation are gifts we ask for after we have done harm, and they are the ground on which trust can begin to be rebuilt.

In *A Broken and Contrite Heart God Will Not Despise*, on Psalm 51, John Piper lingers over David’s plea not only for mercy but for renewal: create in me a clean heart, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Today’s official text is Psalm 51:10–13, so we stay with that prayer and do not take up the surrounding verses as today’s official word. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Luke 17:3–4, so Jesus’ word about rebuke, repentance, and forgiveness even seven times in a day is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Luke. The BibleProject guide to the Psalms helps us hear a pure heart as God’s work in a wounded house, not as a way to rush past the hurt.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Luke 17:3–4 has, Be on your guard! If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times a day, and returns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him. Psalm 51:10 has, Create in me a clean heart, O God, And renew a steadfast spirit within me. Psalm 51:11 has, Do not cast me away from Your presence And do not take Your Holy Spirit from me. Psalm 51:12–13 has, Restore to me the joy of Your salvation And sustain me with a willing spirit. Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, And sinners will be converted to You.

Watch yourselves. Rebuke, and if they repent, forgive—even seven times in a day. Ask God to create a pure heart, to restore the joy of his salvation, and to sustain you with a willing spirit. Trust is repaired in the truth, and in mercy.

**Luke 17:3–4 (NIV)**
3 So watch yourselves. “If your brother or sister sins against you, rebuke them; and if they repent, forgive them. 4 Even if they sin against you seven times in a day and seven times come back to you saying ‘I repent,’ you must forgive them.”

**Psalm 51:10–13 (NIV)**
10 Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me. 11 Do not cast me from your presence or take your Holy Spirit from me. 12 Restore to me the joy of your salvation and grant me a willing spirit, to sustain me. 13 Then I will teach transgressors your ways, so that sinners will turn back to you.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a hurt in your house been left without a true rebuke, or without a real willingness to forgive? What would it look like today to tell the truth, to seek a pure heart, and to forgive when repentance comes?

lessons.title: Shared mission: building a house on the rock

sources.label: John Piper, Don’t Eat the Bread of Anxious Toil (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 282: Shared mission: building a house on the rock**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that trust can be repaired after hurt, with a true rebuke, repentance, and forgiveness. Today Jesus and the psalm turn a marriage toward a shared mission: building a house on the rock. Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because it had its foundation on the rock.

But everyone who hears these words of mine and does not put them into practice is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell with a great crash. We hear the storm simply, not as a spectacle. The difference is not who heard Jesus. The difference is who put his words into practice. A shared mission in a home is not a shared set of plans on paper. It is hearing the Lord together, and doing what he says.

The psalm names the same dependence from another side: Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the guards stand watch in vain. Work in the house is real. It is not enough. If the LORD does not build, the labor is empty. A couple can be busy, careful, and still be building on sand, if Jesus’ words are only heard and not practiced, and if the LORD is not the one who builds.

In *Don’t Eat the Bread of Anxious Toil*, on Psalm 127, John Piper treats the first verse as a holy limit on our labor: unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Today’s official text is Psalm 127:1, so we stay with that line and do not take up the next verse as today’s official word. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Matthew 7:24–27, so the house on the rock, and the house on the sand, are taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Matthew. The BibleProject guide to the Psalms helps us hear a house that the LORD must build, not a house we can finish in our own strength.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Matthew 7:24 has, Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and does them, may be compared to a wise man who built his house on the rock. Matthew 7:26–27 has, And everyone hearing these words of Mine and not doing them, may be compared to a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And it fell—and great was its fall. Psalm 127:1 has, Unless Yahweh builds the house, They labor in vain who build it; Unless Yahweh watches the city, The watchman keeps awake in vain.

Hear these words of Jesus, and put them into practice. Build on the rock, not on the sand. Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. A shared mission begins there.

**Matthew 7:24–27 (NIV)**
24 “Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. 25 The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because it had its foundation on the rock. 26 But everyone who hears these words of mine and does not put them into practice is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. 27 The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell with a great crash.”

**Psalm 127:1 (NIV)**
1 Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the guards stand watch in vain.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has your house been busy with labor, but thin on putting Jesus’ words into practice? What would it look like today to build on the rock together, and to ask the LORD to build the house?

lessons.title: Honoring in-laws, and leaving well

sources.label: John Piper, Staying Married Is Not About Staying in Love (Desiring God)
John Piper, Ruth: Sweet and Bitter Providence (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 283: Honoring in-laws, and leaving well**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that a shared mission is to hear Jesus’ words and put them into practice, because unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Today the house is given a holy shape: leaving well, and honoring the family you leave and the family you enter. That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh. Leaving is not a slam of the door. It is the making of a new first loyalty, so that the two can be one. Father and mother are not erased. They are no longer the center of the new house.

Ruth shows what honor can look like toward a mother-in-law, in a hard day. But Ruth replied, Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me. We hear this as Ruth’s word to Naomi, not as a joke about in-laws, and not as a line we lift out of its story. Honor can cling with faith and kindness, even when the path is bitter.

Paul then brings the same honor down to ordinary family care: But if a widow has children or grandchildren, these should learn first of all to put their religion into practice by caring for their own family and so repaying their parents and grandparents, for this is pleasing to God. Leaving well does not mean neglecting a parent in need. Religion that stays only in words, and does not care for its own house, is not yet practiced.

In *Staying Married Is Not About Staying in Love*, on Genesis 2:18–25, John Piper treats leaving father and mother and being united as God’s design for a new one-flesh house. Today’s official text is Genesis 2:24, so we stay with that verse and do not take up the surrounding lines as today’s official word. In *Ruth: Sweet and Bitter Providence*, on Ruth 1, he lingers over Ruth’s clinging to Naomi and to Naomi’s God. Today’s official text is Ruth 1:16–17, so we stay with that vow of going, staying, and belonging. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is 1 Timothy 5:4, so the call to put religion into practice by caring for parents and grandparents is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to 1 Timothy. The BibleProject guides to Genesis and Ruth help us hear leaving and honoring as one holy work, not as a contest between a spouse and a parent.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Genesis 2:24 has, Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and cleave to his wife; and they shall become one flesh. Ruth 1:16–17 has, Do not press me to forsake you in turning back from following you; for where you go, I will go, and where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God, my God. Thus may Yahweh do to me, and more, if anything but death separates you and me. 1 Timothy 5:4 has, they must first learn to practice piety in regard to their own family and to make some return to their parents; for this is acceptable in the sight of God.

A man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh. Honor can still go with a mother-in-law, and care can still repay a parent. Leave well. Honor well. This is pleasing to God.

**Genesis 2:24 (NIV)**
24 That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.

**Ruth 1:16–17 (NIV)**
16 But Ruth replied, “Don’t urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God. 17 Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.”

**1 Timothy 5:4 (NIV)**
4 But if a widow has children or grandchildren, these should learn first of all to put their religion into practice by caring for their own family and so repaying their parents and grandparents, for this is pleasing to God.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where does leaving well still need to become a clearer first loyalty in your house, and where does honor toward a parent or in-law still need to be practiced? What would it look like today to be united, and also to care in a way that pleases God?

lessons.title: Joy, friendship, and laughing together
lessons.body:
**Lesson 284: Joy, friendship, and laughing together**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and that honor toward a family can still be practiced with care. Today the house is invited into joy. Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor: If either of them falls down, one can help the other up. But pity anyone who falls and has no one to help them up. Also, if two lie down together, they will keep warm. But how can one keep warm alone? Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken.

Friendship in a marriage is not an extra, added after the work is done. It is one of the gifts of being two: help when one falls, warmth, and a strength that is not quickly broken. We hear two lie down together simply, as the Teacher’s picture of comfort, not as a scene to linger on. The cord of three strands is a mercy. A couple is not left to hold themselves together alone.

A cheerful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones. We hear this with care. A cheerful heart is a gift, and laughter in a house can be good medicine. A crushed spirit is not a joke, and it is not a failure to laugh on command. The proverb tells the truth about both: joy can strengthen, and a crushed spirit is heavy in the body too.

The Song then names a holy friendship at the heart of love: His mouth is sweetness itself; he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem. We stay with this verse. Beloved and friend belong together. Desire is not taught here as a spectacle. The gift is that the one you love can also be named as friend.

lessons.title: Love never fails

sources.label: John Piper, A Call to Love — and to Death (Desiring God)
John Piper, When Will Prophecy Cease? (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 285: Love never fails**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that two are better than one, that a cheerful heart is good medicine, and that the beloved can also be named as friend. Today Paul sets love over every gift. If I speak in the tongues of men or of angels, but do not have love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have a faith that can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. If I give all I possess to the poor and give over my body to hardship that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing. Great gifts, even costly ones, are empty without love. We hear the hardship simply, not as a spectacle.

Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres. Love never fails. We have already heard the middle of this chapter in a hard season of marriage. We hear it again now as the whole way of love, and as the word that does not fail.

But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be stilled; where there is knowledge, it will pass away. For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when completeness comes, what is in part disappears. When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I put the ways of childhood behind me. For now we see only a reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love. What is partial will pass. Love remains. In a marriage, this is not a slogan. It is the greatest thing that can hold a house when gifts and seasons change.

In *A Call to Love — and to Death*, on 1 Corinthians 13:4–7, John Piper treats this love as more than a feeling: it is patient and kind, it keeps no record of wrongs, and it perseveres. In *When Will Prophecy Cease?*, on 1 Corinthians 13:8–14:5, he lingers over love that never fails, and over the day when what is in part will pass away. Today’s official text is 1 Corinthians 13:1–13, so we stay inside that chapter and do not take up the next chapter as today’s official word. The opening verses, about tongues, knowledge, and costly gifts that gain nothing without love, are taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to 1 Corinthians. The greatest of these is love.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 1 Corinthians 13:1 has, I have become a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. 1 Corinthians 13:3 has, And if I give all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I surrender my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing. 1 Corinthians 13:7–8 has, it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails. 1 Corinthians 13:10 has, but when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away. 1 Corinthians 13:12–13 has, For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. But now abide faith, hope, love—these three; but the greatest of these is love.

Without love, even the greatest gift is nothing. Love is patient and kind, and it never fails. Faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love.

**1 Corinthians 13:1–13 (NIV)**
1 If I speak in the tongues of men or of angels, but do not have love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have a faith that can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. 3 If I give all I possess to the poor and give over my body to hardship that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing. 4 Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5 It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. 6 Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. 7 It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres. 8 Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be stilled; where there is knowledge, it will pass away. 9 For we know in part and we prophesy in part, 10 but when completeness comes, what is in part disappears. 11 When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I put the ways of childhood behind me. 12 For now we see only a reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. 13 And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where have gifts, knowledge, or even costly sacrifice been easier to offer than patience and kindness? What would it look like today to let love be the greatest thing in your house, the kind that keeps no record of wrongs and never fails?

lessons.title: A lifetime of cherishing
lessons.body:
**Lesson 286: A lifetime of cherishing**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that love never fails, and that the greatest of these is love. Today the word turns to a lifetime of cherishing. May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth. A loving doe, a graceful deer— may her breasts satisfy you always, may you ever be intoxicated with her love. We hear this with dignity, not as a spectacle and not as a set of instructions. The call is to rejoice in the wife of your youth, and to be gladly held by her love, all the years you are given.

The Teacher says the same in another key: Enjoy life with your wife, whom you love, all the days of this meaningless life that God has given you under the sun—all your meaningless days. For this is your lot in life and in your toilsome labor under the sun. Meaningless here is the Teacher’s honest word about life under the sun, not a command to despair, and not a dismissal of the wife you love. The days are given by God. The lot includes toil. And in those days, enjoy life with your wife, whom you love. Cherishing is not only for a young beginning. It is for all the days.

A lifetime of cherishing will have ordinary mornings, hard seasons, and bodies that change. The proverb still says, may you rejoice, and may you ever be intoxicated with her love. The Teacher still says, enjoy life with your wife, whom you love. The work is to keep delight at home, with honor, over a long life.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 5:18–19 or Ecclesiastes 9:9, so today’s word is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. Rejoice in the wife of your youth. Enjoy life with your wife, whom you love, all the days God has given under the sun. Cherishing is a long faithfulness, not a brief feeling.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 5:18–19 has, Let your fountain be blessed, And be glad in the wife of your youth. As a loving hind and a graceful doe, Let her breasts satisfy you at all times; Be intoxicated always with her love. Ecclesiastes 9:9 has, See life with the woman whom you love all the days of your vain life, which He has given to you under the sun—all the days of your vanity; for this is your portion in life and in your labor in which you have labored under the sun.

Rejoice in the wife of your youth. Be intoxicated with her love. Enjoy life with your wife, whom you love, all the days God has given you under the sun. Cherish her for a lifetime.

**Proverbs 5:18–19 (NIV)**
18 May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth. 19 A loving doe, a graceful deer— may her breasts satisfy you always, may you ever be intoxicated with her love.

**Ecclesiastes 9:9 (NIV)**
9 Enjoy life with your wife, whom you love, all the days of this meaningless life that God has given you under the sun—all your meaningless days. For this is your lot in life and in your toilsome labor under the sun.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has cherishing become ordinary duty, and lost its gladness? What would it look like today to rejoice in the one you married, and to enjoy life together in the days God has given?

lessons.title: When you disagree: unity without erasing each other

sources.label: John Piper, The Mind of Christ: Looking Out for the Interests of Others (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 287: When you disagree: unity without erasing each other**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard a lifetime of cherishing: rejoice in the wife of your youth, and enjoy life with your wife, whom you love, all the days God has given. Today the house is taught how to disagree without erasing one another. Let us therefore make every effort to do what leads to peace and to mutual edification. Effort is the word. Peace does not fall on a hard conversation by accident. Mutual edification means we aim to build one another up, not to win. A disagreement can be real. The other person must still be a person we are trying to build, not a problem we are trying to erase.

Paul then gives the manner: then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind. Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves, not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others. Today’s official word begins here, with that then, and we do not take up the verses around it as today’s official text. Like-minded is not the erasing of every difference. It is the same love, one in spirit, without selfish ambition. You can disagree and still value the other above yourself. You can keep your mind, and still look to the interests of the other.

Unity in a marriage is holy work. It is not sameness for its own sake, and it is not a contest in which one voice disappears. Make every effort toward peace and mutual edification. Have the same love. In humility, look to the other’s interests as well as your own.

In *The Mind of Christ: Looking Out for the Interests of Others*, on Philippians 2, John Piper lingers over the humility that values others and looks to their interests, the shared mind that is not selfish ambition. Today’s official text is Philippians 2:2–4, so we stay inside that range. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Romans 14:19, so the call to make every effort to do what leads to peace and to mutual edification is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Romans. The BibleProject guide to Philippians helps us hear unity as the gospel’s ordinary posture, not as a tool for winning the argument.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Romans 14:19 has, So then let us pursue the things which make for peace and the building up of one another. Philippians 2:2 has, fulfill my joy, that you think the same way, by maintaining the same love, being united in spirit, thinking on one purpose. Philippians 2:3–4 has, doing nothing from selfish ambition or vain glory, but with humility of mind regarding one another as more important than yourselves, not merely looking out for your own personal interests, but also for the interests of others.

Make every effort to do what leads to peace and to mutual edification. Be like-minded, having the same love. In humility value others above yourselves, and look to the interests of the other. You can disagree without erasing one another.

**Romans 14:19 (NIV)**
19 Let us therefore make every effort to do what leads to peace and to mutual edification.

**Philippians 2:2–4 (NIV)**
2 then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind. 3 Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves, 4 not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a disagreement in your house aimed at winning, rather than at peace and mutual edification? What would it look like today to keep the same love, to value the other above yourself, and to look to their interests as well as your own?

Unity in a marriage is holy work. It is not sameness for its own sake, and it is not a contest in which one voice disappears. Make every effort toward peace and mutual edification. Have the same love. In humility, look to the other’s interests as well as your own.

Today’s official text is Philippians 2:2–4, so we stay inside that range. Philippians 2:2 has, fulfill my joy, that you think the same way, by maintaining the same love, being united in spirit, thinking on one purpose. Philippians 2:3–4 has, doing nothing from selfish ambition or vain glory, but with humility of mind regarding one another as more important than yourselves, not merely looking out for your own personal interests, but also for the interests of others.

19 Let us therefore make every effort to do what leads to peace and to mutual edification.

**Philippians 2:2–4 (NIV)**
2 then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind. 3 Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves, 4 not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others.

lessons.body:
**Lesson 288: A charge to husbands and wives**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard how to disagree without erasing one another, making every effort toward peace and mutual edification. Today the marriage series comes to a charge for the house. Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything. This is not a license to dominate, and it is not a joke. Mutual honor stands at the front of the charge, and the wife’s submission is as to the Lord, not a replacing of the Lord.

Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other blemish, but holy and blameless. In this same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. After all, no one ever hated their own body, but they feed and care for their body, just as Christ does the church—for we are members of his body. The husband’s charge is not a right to command for himself. It is a call to give himself up, as Christ did, and to feed and care as Christ does the church.

“For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” This is a profound mystery—but I am talking about Christ and the church. However, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband. The one-flesh union points beyond itself to Christ and the church, and then comes back to the house: love, and respect.

Peter gives the same holy order another way. Wives, in the same way submit yourselves to your own husbands so that, if any of them do not believe the word, they may be won over without words by the behavior of their wives, when they see the purity and reverence of your lives. Without words is not a muzzle. It is the power of a holy life, especially where a husband does not yet believe. Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles and the wearing of gold jewelry or fine clothes. Rather, it should be that of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God’s sight. We do not turn this into a rule about jewelry or a slight toward a woman’s voice. The unfading beauty is a gentle and quiet spirit, of great worth in God’s sight. For this is the way the holy women of the past who put their hope in God used to adorn themselves. They submitted themselves to their own husbands, like Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him her lord. You are her daughters if you do what is right and do not give way to fear. We hear Sarah’s word as the text’s example of hope in God, not as a demand that a wife take up that title. The end of the charge is courage: do what is right, and do not give way to fear.

Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers. Weaker partner is not a slur, and it is not a license to rule a wife as less. She is an heir with you of the gracious gift of life. Consideration and respect belong to that shared gift. If they are withheld, prayers in the house can be hindered.

In *Husbands Who Love Like Christ and the Wives Who Submit to Them*, on Ephesians 5:21–33 and 1 Peter 3:1–7, John Piper treats headship as a husband’s responsibility to love like Christ, and submission as a wife’s honor that does not put a husband in the place of Christ, and does not follow him into sin. In *Lionhearted and Lamblike: The Christian Husband as Head, Part 1*, on Ephesians 5:21–33, he lingers over a husband’s call to nourish and cherish, not to control. In *Honor, Guard, and Cherish*, on 1 Peter 3:7, he treats a wife as a fellow heir of the grace of life, to be honored so that prayers are not hindered. The BibleProject guides to Ephesians and 1 Peter help us hear this charge as the gospel’s work in a house, not as a tool for winning.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Ephesians 5:21 has, and being subject to one another in the fear of Christ. Ephesians 5:29 has, for no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the church. Ephesians 5:32 has, This mystery is great, but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the church. 1 Peter 3:4 has, but let it be the hidden person of the heart, with the incorruptible quality of a lowly and quiet spirit, which is precious in the sight of God. 1 Peter 3:6–7 has, just as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You have become her children if you do good, not fearing any intimidation. You husbands in the same way, live with your wives in an understanding way, as with a weaker vessel, since she is a woman; and show her honor as a fellow heir of the grace of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.

Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. The wife must respect her husband. Live as heirs together of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

**Ephesians 5:21–33 (NIV)**
21 Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. 22 Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord. 23 For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, his body, of which he is the Savior. 24 Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything. 25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her 26 to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, 27 and to present her to himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any other blemish, but holy and blameless. 28 In this same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. 29 After all, no one ever hated their own body, but they feed and care for their body, just as Christ does the church— 30 for we are members of his body. 31 “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” 32 This is a profound mystery—but I am talking about Christ and the church. 33 However, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

**1 Peter 3:1–7 (NIV)**
1 Wives, in the same way submit yourselves to your own husbands so that, if any of them do not believe the word, they may be won over without words by the behavior of their wives, 2 when they see the purity and reverence of your lives. 3 Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles and the wearing of gold jewelry or fine clothes. 4 Rather, it should be that of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God’s sight. 5 For this is the way the holy women of the past who put their hope in God used to adorn themselves. They submitted themselves to their own husbands, 6 like Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him her lord. You are her daughters if you do what is right and do not give way to fear. 7 Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has this charge been easier to require of the other than to take up yourself—love that gives itself up, or honor that does not give way to fear? What would it look like today to live this word with reverence for Christ?

lessons.title: Teach your children diligently
lessons.body:
**Lesson 289: Teach your children diligently**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the marriage series ended with a charge to husbands and wives: love as Christ loved the church, and honor one another as heirs of the gracious gift of life. Today the word turns to the children in the house. Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. Love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. The first work is not a technique for parenting. It is to love the LORD who is one, with all that we are.

These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates. Diligence here is ordinary and constant. The words must first be on your hearts, then impressed on your children, in the sitting, the walking, the lying down, and the getting up. Family teaching is not only a formal lesson. It is a life that talks of the LORD in the ordinary hours of a house.

We do not turn the symbols, the hands, the foreheads, and the doorframes into a costume. The point is that the commandment is kept close, where the family lives and goes out and comes in. A parent cannot hand this work off and still call it done. Impress them on your children is a charge to the house.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Deuteronomy 6:4–9, so today’s word is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Deuteronomy. The LORD our God, the LORD is one. Love him with all your heart, keep his commandments on your hearts, and impress them on your children in the ordinary walk of the day. This is how a house begins to teach diligently.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Deuteronomy 6:4–5 has, Hear, O Israel! Yahweh is our God, Yahweh is one! You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might. Deuteronomy 6:7 has, You shall teach them diligently to your sons and shall speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way and when you lie down and when you rise up. Deuteronomy 6:8–9 has, You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as phylacteries between your eyes. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.

The LORD our God, the LORD is one. Love him with all your heart. Keep these commandments on your hearts, and impress them on your children when you sit, walk, lie down, and get up. Teach them diligently, in ordinary time.

**Deuteronomy 6:4–9 (NIV)**
4 Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. 5 Love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. 6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 8 Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 9 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, are these commandments first on your own heart, or only a speech you hope your children will hear? What would it look like today to talk of the LORD in an ordinary moment—at the table, on the road, at bedtime, or in the morning?
