lessons.title: Fathers, do not exasperate; bring them up in the Lord

sources.label: John Piper, Fathers Who Give Hope (Desiring God)
John Piper, Fathers, Bring Them Up in the Discipline & Instruction of the Lord (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 290: Fathers, do not exasperate; bring them up in the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the LORD is one, and that his commandments are to be on our hearts and impressed on our children in the ordinary hours of the day. Today the word comes to fathers in a shorter, sharper line. Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. The charge is double: do not exasperate, and do bring them up in the Lord. A father can be busy with rules and still leave a child raw. The training that is needed is the Lord’s, not a father’s raw will.

Paul says it again in another letter: Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged. Embitter and exasperate name a real wound. A child can be crossed in love, for a holy reason, and still be brought up in hope. A child can also be worn down by pettiness, by harshness, or by a father’s empty anger, until the heart loses heart. We hear this pastorally, not as a license for a child to rule the house, and not as a shame for a father who is already trying to be gentle. The warning is serious. Discouragement is a fruit we are told not to grow.

The text addresses fathers. A mother is not excluded from refusing to embitter a child, and she shares the work of bringing them up. Paul still names fathers here, and the house should hear that leading charge without using it to erase a mother’s wisdom, or to excuse a father from the work.

In *Fathers Who Give Hope*, on Colossians 3:21, John Piper treats a father’s power to discourage, and the call not to embitter children so that they do not lose heart. In *Fathers, Bring Them Up in the Discipline & Instruction of the Lord*, on Ephesians 6:1–4, he lingers over the second half of the charge: bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord, not merely in a father’s preferences. Today’s official text is Ephesians 6:4 and Colossians 3:21, so we stay with those verses and do not take up the surrounding lines as today’s official word. The BibleProject guides to Ephesians and Colossians help us hear this as the gospel’s way with children in the house, not as a method for control.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Ephesians 6:4 has, Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Colossians 3:21 has, Fathers, do not exasperate your children, so that they will not lose heart.

Do not exasperate your children. Do not embitter them, or they will become discouraged. Bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

**Ephesians 6:4 (NIV)**
4 Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

**Colossians 3:21 (NIV)**
21 Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a word or a rule in your house been more likely to embitter than to bring a child up in the Lord? What would it look like today to correct without exasperating, and to train with the Lord’s instruction rather than with mere frustration?

lessons.body:
**Lesson 290: Fathers, do not exasperate; bring them up in the Lord**

Good morning. Yesterday we heard that the LORD is one, and that his commandments are to be on our hearts and impressed on our children in the ordinary hours of the day. Today the word comes to fathers in a shorter, sharper line. Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. The charge is double: do not exasperate, and do bring them up in the Lord. A father can be busy with rules and still leave a child raw. The training that is needed is the Lord’s, not a father’s raw will.

Paul says it again in another letter: Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged. Embitter and exasperate name a real wound. A child can be crossed in love, for a holy reason, and still be brought up in hope. A child can also be worn down by pettiness, by harshness, or by a father’s empty anger, until the heart loses heart. We hear this pastorally, not as a license for a child to rule the house, and not as a shame for a father who is already trying to be gentle. The warning is serious. Discouragement is a fruit we are told not to grow.

The text addresses fathers. A mother is not excluded from refusing to embitter a child, and she shares the work of bringing them up. Paul still names fathers here, and the house should hear that leading charge without using it to erase a mother’s wisdom, or to excuse a father from the work.

In *Fathers Who Give Hope*, on Colossians 3:21, John Piper treats a father’s power to discourage, and the call not to embitter children so that they do not lose heart. In *Fathers, Bring Them Up in the Discipline & Instruction of the Lord*, on Ephesians 6:1–4, he lingers over the second half of the charge: bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord, not merely in a father’s preferences. Today’s official text is Ephesians 6:4 and Colossians 3:21, so we stay with those verses and do not take up the surrounding lines as today’s official word. The BibleProject guides to Ephesians and Colossians help us hear this as the gospel’s way with children in the house, not as a method for control.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Ephesians 6:4 has, Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Colossians 3:21 has, Fathers, do not exasperate your children, so that they will not lose heart.

Do not exasperate your children. Do not embitter them, or they will become discouraged. Bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

**Ephesians 6:4 (NIV)**
4 Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

**Colossians 3:21 (NIV)**
21 Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged.

**For reflection.** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where has a word or a rule in your house been more likely to embitter than to bring a child up in the Lord? What would it look like today to correct without exasperating, and to train with the Lord’s instruction rather than with mere frustration?

lessons.title: Children, honor your father and mother

sources.label: John Piper, Marriage Is Meant for Making Children . . . Disciples of Jesus, Part 2 (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 291: Children, honor your father and mother**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday fathers were told not to exasperate their children, but to bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. Today the children are addressed, and the house is told to hear the fifth commandment again. Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you. Honor is a holy weight. It is not flattery, and it is not a child’s job to pretend a parent has not sinned. It is the honor due to father and mother in the land the LORD gives.

Paul takes the commandment into the church’s house: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. “Honor your father and mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise— “so that it may go well with you and that you may enjoy long life on the earth.” Obey your parents in the Lord names both the duty and the limit. In the Lord is not a small phrase. A child is not being told to follow a parent into sin. The command is still a real command, and it is the first commandment with a promise: that it may go well with you, and that you may enjoy long life on the earth.

This is an adult lesson, and the word is still for the children in the house. Parents receive it first as a charge to teach, to live honorably, and not to make honor harder than it already is. A father who will not exasperate, and a mother who honors her own parents, make this commandment more than a speech. The promise is God’s. The honor is the child’s. The atmosphere of the house is ours to tend.

In *Marriage Is Meant for Making Children . . . Disciples of Jesus, Part 2*, on Ephesians 6:1–4, John Piper treats the command to children as a real obedience in the Lord, and the honor of father and mother as the first commandment with a promise. Today’s official text is Exodus 20:12 and Ephesians 6:1–3, so we stay inside that range and do not take up Ephesians 6:4 as today’s official word. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Exodus 20:12, so the fifth commandment is taught from the text itself, from its use in Ephesians 6, and from the BibleProject guide to Exodus. The BibleProject guide to Ephesians helps us hear a household where honor and obedience belong in the Lord.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Exodus 20:12 has, Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be prolonged in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. Ephesians 6:2–3 has, Honor your father and mother (which is the first commandment with a promise), so that it may be well with you, and that you may live long in the land.

Honor your father and your mother. Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. It is the first commandment with a promise, that it may go well with you, and that you may enjoy long life on the earth.

**Exodus 20:12 (NIV)**
12 “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you.

**Ephesians 6:1–3 (NIV)**
1 Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2 “Honor your father and mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise— 3 “so that it may go well with you and that you may enjoy long life on the earth.”

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, how are you making it either easier or harder for a child to honor father and mother in your house? What would it look like today to teach this commandment, and to live in a way that is worthy of honor, in the Lord?

lessons.title: Children are a heritage from the Lord

sources.label: John Piper, Don’t Eat the Bread of Anxious Toil (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 292: Children are a heritage from the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard the fifth commandment: honor your father and your mother, and children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Today the psalms teach us how to receive the children themselves. Children are a heritage from the LORD, offspring a reward from him. Like arrows in the hands of a warrior are children born in one’s youth. Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. They will not be put to shame when they contend with their opponents in court. We hear this as a gift, not as a contest. A heritage is something received, not something a parent invented. A full quiver is named as a blessing, and we do not turn it into a score, or a shame for a house that has walked a harder road.

The next psalm sets the blessing in the fear of the LORD. Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in obedience to him. You will eat the fruit of your labor; blessings and prosperity will be yours. Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table. Yes, this will be the blessing for the man who fears the LORD. The vine and the olive shoots are a picture of a household at peace under the LORD’s fear, not a demand that a woman’s worth be measured by fruitfulness, and not a slight if a table has known grief. The blessing is for those who fear the LORD and walk in obedience to him. The table is a place of life he gives.

Children are a heritage from the LORD. The warrior’s arrows, the vine, and the olive shoots all say the same thing with care: the children in the house are not an interruption of the real work. They are a reward from him, to be received with honor and raised in his fear.

In *Don’t Eat the Bread of Anxious Toil*, on Psalm 127, John Piper treats children as a heritage from the Lord, a reward, not a reason for anxious toil. Today’s official text is Psalm 127:3–5, so we stay with those verses and do not take up the earlier lines as today’s official word. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Psalm 128:1–4, so the blessing of those who fear the LORD, the fruitful vine, and the olive shoots around the table are taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to the Psalms.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Psalm 127:3–5 has, Behold, children are an inheritance of Yahweh, The fruit of the womb is a reward. Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, So are the children of one’s youth. How blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them; They will not be ashamed When they speak with enemies in the gate. Psalm 128:1–3 has, How blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh, Who walks in His ways. Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine In the innermost parts of your house, Your children like olive plants All around your table.

Children are a heritage from the LORD, offspring a reward from him. Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in obedience to him. Around a table like that, a wife is honored, and children are received as olive shoots, a gift from his hand.

**Psalm 127:3–5 (NIV)**
3 Children are a heritage from the LORD, offspring a reward from him. 4 Like arrows in the hands of a warrior are children born in one’s youth. 5 Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. They will not be put to shame when they contend with their opponents in court.

**Psalm 128:1–4 (NIV)**
1 Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in obedience to him. 2 You will eat the fruit of your labor; blessings and prosperity will be yours. 3 Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table. 4 Yes, this will be the blessing for the man who fears the LORD.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, have the children in your house been received as a heritage from the LORD, or mainly as a load to manage? What would it look like today to fear the LORD at the table, and to treat the children around it as a reward from him?

lessons.title: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord
lessons.body:
**Lesson 293: As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that children are a heritage from the LORD, and that the blessing of a house is for those who fear him. Today Joshua puts a choice before a whole household. Now fear the LORD and serve him with all faithfulness. Throw away the gods your ancestors worshiped beyond the Euphrates River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD. Fear and service go together. Faithfulness is not a mood. It includes a real throwing away of other gods, the ones a family can inherit without noticing.

But if serving the LORD seems undesirable to you, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your ancestors served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are living. But as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD. Joshua does not pretend the choice is unreal. Serving the LORD may seem undesirable. Other gods are named, old ones and near ones. Then he speaks for his house: as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD. A parent cannot believe for a child, and a child cannot make this choice for a father. Still, a house can be pointed, clearly, toward the LORD, and led there in the open.

This is not a slogan to hang and forget. Choose this day is a present word. The gods of a land can be quiet and respectable. The charge is to fear the LORD, serve him with all faithfulness, and let the household hear where the parents intend to stand.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Joshua 24:14–15, so today’s word is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Joshua. Fear the LORD and serve him with all faithfulness. Choose this day whom you will serve. As for me and my household, we will serve the LORD. That is a word for a house, spoken in the open, against every other god.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Joshua 24:14 has, So now, fear Yahweh and serve Him in integrity and truth; and put away the gods which your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve Yahweh. Joshua 24:15 has, If it is evil in your sight to serve Yahweh, choose for yourselves today whom you will serve; but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.

Fear the LORD and serve him with all faithfulness. Throw away the other gods. Choose this day whom you will serve. As for me and my household, we will serve the LORD.

**Joshua 24:14–15 (NIV)**
14 “Now fear the LORD and serve him with all faithfulness. Throw away the gods your ancestors worshiped beyond the Euphrates River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD. 15 But if serving the LORD seems undesirable to you, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your ancestors served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are living. But as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD.”

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, if your household heard you speak Joshua’s line today, would it match the way you actually spend a day? What would it look like to choose, this day, to serve the LORD with all faithfulness, and to throw away a quieter god that has had a place in the house?

lessons.title: Family worship in ordinary time

sources.label: John Piper, Educating for Hope (Desiring God)
John Piper, Raising Children Who Are Confident in God (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 294: Family worship in ordinary time**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Joshua said, as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD. Today that choice comes down to ordinary time: the words on the heart, and the story told to the next generation. These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates. We heard this charge earlier in the week, with the Shema around it. Today we stay with the ordinary practice itself. Family worship is not only a formal hour. It is the commandments on the heart, spoken in the sitting, the walking, the lying down, and the getting up.

The psalm shows why the telling matters. My people, hear my teaching; listen to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth with a parable; I will utter hidden things, things from of old— things we have heard and known, things our ancestors have told us. We will not hide them from their descendants; we will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done. He decreed statutes for Jacob and established the law in Israel, which he commanded our ancestors to teach their children, so the next generation would know them, even the children yet to be born, and they in turn would tell their children. Then they would put their trust in God and would not forget his deeds but would keep his commands. They would not be like their ancestors— a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose hearts were not loyal to God, whose spirits were not faithful to him.

The aim is not a perfect performance at a family altar. The aim is that the next generation would put their trust in God, remember his deeds, and keep his commands. Hide nothing that should be told. Tell the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD in ordinary time, so that the children yet to be born may hear, and tell their children in turn.

In *Educating for Hope* and in *Raising Children Who Are Confident in God*, on Psalm 78:1–8, John Piper treats the psalm as a charge to tell the next generation the deeds of the Lord, so that they would set their hope in God and not forget his works. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Deuteronomy 6:6–9, so the ordinary practice—commandments on the heart, impressed on the children in the sitting and the walking—is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Deuteronomy, as we also heard it earlier this week. The BibleProject guide to the Psalms helps us hear family worship as a telling that aims at trust, not as a mere routine.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Deuteronomy 6:6–7 has, These words, which I am commanding you today, shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your sons and shall speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way and when you lie down and when you rise up. Psalm 78:4 has, We will not conceal them from their children, But recount to the generation to come the praises of Yahweh, And His strength and His wondrous deeds that He has done. Psalm 78:7–8 has, That they should set their confidence in God And not forget the deeds of God, But observe His commandments, And not be like their fathers, A stubborn and rebellious generation, A generation that did not prepare its heart And whose spirit was not faithful to God.

Let the commandments be on your hearts, and impress them on your children in ordinary time. Tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, so they would put their trust in God, and not forget his deeds.

**Deuteronomy 6:6–9 (NIV)**
6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. lessons.title: Discipline that loves, not that crushes

sources.label: John Piper, The Painful Discipline of Our Heavenly Father (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 295: Discipline that loves, not that crushes**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that family worship belongs in ordinary time: the commandments on the heart, and the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD told to the next generation. Today the word turns to discipline that loves, and does not crush. Whoever spares the rod hates their children, but the one who loves their children is careful to discipline them. The rod here is not a license to harm, and it is not a how-to we will linger on. The proverb’s contrast is hate and love. Love is careful. A parent who will not correct at all is not called kind in this verse. A parent who crushes is not called careful. The one who loves is careful to discipline.

Hebrews takes us into the Father’s own way with his children. And have you completely forgotten this word of encouragement that addresses you as a father addresses his son? It says, “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, and do not lose heart when he rebukes you, because the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he chastens everyone he accepts as his son.” We hear chasten as the text’s hard word for a Father’s serious correction, not as a scene to describe. The Lord disciplines the one he loves. Discipline is not the opposite of love. It is one of love’s forms.

Endure hardship as discipline; God is treating you as his children. For what children are not disciplined by their father? If you are not disciplined—and everyone undergoes discipline—then you are not legitimate, not true sons and daughters at all. We hear this pastorally, not as a slight against a child, and not as a threat to a tender conscience. The writer’s point is belonging: the Father does not leave his children without training. Moreover, we have all had human fathers who disciplined us and we respected them for it. How much more should we submit to the Father of spirits and live! They disciplined us for a little while as they thought best; but God disciplines us for our good, in order that we may share in his holiness. No discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it.

Painful is honest. Crushing is not the aim. The harvest is righteousness and peace, for those who have been trained by it. A house that loves a child will be careful to discipline, and will refuse to make light of the Lord’s own discipline, and will refuse to lose heart.

In *The Painful Discipline of Our Heavenly Father*, on Hebrews 12:3–11, John Piper treats the Lord’s discipline as the love of a Father, not as an accident, and as training that later yields a harvest of righteousness and peace. Today’s official text is Hebrews 12:5–11, so we stay inside that range and do not take up the earlier verses as today’s official word. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 13:24, so the careful love that disciplines, and does not spare the child by refusing to correct, is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Proverbs. The BibleProject guide to Hebrews helps us hear a Father who disciplines for our good, that we may share in his holiness, not a Father who crushes.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 13:24 has, He who holds back his rod hates his son, But he who loves him disciplines him diligently. Hebrews 12:5–6 has, My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the LORD, Nor faint when you are reproved by Him; For those whom the Lord loves He disciplines, And He flogs every son whom He receives. Hebrews 12:11 has, And all discipline for the moment seems not to be joyful, but sorrowful, but to those who have been trained by it, afterwards it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

The one who loves their children is careful to discipline them. The Lord disciplines the one he loves. No discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful. Later on it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace. Love corrects. Love does not crush.

**Proverbs 13:24 (NIV)**
24 Whoever spares the rod hates their children, but the one who loves their children is careful to discipline them.

**Hebrews 12:5–11 (NIV)**
5 And have you completely forgotten this word of encouragement that addresses you as a father addresses his son? It says, “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, and do not lose heart when he rebukes you, 6 because the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he chastens everyone he accepts as his son.” 7 Endure hardship as discipline; God is treating you as his children. For what children are not disciplined by their father? 8 If you are not disciplined—and everyone undergoes discipline—then you are not legitimate, not true sons and daughters at all. 9 Moreover, we have all had human fathers who disciplined us and we respected them for it. How much more should we submit to the Father of spirits and live! 10 They disciplined us for a little while as they thought best; but God disciplines us for our good, in order that we may share in his holiness. 11 No discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has discipline in your house been either spared out of weariness, or made harsher than love? What would it look like today to be careful, to correct without crushing, and to trust the Father who disciplines the one he loves?

lessons.title: Train a child in the way they should go
lessons.body:
**Lesson 296: Train a child in the way they should go**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the one who loves their children is careful to discipline them, and that the Lord disciplines the one he loves, for a harvest of righteousness and peace. Today the word turns to the long path of a child’s way. Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it. This is the proverb’s ordinary wisdom, not a guarantee we can use to crush a parent whose child has wandered, and not a reason to grow careless. Starting a child off is real work. The way they should go is the LORD’s way, not merely a family style. We plant, we pray, and we leave the years in God’s hands.

Moses then shows what that starting looks like in a house. Fix these words of mine in your hearts and minds; tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. Teach them to your children, talking about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates, so that your days and the days of your children may be many in the land the LORD swore to give your ancestors, as many as the days that the heavens are above the earth. We heard a word like this earlier, in Deuteronomy 6. Today the charge comes again, with a promise of days in the land. The words must first be fixed in the parents’ hearts and minds. Then they are taught in the sitting, the walking, the lying down, and the getting up. Training a child is not only a formal hour. It is a life soaked in the LORD’s words, aimed at the long years.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 22:6 or Deuteronomy 11:18–21, so today’s word is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Proverbs and Deuteronomy. Start children off on the way they should go. Fix the LORD’s words in your hearts, and teach them to your children in the ordinary hours of the day, so that your days and their days may be many in the land the LORD swore to give.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 22:6 has, Train up a child according to his way, Even when he is old he will not depart from it. Deuteronomy 11:18–19 has, You shall therefore place these words of mine on your heart and on your soul; and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as phylacteries between your eyes. And you shall teach them to your sons, speaking of them when you sit in your house and when you walk along the road and when you lie down and when you rise up. Deuteronomy 11:21 has, so that your days and the days of your sons may be multiplied on the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens remain above the earth.

Start children off on the way they should go. Fix these words in your hearts and minds, and teach them when you sit, walk, lie down, and get up. The way is long. The LORD’s words are to be near, all the days.

**Proverbs 22:6 (NIV)**
6 Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.

**Deuteronomy 11:18–21 (NIV)**
18 Fix these words of mine in your hearts and minds; tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 19 Teach them to your children, talking about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 20 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates, 21 so that your days and the days of your children may be many in the land the LORD swore to give your ancestors, as many as the days that the heavens are above the earth.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, what “way” are you actually starting your children on in the ordinary hours of this week? What would it look like today to fix the LORD’s words in your own heart, and to talk of them when you sit or walk or lie down or get up?

lessons.body:
**Lesson 297: Tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we were told to start children off on the way they should go, and to teach the LORD’s words in the ordinary hours of the day. Today the charge is to tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD. We will not hide them from their descendants; we will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done. We heard the first lines of this psalm earlier in the week of ordinary worship. Today we stay with the telling itself, and with the aim of that telling.

He decreed statutes for Jacob and established the law in Israel, which he commanded our ancestors to teach their children, so the next generation would know them, even the children yet to be born, and they in turn would tell their children. Then they would put their trust in God and would not forget his deeds but would keep his commands. They would not be like their ancestors— a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose hearts were not loyal to God, whose spirits were not faithful to him. The aim is not a full head only. The aim is trust in God, memory of his deeds, and kept commands, so that the children yet to be born may tell their children in turn. A stubborn and rebellious generation is named as a warning, not as a sneer at the children in the house.

Joel makes the same chain short and clear: Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation. The story is not to stop with us. What God has done is to be told on, down the line.

In *Educating for Hope* and in *Raising Children Who Are Confident in God*, on Psalm 78:1–8, John Piper treats the psalm as a charge to tell the next generation the deeds of the Lord, so that they would set their hope in God and not forget his works. Today’s official text is Psalm 78:4–8, so we stay with those verses and do not take up the opening lines as today’s official word. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Joel 1:3, so the call to tell it to your children, and let them tell the next generation, is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Joel. The BibleProject guide to the Psalms helps us hear a telling that aims at trust, not at a mere performance of family memory.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Psalm 78:4 has, We will not conceal them from their children, But recount to the generation to come the praises of Yahweh, And His strength and His wondrous deeds that He has done. Psalm 78:7–8 has, That they should set their confidence in God And not forget the deeds of God, But observe His commandments, And not be like their fathers, A stubborn and rebellious generation, A generation that did not prepare its heart And whose spirit was not faithful to God. Joel 1:3 has, Recount about it to your sons, And let your sons recount about it to their sons, And their sons to the next generation.

We will not hide them. We will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done, so they would put their trust in God. Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to theirs.

**Psalm 78:4–8 (NIV)**
4 We will not hide them from their descendants; we will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done. 5 He decreed statutes for Jacob and established the law in Israel, which he commanded our ancestors to teach their children, 6 so the next generation would know them, even the children yet to be born, and they in turn would tell their children. 7 Then they would put their trust in God and would not forget his deeds but would keep his commands. 8 They would not be like their ancestors— a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose hearts were not loyal to God, whose spirits were not faithful to him.

**Joel 1:3 (NIV)**
3 Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, what praiseworthy deed of the LORD have your children actually heard from your mouth lately? What would it look like today to tell one wonder, so that it might be told again to the next generation?

sources.label: John Piper, Educating for Hope (Desiring God)
John Piper, Raising Children Who Are Confident in God (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 297: Tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the Lord**

Good morning. Yesterday we were told to start children off on the way they should go, and to teach the LORD’s words in the ordinary hours of the day. Today the charge is to tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD. We will not hide them from their descendants; we will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done. We heard the first lines of this psalm earlier in the week of ordinary worship. Today we stay with the telling itself, and with the aim of that telling.

He decreed statutes for Jacob and established the law in Israel, which he commanded our ancestors to teach their children, so the next generation would know them, even the children yet to be born, and they in turn would tell their children. Then they would put their trust in God and would not forget his deeds but would keep his commands. They would not be like their ancestors— a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose hearts were not loyal to God, whose spirits were not faithful to him. The aim is not a full head only. The aim is trust in God, memory of his deeds, and kept commands, so that the children yet to be born may tell their children in turn. A stubborn and rebellious generation is named as a warning, not as a sneer at the children in the house.

Joel makes the same chain short and clear: Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation. The story is not to stop with us. What God has done is to be told on, down the line.

In *Educating for Hope* and in *Raising Children Who Are Confident in God*, on Psalm 78:1–8, John Piper treats the psalm as a charge to tell the next generation the deeds of the Lord, so that they would set their hope in God and not forget his works. Today’s official text is Psalm 78:4–8, so we stay with those verses and do not take up the opening lines as today’s official word. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Joel 1:3, so the call to tell it to your children, and let them tell the next generation, is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Joel. The BibleProject guide to the Psalms helps us hear a telling that aims at trust, not at a mere performance of family memory.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Psalm 78:4 has, We will not conceal them from their children, But recount to the generation to come the praises of Yahweh, And His strength and His wondrous deeds that He has done. Psalm 78:7–8 has, That they should set their confidence in God And not forget the deeds of God, But observe His commandments, And not be like their fathers, A stubborn and rebellious generation, A generation that did not prepare its heart And whose spirit was not faithful to God. Joel 1:3 has, Recount about it to your sons, And let your sons recount about it to their sons, And their sons to the next generation.

We will not hide them. We will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done, so they would put their trust in God. Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to theirs.

**Psalm 78:4–8 (NIV)**
4 We will not hide them from their descendants; we will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, his power, and the wonders he has done. 5 He decreed statutes for Jacob and established the law in Israel, which he commanded our ancestors to teach their children, 6 so the next generation would know them, even the children yet to be born, and they in turn would tell their children. 7 Then they would put their trust in God and would not forget his deeds but would keep his commands. 8 They would not be like their ancestors— a stubborn and rebellious generation, whose hearts were not loyal to God, whose spirits were not faithful to him.

**Joel 1:3 (NIV)**
3 Tell it to your children, and let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation.

**For reflection.** As a woman, wife, and a mother, what praiseworthy deed of the LORD have your children actually heard from your mouth lately? What would it look like today to tell one wonder, so that it might be told again to the next generation?

lessons.title: Your example preaches louder than your rules
lessons.body:
**Lesson 298: Your example preaches louder than your rules**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we were told to tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the LORD, so they would put their trust in God. Today the word comes closer to the parent’s own life: your example preaches louder than your rules. Follow my example, as I follow the example of Christ. Paul does not offer himself as the end. He is worth following only as he follows Christ. A house can be full of good rules and still be thin if the parent’s life points another way. The first example in the room is not the child’s. It is ours, under Christ.

Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me—put it into practice. And the God of peace will be with you. Learned, received, heard, and seen: the whole of a life is in view, not only a lesson spoken once. What a child can put into practice is often what has been seen. The promise at the end is not a technique. The God of peace will be with you, where what has been received is actually practiced.

Moses had already warned the heart that forgets. Only be careful, and watch yourselves closely so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen or let them fade from your heart as long as you live. Teach them to your children and to their children after them. Watch yourselves. The things your eyes have seen must not fade from your heart. Teaching the children, and the children after them, is bound to a parent who still remembers. A faded heart will have a hard time leaving a living example.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is 1 Corinthians 11:1, Philippians 4:9, or Deuteronomy 4:9, so today’s word is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to 1 Corinthians, Philippians, and Deuteronomy. Follow my example, as I follow the example of Christ. Put into practice what has been learned and seen. Watch yourselves, so that what your eyes have seen does not fade from your heart, and teach it to your children and to their children after them.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 1 Corinthians 11:1 has, Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ. Philippians 4:9 has, The things you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you. Deuteronomy 4:9 has, Only keep yourself and keep your soul very carefully, lest you forget the things which your eyes have seen and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. But make them known to your sons and to your grandsons.

Follow my example, as I follow the example of Christ. Put into practice what has been learned and seen in me. Watch yourselves, and do not let what your eyes have seen fade from your heart. Teach it to your children, and to their children after them.

**1 Corinthians 11:1 (NIV)**
1 Follow my example, as I follow the example of Christ.

**Philippians 4:9 (NIV)**
9 Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me—put it into practice. And the God of peace will be with you.

**Deuteronomy 4:9 (NIV)**
9 Only be careful, and watch yourselves closely so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen or let them fade from your heart as long as you live. Teach them to your children and to their children after them.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, if your children put into practice only what they have seen in you this week, what would they be practicing? What would it look like today to follow Christ’s example in one visible way, and to keep what you have seen from fading out of your heart?

lessons.title: Patience with little hearts

sources.label: John Piper, We Were Eager to Share with You Our Own Souls (Desiring God)
John Piper, On Sharing Your Own Soul (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 299: Patience with little hearts**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that a parent’s example preaches louder than rules: follow Christ, put into practice what has been seen, and do not let the things you have seen fade from your heart. Today the word is patience with little hearts. Instead, we were like young children among you. Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, so we cared for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God but our lives as well. We hear the nursing mother simply, as a picture of gentle, costly care, not as a scene to describe. Patience with little hearts looks like this: not only words about God, but a life shared, because they are dear.

Surely you remember, brothers and sisters, our toil and hardship; we worked night and day in order not to be a burden to anyone while we preached the gospel of God to you. You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous and blameless we were among you who believed. For you know that we dealt with each of you as a father deals with his own children, encouraging, comforting and urging you to live lives worthy of God, who calls you into his kingdom and glory. A father with his own children does not only lay down a law. He encourages, comforts, and urges, toward a life worthy of God. Little hearts need all three. Night-and-day work is honest. Patience is not laziness. It is care that stays, and a life that can be witnessed.

The same patience shows in another letter. And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, not resentful. Opponents must be gently instructed, in the hope that God will grant them repentance leading them to a knowledge of the truth. Today’s official word ends there. We do not take up the next line as today’s official text. A parent is not being told to treat a child as an enemy. We do hear the manner: not quarrelsome, kind, able to teach, not resentful, gently instructing, in the hope that God will grant what we cannot force. Patience with little hearts leaves room for God to work.

In *We Were Eager to Share with You Our Own Souls* and in *On Sharing Your Own Soul*, on 1 Thessalonians 2:1–12, John Piper lingers over a care like a nursing mother, and a father’s encouraging, comforting, and urging, and over a life shared with the gospel, not only spoken. Today’s official text is 1 Thessalonians 2:7–12, so we stay inside that range. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is 2 Timothy 2:24–25, so the Lord’s servant who is not quarrelsome, but kind, able to teach, and gentle, is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to 2 Timothy. The BibleProject guide to 1 Thessalonians helps us hear patience as a shared life, not as a thin niceness.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 1 Thessalonians 2:7–8 has, But we proved to be gentle among you, as a nursing mother tenderly cares for her own children. In this way, having fond affection for you, we were pleased to impart to you not only the gospel of God but also our own lives, because you had become beloved to us. 1 Thessalonians 2:11–12 has, just as you know how we were exhorting and encouraging and bearing witness to each one of you as a father would his own children, so that you would walk in a manner worthy of the God who calls you into His own kingdom and glory. 2 Timothy 2:24–25 has, And the Lord’s slave must not be quarrelsome, but be kind to all, able to teach, patient when wronged, with gentleness correcting those who are in opposition, if perhaps God may give them repentance leading to the full knowledge of the truth.

Care like a nursing mother, and deal with them as a father deals with his own children: encouraging, comforting, and urging them to live lives worthy of God. Be kind, able to teach, not resentful. Instruct gently, and hope in God.

**1 Thessalonians 2:7–12 (NIV)**
7 Instead, we were like young children among you. Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, 8 so we cared for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God but our lives as well. 9 Surely you remember, brothers and sisters, our toil and hardship; we worked night and day in order not to be a burden to anyone while we preached the gospel of God to you. 10 You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous and blameless we were among you who believed. 11 For you know that we dealt with each of you as a father deals with his own children, 12 encouraging, comforting and urging you to live lives worthy of God, who calls you into his kingdom and glory.

**2 Timothy 2:24–25 (NIV)**
24 And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, not resentful. 25 Opponents must be gently instructed, in the hope that God will grant them repentance leading them to a knowledge of the truth,

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a little heart in your house met a quarrelsome word more often than a shared life? What would it look like today to encourage, comfort, and urge, with kindness, and to share not only instruction but your life as well?

lessons.title: Let the little children come to me

sources.label: John Piper, God, Marriage and Children (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
**Lesson 300: Let the little children come to me**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard patience with little hearts: a shared life, a father’s encouraging and comforting, and a servant who is kind and not quarrelsome. Today Jesus himself meets the children. People were bringing little children to Jesus for him to place his hands on them, but the disciples rebuked them. When Jesus saw this, he was indignant. He said to them, “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you, anyone who will not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” And he took the children in his arms, placed his hands on them and blessed them.

The disciples rebuked the people who brought the children. Jesus was indignant. The children were not a interruption of the real work. He said to let them come, and not to hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. We hear the whole word together, through the warning that anyone who will not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it. A house can hinder children from Jesus without meaning to: by impatience, by unbelief, by making them wait until they seem more useful. The charge is to bring them, not to stand in the way.

And he took the children in his arms, placed his hands on them and blessed them. The blessing is not a vague kindness. It is Jesus’ own hands, his own arms, his own word over little lives. Parents and a church are not the Savior. We are the ones who must not hinder, and who must bring them to him.

In *God, Marriage and Children*, on Mark 10:1–16, John Piper treats the children brought to Jesus as more than a sweet scene: the kingdom belongs to such as these, and we must not hinder them. Today’s official text is Mark 10:13–16, so we stay with the children, the indignation, the invitation, and the blessing, and we do not take up the earlier verses as today’s official word. The BibleProject guide to Mark helps us hear Jesus’ arms as the place the little ones are welcomed, not as an afterthought in the gospel.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Mark 10:14–16 has, Permit the children to come to Me; do not hinder them; for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it at all. And He took them in His arms and began blessing them, laying His hands on them.

Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Anyone who will not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it. He took the children in his arms and blessed them.

**Mark 10:13–16 (NIV)**
13 People were bringing little children to Jesus for him to place his hands on them, but the disciples rebuked them. 14 When Jesus saw this, he was indignant. He said to them, “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. 15 Truly I tell you, anyone who will not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” 16 And he took the children in his arms, placed his hands on them and blessed them.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where might you be hindering a little child from coming to Jesus—by hurry, by unbelief, or by treating them as in the way? What would it look like today to bring them to him, and to receive the kingdom like a little child yourself?

lessons.title: A parent's prayer
lessons.body:
**Lesson 301: A parent's prayer**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Jesus said, Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, and he took them in his arms and blessed them. Today the week ends with a parent’s prayer. I prayed for this child, and the LORD has granted me what I asked of him. So now I give him to the LORD. For his whole life he will be given over to the LORD. And he worshiped the LORD there. We hear Hannah’s word as a prayer already answered, and as a life then given over to the LORD. We do not turn it into a demand that a parent leave a child at the church door. The child was asked of the LORD, granted by the LORD, and given back to the LORD, for his whole life. A parent’s prayer begins and ends there: this child is the LORD’s.

John’s short letter names the joy that prayer is aiming at. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth. Greater joy, he says, than this: not that the children are impressive, or easy, or successful in the usual ways, but that they are walking in the truth. A parent’s prayer can ask for many things. This is the joy worth naming first. Walking in the truth is a path, not a moment we can force. We pray, we give the child to the LORD, and we ask to hear, in time, that they are walking in the truth.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is 1 Samuel 1:27–28 or 3 John 1:4, so today’s word is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to 1 Samuel and 3 John. I prayed for this child, and the LORD has granted me what I asked of him. So now I give him to the LORD, for his whole life. And there is no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 1 Samuel 1:27–28 has, For this young boy I prayed, and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of Him. So I have also dedicated him to Yahweh; as long as he lives, he is dedicated to Yahweh. So he worshiped Yahweh there. 3 John 1:4 has, I have no greater joy than this, to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

I prayed for this child, and the LORD has granted me what I asked of him. So now I give him to the LORD, for his whole life. There is no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

**1 Samuel 1:27–28 (NIV)**
27 I prayed for this child, and the LORD has granted me what I asked of him. 28 So now I give him to the LORD. For his whole life he will be given over to the LORD.” And he worshiped the LORD there.

**3 John 1:4 (NIV)**
4 I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, have you actually given this child to the LORD in prayer, or mainly asked the LORD to give the child to you? What would it look like today to pray for them to walk in the truth, and to leave their whole life in the LORD’s hands?

lessons.title: When a child wanders: the Father who runs

sources.label: John Piper, Coming to Yourself and Coming to the Father (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard a parent's prayer: a child asked of the Lord, and given back to him, and no greater joy than to hear that children are walking in the truth. Today Jesus tells of a father who runs when a child wanders. Jesus continued: There was a man who had two sons. The younger one said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ So he divided his property between them. We say that simply. It is not a joke about a house, and it is not a scene to dress up. The son asked for the share, and the father gave it.

Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country and there squandered his wealth in wild living. After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs. He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything. We hear the need without lingering on the shame as a spectacle. Running from the father's house felt free for a while. It ended in hunger.

When he came to his senses, he said, How many of my father’s hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death! I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants. So he got up and went to his father. Coming to his senses is not a small thing. He tells the truth about the sin, and he goes home.

But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him. The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ But the father said to his servants, Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found. So they began to celebrate. Today's official word ends here. We do not take up the older brother as today's text. The father runs. Compassion reaches a long way off. The child who was lost is found, and the house celebrates.

In *Coming to Yourself and Coming to the Father*, on Luke 15:11–24, John Piper traces the son's misery, his coming to himself, and the father's lavish welcome—running, embracing, and celebrating a son who was lost and is found. The BibleProject guide to Luke helps us hear Jesus telling this story so that we would know the Father's joy when a wanderer comes home.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Luke 15:17 has, But when he came to himself, he said, How many of my father’s hired men have more than enough bread, but I am dying here with hunger! Luke 15:20 has, But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. Luke 15:24 has, for this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found. And they began to celebrate.

The father saw him while he was still a long way off, and was filled with compassion, and ran. A child may wander. The Father still runs. Come home is not a small word in this house, and celebration is not delayed until the child has earned it.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a child, or your own heart, wandered? What would it look like today to be the kind of parent who keeps watch a long way off, runs with compassion, and tells the truth about sin without closing the door of the house?

**Luke 15:11–24 (NIV)**
11 Jesus continued: “There was a man who had two sons. 12 The younger one said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ So he divided his property between them. 13 “Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country and there squandered his wealth in wild living. 14 After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need. 15 So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs. 16 He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything. 17 “When he came to his senses, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death! 18 I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19 I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.’ 20 So he got up and went to his father. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him. 21 “The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ 22 “But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’ So they began to celebrate.

lessons.title: Wisdom for daughters and sons

sources.label: John Piper, Do Not Forsake Your Mother's Teaching (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the Father ran to a child who had wandered, and the house began to celebrate. Today the word turns to wisdom for daughters and sons. Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction and do not forsake your mother’s teaching. They are a garland to grace your head and a chain to adorn your neck. Father and mother both teach. The instruction is not an extra. It is meant to grace a life.

Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction; pay attention and gain understanding. I give you sound learning, so do not forsake my teaching. For I too was a son to my father, still tender, and cherished by my mother. Then he taught me, and he said to me, Take hold of my words with all your heart; keep my commands, and you will live. Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget my words or turn away from them. Do not forsake wisdom, and she will protect you; love her, and she will watch over you. The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom. Though it cost all you have, get understanding. Cherish her, and she will exalt you; embrace her, and she will honor you. She will give you a garland to grace your head and present you with a glorious crown. Today's official word in this chapter ends at verse 9. We do not take up the later verses as today's text.

Wisdom is not a finishing school for manners only. Daughters and sons are called to take hold of the words, to get wisdom even when it costs, and not to forsake a mother's teaching or a father's instruction. A house that loves its children will teach, and will keep teaching, until wisdom is prized.

In *Do Not Forsake Your Mother's Teaching*, on Proverbs 1:7–9, John Piper treats the family as God's basic school, where a father's instruction and a mother's teaching belong together. Today's official text is Proverbs 1:8–9, so we stay inside that range and do not take up verse 7 as today's official word. In *Get Wisdom*, on Proverbs 4:1–13, he urges us to get wisdom and to prize it. Today's official text is Proverbs 4:1–9, so we do not take up the later verses as today's official word. The BibleProject guide to Proverbs helps us hear wisdom as a path to walk, not a slogan to post.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 1:8–9 has, Hear, my son, your father’s discipline And do not abandon your mother’s instruction; For they are a garland of grace for your head And ornaments about your neck. Proverbs 4:1 has, Hear, O sons, the discipline of a father, And pay attention that you may know understanding. Proverbs 4:7–8 has, The beginning of wisdom is : Acquire wisdom; And with all your acquiring, acquire understanding. Prize her, and she will exalt you; She will honor you if you embrace her.

Listen to a father's instruction. Do not forsake a mother's teaching. Get wisdom. Though it cost all you have, get understanding. That is a grace for a daughter's head and a son's, and it is work worth doing in an ordinary house.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has instruction been left to someone else, or wisdom treated as optional, in your house? What is one word you will take hold of with your children today, and one way you will refuse to forsake a father's or a mother's teaching?

**Proverbs 1:8–9 (NIV)**
8 Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction and do not forsake your mother’s teaching. 9 They are a garland to grace your head and a chain to adorn your neck.

**Proverbs 4:1–9 (NIV)**
1 Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction; pay attention and gain understanding. 2 I give you sound learning, so do not forsake my teaching. 3 For I too was a son to my father, still tender, and cherished by my mother. 4 Then he taught me, and he said to me, “Take hold of my words with all your heart; keep my commands, and you will live. 5 Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget my words or turn away from them. 6 Do not forsake wisdom, and she will protect you; love her, and she will watch over you. 7 The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom. Though it cost all you have, get understanding. 8 Cherish her, and she will exalt you; embrace her, and she will honor you. 9 She will give you a garland to grace your head and present you with a glorious crown.”

lessons.title: Protecting innocence, and preparing them for the world

sources.label: John Piper, ‘I Am Sending You Out as Sheep in the Midst of Wolves’ (Desiring God)
John Piper, Holding Fast the Word of Life (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard wisdom for daughters and sons: a father's instruction, a mother's teaching, and the call to get wisdom. Today the word turns to protecting innocence, and preparing them for the world. Jesus said, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. We hear both sides of the sentence. Shrewd is not sly harm. Innocent is not naivete that never notices danger. The sending is real, and the world is not safe in every place, and still Jesus does not tell his people to become wolves.

Today's official word in Matthew is this verse only. We do not take up the later costs as today's text. The point we keep is the pair: shrewd and innocent. A parent who only hides a child may forget that Jesus sends. A parent who only exposes a child may forget that he also says, be innocent as doves.

Paul writes, so that you may become blameless and pure, “children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation.” Then you will shine among them like stars in the sky. Today's official word here is this verse only, so we stay with it and do not take up the verses around it as today's official text. Blameless and pure is not a sneer at the world, and it is not a plan to shine by mocking it. The children of God live in a warped and crooked generation, and they shine among them.

Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it. The heart is not guarded by panic, and it is not guarded by pretending there is nothing to guard. Everything you do flows from it. Preparing a child for the world includes guarding what is loved, what is watched, and what is named as good, without turning the house into a scare, and without sending them out unprepared.

In *I Am Sending You Out as Sheep in the Midst of Wolves*, on Matthew 10:16–31, John Piper lingers on Jesus' sending, and on the call to be wise and innocent. Today's official text is Matthew 10:16 only, so we stay with that verse and do not take up the later costs as today's official word. He treats being sent by Christ as a blessing, even when the sending is into a hard world. *Holding Fast the Word of Life* is on Philippians 2:14–16; today's official text is Philippians 2:15, so we stay inside that verse. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 4:23, so the call to guard the heart is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Proverbs. The BibleProject guides to Matthew and Philippians help us hear a people sent into the world, shining among them, not becoming like the harm around them.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Matthew 10:16 has, Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves. Philippians 2:15 has, so that you will be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world. Proverbs 4:23 has, Guard your heart with all diligence, For from it flow the springs of life.

Be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. Become blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation, and shine among them like stars in the sky. Above all else, guard your heart. Protect innocence. Prepare them. Do not choose only one of those tasks.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where have you protected a child without preparing them, or prepared them without guarding what should stay innocent? What would shrewd and innocent look like in one ordinary choice this week?

**Matthew 10:16 (NIV)**
16 “I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.

lessons.title: Protecting innocence, and preparing them for the world

sources.label: John Piper, ‘I Am Sending You Out as Sheep in the Midst of Wolves’ (Desiring God)
John Piper, Holding Fast the Word of Life (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning. Yesterday we heard wisdom for daughters and sons: a father's instruction, a mother's teaching, and the call to get wisdom. Today the word turns to protecting innocence, and preparing them for the world. Jesus said, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. We hear both sides of the sentence. Shrewd is not sly harm. Innocent is not naivete that never notices danger. The sending is real, and the world is not safe in every place, and still Jesus does not tell his people to become wolves.

Today's official word in Matthew is this verse only. We do not take up the later costs as today's text. The point we keep is the pair: shrewd and innocent. A parent who only hides a child may forget that Jesus sends. A parent who only exposes a child may forget that he also says, be innocent as doves.

Paul writes, so that you may become blameless and pure, “children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation.” Then you will shine among them like stars in the sky. Today's official word here is this verse only, so we stay with it and do not take up the verses around it as today's official text. Blameless and pure is not a sneer at the world, and it is not a plan to shine by mocking it. The children of God live in a warped and crooked generation, and they shine among them.

Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it. The heart is not guarded by panic, and it is not guarded by pretending there is nothing to guard. Everything you do flows from it. Preparing a child for the world includes guarding what is loved, what is watched, and what is named as good, without turning the house into a scare, and without sending them out unprepared.

In *I Am Sending You Out as Sheep in the Midst of Wolves*, on Matthew 10:16–31, John Piper lingers on Jesus' sending, and on the call to be wise and innocent. Today's official text is Matthew 10:16 only, so we stay with that verse and do not take up the later costs as today's official word. He treats being sent by Christ as a blessing, even when the sending is into a hard world. *Holding Fast the Word of Life* is on Philippians 2:14–16; today's official text is Philippians 2:15, so we stay inside that verse. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 4:23, so the call to guard the heart is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guide to Proverbs. The BibleProject guides to Matthew and Philippians help us hear a people sent into the world, shining among them, not becoming like the harm around them.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Matthew 10:16 has, Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves. Philippians 2:15 has, so that you will be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world. Proverbs 4:23 has, Guard your heart with all diligence, For from it flow the springs of life.

Be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. Become blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation, and shine among them like stars in the sky. Above all else, guard your heart. Protect innocence. Prepare them. Do not choose only one of those tasks.

**For reflection.** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where have you protected a child without preparing them, or prepared them without guarding what should stay innocent? What would shrewd and innocent look like in one ordinary choice this week?

16 “I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.

**Philippians 2:15 (NIV)**
15 so that you may become blameless and pure, “children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation.” Then you will shine among them like stars in the sky

**Proverbs 4:23 (NIV)**
23 Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.

lessons.title: Justice, kindness, and humility at home
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard how to protect innocence and still prepare children for the world: shrewd and innocent, a guarded heart, shining like stars. Today the word comes home to justice, kindness, and humility under our own roof. He has shown you, O mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you? To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God. The requirement is not hidden. Justice, mercy, and a humble walk with God belong together. A house can love mercy in public and still be unfair in the hallway. The LORD has shown what is good, and he requires it here.

Therefore, as God’s chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which binds them all together in perfect unity. Today's official word in Colossians ends at verse 14. We do not take up the next verse as today's text.

Holy and dearly loved is the starting place, not a prize at the end of a well-run morning. Compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience are clothes for a family, not ornaments for company. Bearing with each other is honest about grievance. Forgiveness is as the Lord forgave you. Love binds them all together. Justice at home is not harshness with a Bible verse attached. Kindness is not the refusal to name what is wrong. Humility walks with God, and does not need to win every small dispute.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Micah 6:8 or Colossians 3:12–14, so justice, kindness, and humility at home are taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Micah and Colossians. Micah shows what the LORD requires. Colossians shows how a people holy and dearly loved put those things on, and put on love over them all.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Micah 6:8 has, He has told you, O man, what is good; And what does Yahweh require of you But to do justice, to love lovingkindness, And to walk humbly with your God? Colossians 3:12 has, So, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Colossians 3:13 has, bearing with one another, and graciously forgiving each other, whoever has a complaint against anyone, just as the Lord graciously forgave you, so also should you. Colossians 3:14 has, Above all these things put on love, which is the perfect bond of unity.

Act justly. Love mercy. Walk humbly with your God. Clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love. That is what is good, and it is required at home.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has your house been quicker to demand justice than to love mercy, or quicker to be kind than to be fair? What would it look like today to walk humbly with God in one grievance, and to put on love over the whole of it?

**Micah 6:8 (NIV)**
8 He has shown you, O mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you? To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God.

**Colossians 3:12–14 (NIV)**
12 Therefore, as God’s chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. 13 Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. 14 And over all these virtues put on love, which binds them all together in perfect unity.
