lessons.title: Honor the Lord with your wealth
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that wealth can rust, and that those who are rich should hope in God and be rich in good deeds. Today the word turns to honoring the Lord with your wealth. Honor the LORD with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops; then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine. Better the little that the righteous have than the wealth of many wicked.

Honor is not a tip left at the end if anything remains. It is firstfruits: the first of what you have, given to the Lord as recognition that the harvest is his. The promise of full barns is real in the proverb, and it is not a machine you can work for private gain. We have already heard firstfruits beside the tithe; today’s official texts are Proverbs 3:9–10 and Psalm 37:16–26, so we stay with these words. Honor the LORD with your wealth. Then trust him with the barns.

Psalm 37 holds little and plenty together. Better the little that the righteous have than the wealth of many wicked. The LORD makes firm the steps of the one who delights in him; though he may stumble, he will not fall, for the LORD upholds him with his hand. The righteous give generously. They are always generous and lend freely; their children will be a blessing. The psalmist says, I was young and now I am old, yet I have never seen the righteous forsaken or their children begging bread. Hear that as a testimony of God’s care, not as a taunt against a household in poverty, and not as a promise that no faithful family will ever struggle. The same psalm says it is better to have a little and be righteous, and that in days of famine they will enjoy plenty. The point is the Lord’s faithfulness, not a sneer at people in want.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 3:9–10 or Psalm 37:16–26, so honoring the Lord with wealth is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Proverbs and Psalms. Honor the LORD with your firstfruits. Prefer a righteous little to wicked wealth. Be generous, and trust the Lord who upholds his people.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 3:9 has, Honor Yahweh from your wealth And from the first of all your produce. Proverbs 3:10 has, So your barns will be filled with plenty And your vats will burst with new wine. Psalm 37:16 has, Better is the little of the righteous Than the abundance of many wicked. Psalm 37:25 has, I was young and now I am old, Yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken Or his seed begging bread.

Honor the LORD with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops. Better the little that the righteous have than the wealth of many wicked. Delight in the Lord. Give generously. Trust him to uphold you, and do not use a psalm of care as a wound against the poor.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where could firstfruits, rather than leftovers, honor the Lord in your house this week? What would it look like to prefer a righteous little to a larger pile, and to be generous while you trust him?

**Proverbs 3:9–10 (NIV)**
9 Honor the LORD with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops; 10 then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine.

**Psalm 37:16–26 (NIV)**
16 Better the little that the righteous have than the wealth of many wicked; 17 for the power of the wicked will be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous. 18 The blameless spend their days under the LORD’s care, and their inheritance will endure forever. 19 In times of disaster they will not wither; in days of famine they will enjoy plenty. 20 But the wicked will perish: Though the LORD’s enemies are like the flowers of the field, they will be consumed, they will go up in smoke. 21 The wicked borrow and do not repay, but the righteous give generously; 22 those the LORD blesses will inherit the land, but those he curses will be destroyed. 23 The LORD makes firm the steps of the one who delights in him; 24 though he may stumble, he will not fall, for the LORD upholds him with his hand. 25 I was young and now I am old, yet I have never seen the righteous forsaken or their children begging bread. 26 They are always generous and lend freely; their children will be a blessing.

lessons.title: A budget of the heart: where your treasure is

sources.label: John Piper, Free from Money, Rich Toward God (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we are to honor the Lord with our wealth and firstfruits, and that a righteous little is better than the wealth of many wicked. Today the word turns to a budget of the heart: where your treasure is. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Jesus also says, “No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.”

Today’s official reading in Matthew is 6:21 only. We may remember, in our own words, that moth, rust, and thieves undo earth’s piles, but we do not take those nearby verses as official text today. The sentence itself is enough: your heart follows your treasure. A budget is not only a list of numbers. It is a map of loves. What you fund, delay, hide, or refuse will train the heart, whether the amount is large or small.

Luke 16:10–13 makes the test ordinary. Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much. The official wording of verses 10–12 does not come to us as a short closed quotation, so we hear it in the words themselves. If you have not been trustworthy in handling worldly wealth, who will trust you with true riches? If you have not been trustworthy with someone else’s property, who will give you property of your own? Then comes the closed word: “No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.” Faithfulness in little is not small. A split loyalty will not hold.

In *Free from Money, Rich Toward God*, on Matthew 6:19–21, John Piper teaches that being rich toward God means counting God as your riches, and handling money so as to show that God, not money, is your treasure. Today’s official text in Matthew is 6:21, so we stay inside that range. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Luke 16:10–13, so faithfulness in little, and the refusal of two masters, are taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guides to Matthew and Luke.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Luke 16:10 has, He who is faithful in a very little thing is faithful also in much, and he who is unrighteous in a very little thing is unrighteous also in much. Luke 16:11 has, Therefore if you have not been faithful in the use of unrighteous wealth, who will entrust the true riches to you? Luke 16:13 has, No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.

Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Be trustworthy in very little, and in worldly wealth that is not finally yours. You cannot serve both God and money. Budget the heart, not only the numbers.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, if someone followed only this week’s spending, delaying, and giving, where would they say your heart is? What is one faithful little thing—an account, a promise, a gift, or a refusal—that would tell the truth that you cannot serve both God and money?

**Matthew 6:21 (NIV)**
21 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

**Luke 16:10–13 (NIV)**
10 “Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much. 11 So if you have not been trustworthy in handling worldly wealth, who will trust you with true riches? 12 And if you have not been trustworthy with someone else’s property, who will give you property of your own? 13 “No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.”

lessons.title: Leaving a wise inheritance
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that where your treasure is, there your heart will be also, and that you cannot serve both God and money. Today the word turns to leaving a wise inheritance. A good person leaves an inheritance for their children’s children, but a sinner’s wealth is stored up for the righteous. Blessed are those who fear the LORD, who find great delight in his commands. Paul tells the Corinthians that what he wants is not their possessions but them, because children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

The proverb is larger than a will. A good person leaves an inheritance for their children’s children. That can include money, and it is not wrong to plan for that. It also includes a name, a way of fearing the Lord, and a house that has learned generosity and justice. Psalm 112:1–5 sets the blessing in that soil: those who fear the LORD and delight in his commands; children mighty in the land; wealth and riches in their houses, and righteousness that endures; light in darkness for the gracious and compassionate; good for those who are generous and lend freely, who conduct their affairs with justice. Hear the promises as the psalm’s testimony of a life that fears the Lord, not as a taunt against a household that has little to leave, and not as a machine that turns fear of God into guaranteed riches.

Paul’s sentence in 2 Corinthians 12:14 is official today, and only this verse. He is ready to visit and not be a burden, because what he wants is not their possessions but them. After all, children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. The image is parental care, not a law against grown children who honor aging parents in real need. Paul will not mine the church. A wise inheritance moves toward the next generation, and it does not treat people as a source of goods.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 13:22, Psalm 112:1–5, or 2 Corinthians 12:14, so a wise inheritance is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Proverbs, Psalms, and 2 Corinthians. Leave what will outlast you. Fear the Lord. Want the people themselves, not only what they have.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 13:22 has, A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, And the wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous. 2 Corinthians 12:14 has, I do not seek what is yours, but you. For children ought not to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. In Psalm 112 the LSB names Yahweh and speaks of the man’s seed and house, with the same sense that those who fear the Lord are blessed, that righteousness endures, and that it is well with the one who is gracious and lends.

A good person leaves an inheritance for their children’s children. Fear the LORD, and delight in his commands. Be generous, and conduct your affairs with justice. Do not seek what is theirs, but them. Parents, where you can, save up for your children, and leave more than a pile.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, what are you actually leaving—money, habits, fear of the Lord, or only a mess to clean up? What would one wise step look like this week toward an inheritance your children’s children could receive?

**Proverbs 13:22 (NIV)**
22 A good person leaves an inheritance for their children’s children, but a sinner’s wealth is stored up for the righteous.

**Psalm 112:1–5 (NIV)**
1 Praise the LORD. Blessed are those who fear the LORD, who find great delight in his commands. 2 Their children will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed. 3 Wealth and riches are in their houses, and their righteousness endures forever. 4 Even in darkness light dawns for the upright, for those who are gracious and compassionate and righteous. 5 Good will come to those who are generous and lend freely, who conduct their affairs with justice.

**2 Corinthians 12:14 (NIV)**
14 Now I am ready to visit you for the third time, and I will not be a burden to you, because what I want is not your possessions but you. After all, children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

lessons.title: Work as worship: from the beginning God worked

sources.label: John Piper, Male and Female He Created Them in the Image of God (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that a good person leaves an inheritance for their children’s children, and that parents should not treat their people as possessions. Today the word turns to work as worship: from the beginning God worked. Then God said, “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.” So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them. God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky and over every living creature that moves on the ground.” The LORD God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it.

Work is not a late punishment that sneaks in after the fall. It is there at the beginning, in the blessing of being made in God’s image. To be made in his likeness is not only a dignity to defend. It is a vocation: fill the earth, subdue it, rule as stewards, not as wreckers. Be fruitful and increase in number is a blessing on human life and family, and we hear it with honor, not as a blunt or graphic word. Male and female he created them: the image is given to both, and the charge to tend the world belongs with that gift.

Genesis 2:15 makes the work plain and close to the ground. The LORD God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it. Work and care belong together. lessons.title: Six days you shall labor

sources.label: John Piper, Remember the Sabbath Day to Keep It Holy (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that from the beginning God worked, and that he put the man in the garden to work it and take care of it. Today the word turns to six days you shall labor. Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your male or female servant, nor your animals, nor any foreigner residing in your towns. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, but he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy. Then Paul says, Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving.

The official wording of Exodus 20:8–11 does not come to us as a short closed quotation in this range, because the commandment stands inside a longer speech, so we hear it in the words themselves. Six days you shall labor is a real command, not a shrug. Work has a place, and it has a limit. The seventh day is a sabbath to the LORD your God, a holy rest, not an aimless collapse and not a chance to keep the work running through someone else in the house. The ground of the command is God’s own work and rest in creation. He blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.

Today’s official text in Colossians is 3:23–24, not the verse just before it. Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters. It is the Lord Christ you are serving, and there is an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. Wholehearted work and holy rest belong together. This is not a license for workaholism, and it is not a wound for people who cannot work, or who must labor in uneven hours. Receive the six days as a call to faithful labor, and receive the seventh as a gift from the God who rested.

In *Remember the Sabbath Day to Keep It Holy*, on Exodus 20:8–11, John Piper teaches that Israel is to remember to take a holy day, to keep it for the Lord, to work six and rest one, and that this rest is grounded in God’s rest after creation, a day he blessed and hallowed. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Colossians 3:23–24, so working with all your heart for the Lord is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guides to Exodus and Colossians.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Exodus 20:8 has, Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Exodus 20:10 has, the seventh day is a sabbath of Yahweh your God; in it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter, your male or your female slave or your cattle or your sojourner who is within your gates. Exodus 20:11 has, therefore Yahweh blessed the sabbath day and made it holy. Colossians 3:23 has, Whatever you do, do your work heartily, as for the Lord rather than for men. Colossians 3:24 has, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance. Serve the Lord Christ.

Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, and then you shall rest. Work at whatever you do with all your heart, as working for the Lord. It is the Lord Christ you are serving.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has labor swallowed the holy rest, or rest turned into a way to avoid the six days? What would it look like this week to work with all your heart for the Lord, and to keep a day holy to him?

**Exodus 20:8–11 (NIV)**
8 “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. 9 Six days you shall labor and do all your work, 10 but the seventh day is a sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your male or female servant, nor your animals, nor any foreigner residing in your towns. 11 For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, but he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.

**Colossians 3:23–24 (NIV)**
23 Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, 24 since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving.

lessons.title: Work with all your heart, as working for the Lord

sources.label: John Piper, Slavery and Christ’s Supreme Lordship (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard, Six days you shall labor, and also, Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord. Today the word widens that same call: work with all your heart, as working for the Lord. The official range in Colossians is now 3:22–24. Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything; and do it, not only when their eye is on you and to curry their favor, but with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord. Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving. Ephesians 6:5–8 speaks in the same household world: Slaves, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear, and with sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ.

These sentences must be heard with dignity. They address people who were enslaved in the Roman world. They are not a defense of owning people, and they are not a tool for a harsh employer. The wound of that system is real, and we do not soften it, or turn it into a joke, or use the text to tell someone to stay under harm. What the apostle presses, inside that world, is this: do not live by eye-service. Work with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord. It is the Lord Christ you are serving. There is an inheritance from the Lord as a reward, even where an earthly master could give none.

Ephesians 6:5–8 stays inside today’s official range. Obey not only to win favor when an eye is on you, but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart. Serve wholeheartedly, as if you were serving the Lord, not people, because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good they do, whether they are slave or free. The reward does not skip the hidden good. Today’s official texts do not include the next words to masters; we may remember, in our own words, that the letters also bind those who had power, but we do not take those verses as official reading today. For a house now, the living nerve is this: work for Christ, not for the eye, in every rightful task.

In *Slavery and Christ’s Supreme Lordship*, on Colossians 3:22–4:1, John Piper teaches that Christians magnify the supreme lordship of Christ in the way they serve under earthly authorities, and that we work heartily as for the Lord and not for men, because earthly lordship is not ultimate. Today’s official text in Colossians is 3:22–24, so we stay inside that range and do not take 3:25 or 4:1 as official reading for this lesson. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Ephesians 6:5–8, so that word is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guides to Colossians and Ephesians.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Colossians 3:22 has, Slaves, in all things obey those who are your masters according to the flesh, not with eyeservice, as men-pleasers, but with integrity of heart, fearing the Lord. Colossians 3:23 has, do your work heartily, as for the Lord rather than for men. Ephesians 6:5 has, Slaves, be obedient to those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in the integrity of your heart, as to Christ. Ephesians 6:8 has, knowing that whatever good thing each one does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether slave or free.

Do not work only when an eye is on you. Work with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord. Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters. It is the Lord Christ you are serving, and he will reward the good, whether a person is slave or free. Hear the old household words with care, and do not use them to defend harm.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has work in your house become eye-service—only the tasks someone will notice? What would it look like today to do one hidden thing with all your heart, as working for the Lord Christ?

**Colossians 3:22–24 (NIV)**
22 Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything; and do it, not only when their eye is on you and to curry their favor, but with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord. 23 Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, 24 since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving.

**Ephesians 6:5–8 (NIV)**
5 Slaves, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear, and with sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ. 6 Obey them not only to win their favor when their eye is on you, but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart. 7 Serve wholeheartedly, as if you were serving the Lord, not people, 8 because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good they do, whether they are slave or free.

lessons.title: Integrity when no one is watching

sources.label: John Piper, Daniel’s Defiance of Darius in Prayer (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we are to work with all our heart as working for the Lord, not only when an eye is on us. Today the word turns to integrity when no one is watching. The integrity of the upright guides them, but the unfaithful are destroyed by their duplicity. Daniel so distinguished himself among the administrators and the satraps by his exceptional qualities that the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom. They tried to find grounds for charges against him in his conduct of government affairs, but they could find no corruption in him, because he was trustworthy and neither corrupt nor negligent.

Integrity is not a pose for an audience. It guides the upright when the room is empty. Duplicity destroys the unfaithful, often first by splitting the inner life, and then by being found out. Daniel’s public work could be inspected. They went looking for a charge in his conduct of government affairs, and they were unable to do so. He was trustworthy, and neither corrupt nor negligent. The exception they finally named was not a hidden crime. They said, “We will never find any basis for charges against this man Daniel unless it has something to do with the law of his God.”

Today’s official reading in Daniel is 6:3–5, not the verses that follow. We do not leave this range to tell the later plot, the decree, or the den as official text. What is in front of us is already enough: a life so clean in its work that the only opening left was his loyalty to God. Integrity when no one is watching is not a small private hobby. It is how a person becomes, over time, either trustworthy or double. The same God who held Daniel’s work will be heard again in a later week, when he keeps praying.

In *Daniel’s Defiance of Darius in Prayer*, on Daniel 6:1–13, John Piper hears Daniel’s name and life as a man who lived as if God, not man, were his judge, and the sermon’s official span includes today’s verses about his excellent and blameless work. Today’s official text is Daniel 6:3–5, so we stay inside that range and do not take 6:1–2 or 6:6–13 as official reading for this lesson. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 11:3, so the integrity of the upright is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guides to Proverbs and Daniel.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 11:3 has, The integrity of the upright will lead them, But the crookedness of the treacherous will destroy them. Daniel 6:3 has, Then this Daniel began distinguishing himself among the commissioners and satraps because an extraordinary spirit was in him. Daniel 6:4 has, they were not able to find any ground of accusation or evidence of corruption, inasmuch as he was faithful, and no negligence or corruption was to be found in him. Daniel 6:5 has, We will not find any ground of accusation against this Daniel unless we find it against him with regard to the law of his God.

The integrity of the upright guides them. Be trustworthy, and neither corrupt nor negligent, when no one is watching. Let there be no hidden charge in the work itself. If a complaint comes, let it have to do with loyalty to God, not with duplicity.

lessons.title: Skill, excellence, and a job done well
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the integrity of the upright guides them, and that Daniel was trustworthy and neither corrupt nor negligent. Today the word turns to skill, excellence, and a job done well. Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank. Then the LORD said to Moses that he had chosen Bezalel of the tribe of Judah, and had filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills, to make artistic designs, to cut and set stones, to work in wood, and to engage in all kinds of crafts. He also appointed Oholiab to help him, and gave ability to all the skilled workers to make everything he had commanded.

The official wording of Exodus 31:1–6 does not come to us as a closed typographic unit in this range, because the LORD’s speech continues, so we hear it in the words themselves. Skill is not a secular leftover, as if the Spirit only fell on preachers. The LORD filled Bezalel with the Spirit of God for wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and crafts: gold, silver, bronze, stone, wood. He appointed a helper, and he put ability in other skilled workers too. Excellence in a job can be obedience. A well-made thing can serve the worship of God.

Proverbs 22:29 asks if you see someone skilled in their work, and says they will serve before kings, not before officials of low rank. Hear the proverb as honor for skill, not as a guarantee that every careful worker will be promoted on a timetable, and not as contempt for humble posts. Kings may notice skill, and God already has. A job done well, whether anyone famous is watching or not, belongs with yesterday’s integrity and with the Spirit who gives ability.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 22:29 or Exodus 31:1–6, so skill and a job done well are taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Proverbs and Exodus. The Spirit can fill a craftsman. Skill can serve before kings. Do the work well.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 22:29 has, Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will stand before kings; He will not stand before obscure men. Exodus 31:2–3 has, See, I have called by name Bezalel, the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. And I have filled him with the Spirit of God in wisdom, in discernment, in knowledge, and in all kinds of craftsmanship. Exodus 31:6 has, in the hearts of all who are wise at heart I have put wisdom, that they may make all that I have commanded you.

Do you see someone skilled in their work? Honor that skill, and pursue it. The LORD filled Bezalel with his Spirit for craft and wisdom, and he gave ability to other workers too. A job done well can be a holy thing.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, what work in your hands has been good enough to get by, but not yet done with the skill you could give it? What would one excellent, honest improvement look like this week?

**Proverbs 22:29 (NIV)**
29 Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank.

**Exodus 31:1–6 (NIV)**
1 Then the LORD said to Moses, 2 “See, I have chosen Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, 3 and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills— 4 to make artistic designs for work in gold, silver and bronze, 5 to cut and set stones, to work in wood, and to engage in all kinds of crafts. 6 Moreover, I have appointed Oholiab son of Ahisamak, of the tribe of Dan, to help him. Also I have given ability to all the skilled workers to make everything I have commanded you:

lessons.title: Whatever you do, do it all for the Lord

sources.label: John Piper, The Joyful Duty of Man (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the LORD filled a craftsman with his Spirit for skill, and that a job done well can serve before kings. Today the word gathers the week into one aim: whatever you do, do it all for the Lord. So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God. And whatever you do, whether in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

The field is as wide as a life. Eating and drinking are not too small for the glory of God, and word and deed are not two separate religions. Whatever you do is the point. The glory of God is not a thin layer you add after the real work is finished. It is the reason for the work, the meal, the sentence, the hidden chore. Colossians 3:17 adds the name: do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him. The name is not a tag you stamp on a selfish plan. It means the work is done under his authority, in a way that can be offered to him, with thanks.

This is a budget of the whole day, not only of money. Six days of labor, a holy rest, integrity when no one is watching, skill in the work, and now the end toward which they run: the glory of God, the name of the Lord Jesus, and thanks to the Father. A small life can hold all of that. A famous life can miss it. Do it all for the Lord.

In *The Joyful Duty of Man*, on 1 Corinthians 10:31, John Piper teaches that if God made us for his glory, then we should live for his glory, and that to glorify him is not empty duty but the way we love, trust, thank, and obey him in ordinary acts, even in eating and drinking. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Colossians 3:17, so doing all in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks, is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guides to 1 Corinthians and Colossians.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 1 Corinthians 10:31 has, Whether, then, you eat or drink or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Colossians 3:17 has, And whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him.

Whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God. Whatever you do, whether in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him. Let the whole day belong to him.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, if someone followed only this day’s ordinary words and deeds, would they be able to tell that you meant them for the glory of God? What is one meal, chore, or sentence you can do today in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks?

**1 Corinthians 10:31 (NIV)**
31 So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God.

**Colossians 3:17 (NIV)**
17 And whatever you do, whether in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

lessons.title: Sloth, excuses, and the sluggard
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that whatever you do, whether you eat or drink, you are to do it all for the glory of God, and in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks. Today the word turns to sloth, excuses, and the sluggard. Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest. How long will you lie there, you sluggard? When will you get up from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest—and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man.

Today’s official range in Proverbs 6 is 6–11, so the ant is still here, and the warning now runs all the way to a little more sleep. We have already heard the ant as a picture of wise provision. Today the same lines confront the sluggard: no commander is needed for the ant to store in summer, but the sluggard keeps folding the hands. The wound is not ordinary tiredness, and it is not the rest God later commands. It is delay that will not rise, and excuse that will not start.

Proverbs 26:13–16 makes the excuses plain. A sluggard says, “There’s a lion in the road, a fierce lion roaming the streets!” As a door turns on its hinges, so a sluggard turns on his bed. A sluggard buries his hand in the dish; he is too lazy to bring it back to his mouth. A sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven people who answer discreetly. Hear this with dignity. The proverb unmasks invented danger and self-trust, not a person who is ill, grieving, or truly unable to work, and not a child to be mocked. Some fears are real. The sluggard’s lion is an excuse that keeps the hands folded. Wisdom gets up, stores in summer, and does not call itself wiser than everyone who would help.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Proverbs 6:6–11 or 26:13–16, so sloth, excuses, and the sluggard are taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guide to Proverbs. Consider the ant. Get up from the delay. Do not let a little more rest become a life of folded hands, and do not invent a lion to keep you in bed.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Proverbs 6:6 has, Go to the ant, O sluggard, Observe her ways and be wise. Proverbs 6:11 has, Your poverty will come in like a vagabond And your want like an armed man. Proverbs 26:14–16 keep the same pictures, with only small differences of wording: the door on its hinges, the hand in the dish, and the sluggard wiser in his own eyes than seven who answer discreetly.

Go to the ant and be wise. Store in summer. Do not lie there with a little more sleep, a little more slumber, a little more folding of the hands. Do not invent a lion in the road to cover delay. Get up, and do not be wiser in your own eyes than those who answer discreetly.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has a little more delay, or a well-dressed excuse, kept a needed task folded in your hands? What would it look like today to rise and do the next faithful thing, without mocking your own weariness or anyone else’s limits?

**Proverbs 6:6–11 (NIV)**
6 Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! 7 It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, 8 yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest. 9 How long will you lie there, you sluggard? When will you get up from your sleep? 10 A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest— 11 and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man.

**Proverbs 26:13–16 (NIV)**
13 A sluggard says, “There’s a lion in the road, a fierce lion roaming the streets!” 14 As a door turns on its hinges, so a sluggard turns on his bed. 15 A sluggard buries his hand in the dish; he is too lazy to bring it back to his mouth. 16 A sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven people who answer discreetly.

lessons.title: Fair bosses and faithful workers

sources.label: John Piper, Jesus Is Precious as the Foundation of the Family (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard the sluggard’s delay and excuses. Today the word turns to the other side of the work: fair bosses and faithful workers. James speaks sharply to rich people who have hoarded wealth, withheld wages, and lived in luxury. Paul says, And masters, treat your slaves in the same way. Do not threaten them, since you know that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with him. Leviticus says, Do not defraud or rob your neighbor. Do not hold back the wages of a hired worker overnight.

James 5:1–6 is a hard passage, and it should be heard again with dignity, not as a sneer and not as a scene to linger on. Wealth has rotted. The wages they failed to pay the workers who mowed their fields are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty. They have lived in luxury and self-indulgence. They have condemned and murdered the innocent one, who was not opposing them. We say that simply, and with care. The warning is about injustice that withholds what is owed and trusts rusting treasure.

Leviticus 19:13 says the same thing in a day’s work: Do not defraud or rob your neighbor. Do not hold back the wages of a hired worker overnight. lessons.title: Ambition, calling, and the gift of limits

sources.label: John Piper, Assessing Ourselves with Our God-Assigned Measure of Faith, Part 2 (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that bosses and workers stand under the same Master in heaven, and that wages must not be held back. Today the word turns to ambition, calling, and the gift of limits. For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgment, in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you. We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. And Moses prays, May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us—yes, establish the work of our hands.

Today’s official reading in Romans is 12:3–8, not the verses just before it. The first word is a limit, and it is a gift. Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought. Think with sober judgment, in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you. Ambition that ignores that measure will swell, and then it will use other people as a stage. Sober judgment is not self-hatred. It is a true size: one body, many members, different functions, each member belonging to the others.

The gifts follow the same grace. If it is prophesying, then prophesy in accordance with your faith; if serving, then serve; if teaching, then teach; if encouraging, then give encouragement; if giving, then give generously; if leading, do it diligently; if showing mercy, do it cheerfully. Calling is not a hunt for the most impressive gift. It is the grace already given, used for the body. Psalm 90:17 then asks the Lord to establish the work of our hands. We do not have to make our work last by thinking more highly of ourselves. We ask him to set it in place, within the limits he has assigned.

In *Assessing Ourselves with Our God-Assigned Measure of Faith, Part 2*, on Romans 12:1–8, John Piper teaches that we must not think more highly of ourselves than we ought, but think with sober judgment according to the measure of faith God has assigned, and that different gifts are given by grace to be used. Today’s official text in Romans is 12:3–8, so we stay inside that range. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Psalm 90:17, so the prayer that God would establish the work of our hands is taught from the text itself and from the BibleProject guides to Romans and Psalms.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Romans 12:3 has, not to think more highly of himself than he ought to think; but to think so as to have sound thinking, as God has allotted to each a measure of faith. Romans 12:6 has, having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us. Psalm 90:17 has, Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us; And establish for us the work of our hands; Establish the work of our hands.

Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought. Think with sober judgment, according to the faith God has distributed to you. Use the gift grace has given, and belong to the other members of the body. Ask the Lord to establish the work of your hands.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has ambition outrun the measure of faith and gift actually given to you? What would it look like this week to serve, teach, give, lead, or show mercy inside that limit, and to ask the Lord to establish the work of your hands?

**Romans 12:3–8 (NIV)**
3 For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgment, in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you. 4 For just as each of us has one body with many members, and these members do not all have the same function, 5 so in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others. 6 We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. If your gift is prophesying, then prophesy in accordance with your faith; 7 if it is serving, then serve; if it is teaching, then teach; 8 if it is to encourage, then give encouragement; if it is giving, then give generously; if it is to lead, do it diligently; if it is to show mercy, do it cheerfully.

**Psalm 90:17 (NIV)**
17 May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us— yes, establish the work of our hands.

lessons.title: Witness at work: salt and light on the job
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we must not think of ourselves more highly than we ought, and that God gives different gifts by grace. Today the word turns to witness at work: salt and light on the job. You are the salt of the earth. You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden. In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven. Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us.

The official wording of Matthew 5:13–16 does not come to us as short closed quotations in this range, because the sermon’s speech continues, so we hear it in the words themselves. Salt can lose its saltiness, and then it is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot. Light is not lit to be put under a bowl, but on a stand, where it gives light to everyone in the house. The aim is not that people would praise you for being useful at work. It is that they would see good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

1 Peter 2:12 sets that life among people who may already be ready to accuse you. Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us. Titus 2:9–10 then speaks inside a Roman household: Teach slaves to be subject to their masters in everything, to try to please them, not to talk back to them, and not to steal from them, but to show that they can be fully trusted, so that in every way they will make the teaching about God our Savior attractive. Hear this with dignity. The text is not a defense of owning people, and it is not a tool for a harsh employer. The living nerve is trustworthy work, a mouth that does not steal or talk back in spite, so that the teaching about the Savior becomes attractive. Salt and light at a job look like good work that can be trusted, not like a speech that leaves the work undone.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Matthew 5:13–16, 1 Peter 2:12, or Titus 2:9–10, so salt and light on the job are taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Matthew, 1 Peter, and Titus. Let your light shine. Live such good lives that even an accusation has to look at the work. Make the teaching about God our Savior attractive by being trustworthy.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Matthew 5:13 has, You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has become tasteless, how will it be made salty again? Matthew 5:16 has, Let your light shine before men in such a way that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven. 1 Peter 2:12 has, by keeping your conduct excellent among the Gentiles, so that in the thing which they slander you as evildoers, they may because of your good works, as they observe them, glorify God in the day of visitation. Titus 2:10 has, not pilfering, but demonstrating all good faith so that they will adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in everything.

You are the salt of the earth. You are the light of the world. Let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven. Live such a good life at work that an accusation cannot hide the work. Be trustworthy, so that the teaching about God our Savior is made attractive.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, if someone at your work, or in the unpaid work of your house, watched only this week’s ordinary tasks, would the teaching about the Savior look more attractive? What is one trustworthy, unshowy good deed that could let the light shine?

**Matthew 5:13–16 (NIV)**
13 “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its saltiness, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot. 14 “You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden. 15 Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a bowl. Instead they put it on its stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. 16 In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

**1 Peter 2:12 (NIV)**
12 Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us.

**Titus 2:9–10 (NIV)**
9 Teach slaves to be subject to their masters in everything, to try to please them, not to talk back to them, 10 and not to steal from them, but to show that they can be fully trusted, so that in every way they will make the teaching about God our Savior attractive.

lessons.title: Rest is obedience, not laziness

sources.label: John Piper, Be Diligent to Enter God’s Rest (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that we are to be salt and light in ordinary work, so that good deeds glorify the Father. Today the word turns to rest as obedience, not laziness. The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all they had done and taught. Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” Six days do your work, but on the seventh day do not work, so that your ox and your donkey may rest, and so that the slave born in your household and the foreigner living among you may be refreshed. There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God.

Jesus does not treat rest as a prize for people who have already finished everything. The apostles had been working, the crowd still pressed, and they had not even had a chance to eat. He said, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” So they went away by themselves in a boat to a solitary place. This is not the sluggard’s little more sleep. It is obedience: coming with him, and actually stopping.

Exodus 23:12 says the same from the other side of the week. The official wording does not come to us as a closed quotation in this single verse, so we hear it in the words themselves. Six days do your work, but on the seventh day do not work, so that your ox and your donkey may rest, and so that the slave born in your household and the foreigner living among you may be refreshed. Rest is not only for the one who can afford it. It is meant to refresh the ones who might otherwise be kept at the work. Hebrews 4:9–11 then opens a larger rest: There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God; for anyone who enters God’s rest also rests from their works, just as God did from his. Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one will perish by following their example of disobedience. Hear that last line with care. The danger is unbelief that will not enter, not a scare to drive a tired household. Rest is a gift to enter, and it takes effort to stop, to trust, and not to copy a hard heart.

In *Be Diligent to Enter God’s Rest*, on Hebrews 4:1–11, John Piper teaches that there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, and that we must be diligent to enter that rest, not falling through the same example of unbelief. Today’s official text in Hebrews is 4:9–11, so we stay inside that range. I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Mark 6:30–32 or Exodus 23:12, so Jesus’ call to a quiet place, and the seventh day’s refreshment for every worker in the house, are taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Mark, Exodus, and Hebrews.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Mark 6:31 has, Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while. lessons.title: Rest is obedience, not laziness

sources.label: John Piper, Be Diligent to Enter God’s Rest (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning. Yesterday we heard that we are to be salt and light in ordinary work, so that good deeds glorify the Father. Today the word turns to rest as obedience, not laziness. The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all they had done and taught. Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” Six days do your work, but on the seventh day do not work, so that your ox and your donkey may rest, and so that the slave born in your household and the foreigner living among you may be refreshed. There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God.

Jesus does not treat rest as a prize for people who have already finished everything. The apostles had been working, the crowd still pressed, and they had not even had a chance to eat. He said, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” So they went away by themselves in a boat to a solitary place. This is not the sluggard’s little more sleep. It is obedience: coming with him, and actually stopping.

Exodus 23:12 says the same from the other side of the week. The official wording does not come to us as a closed quotation in this single verse, so we hear it in the words themselves. Six days do your work, but on the seventh day do not work, so that your ox and your donkey may rest, and so that the slave born in your household and the foreigner living among you may be refreshed. Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one will perish by following their example of disobedience. Hear that last line with care. lessons.title: The Lord blesses the work of your hands
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that rest is obedience, not laziness, and that there remains a Sabbath-rest for the people of God. Today the word turns to the Lord who blesses the work of your hands. If you fully obey the LORD your God and carefully follow all his commands I give you today, the LORD your God will set you high above all the nations on earth. All these blessings will come on you and accompany you if you obey the LORD your God. Then Moses prays, May your deeds be shown to your servants, your splendor to their children. May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us—yes, establish the work of our hands.

Deuteronomy 28:1–8 is a covenant word to Israel: blessed in the city and in the country; the fruit of the womb, the crops, and the young of the livestock; the basket and the kneading trough; blessed when you come in and when you go out; enemies defeated; a blessing on the barns and on everything you put your hand to, in the land he is giving you. Hear this with honor, and with care. It is not a machine you can work for private gain, and it is not a taunt against a household whose work has not been easy, or whose barn is not full. The blessing is tied to listening to the LORD your God, and it is his gift in the land he gives.

Psalm 90:16–17, today’s official pair, asks for something that can be prayed in any house: May your deeds be shown to your servants, your splendor to their children. May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us—yes, establish the work of our hands. We already heard verse 17 beside the gift of limits. Today the prayer is fuller: show your deeds, show your splendor to the children, and set the work of our hands in place. The Lord blesses the work of your hands, and we still have to ask him to establish it.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Deuteronomy 28:1–8 or Psalm 90:16–17, so the Lord who blesses the work of your hands is taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Deuteronomy and Psalms. Obey the LORD your God. Ask him to show his deeds, and to establish the work of your hands.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Deuteronomy 28:1 has, if you diligently listen to the voice of Yahweh your God, being careful to do all His commandments which I am commanding you today, Yahweh your God will set you high above all the nations of the earth. Deuteronomy 28:8 has, Yahweh will command the blessing upon you in your barns and in all that you send forth your hand to do, and He will bless you in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. Psalm 90:16 has, Let Your work appear to Your slaves And Your majesty to their sons. Psalm 90:17 has, Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us; And establish for us the work of our hands; Establish the work of our hands.

If you obey the LORD your God, his blessing is not a small thing: city and country, coming in and going out, barns and the work of the hand. Do not turn that into a boast or a wound. Pray, May your deeds be shown to your servants, your splendor to their children. Ask him to establish the work of your hands.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where have you asked the Lord only for more work, and not for his favor to rest on the work already in your hands? What would it look like today to obey him in one task, and to ask him to establish it?

**Deuteronomy 28:1–8 (NIV)**
1 If you fully obey the LORD your God and carefully follow all his commands I give you today, the LORD your God will set you high above all the nations on earth. 2 All these blessings will come on you and accompany you if you obey the LORD your God: 3 You will be blessed in the city and blessed in the country. 4 The fruit of your womb will be blessed, and the crops of your land and the young of your livestock—the calves of your herds and the lambs of your flocks. 5 Your basket and your kneading trough will be blessed. 6 You will be blessed when you come in and blessed when you go out. 7 The LORD will grant that the enemies who rise up against you will be defeated before you. They will come at you from one direction but flee from you in seven. 8 The LORD will send a blessing on your barns and on everything you put your hand to. The LORD your God will bless you in the land he is giving you.

**Psalm 90:16–17 (NIV)**
16 May your deeds be shown to your servants, your splendor to their children. 17 May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us— yes, establish the work of our hands.

lessons.title: When work is frustrating: thorns and grace
lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the LORD blesses the work of your hands, and we asked him to establish that work. Today the word tells the truth about when work is frustrating: thorns and grace. To Adam he said that the ground was cursed because of him; through painful toil he would eat food from it all the days of his life. It will produce thorns and thistles, and by the sweat of your brow you will eat your food until you return to the ground, since from it you were taken; for dust you are and to dust you will return. The Preacher then asks, What do people get for all the toil and anxious striving with which they labor under the sun? All their days their work is grief and pain; even at night their minds do not rest.

Today’s official reading in Genesis is 3:17–19, not the earlier sentences of the chapter. We hear it with care. The Lord addresses Adam because he ate from the tree about which God had commanded, You must not eat from it. The official typography of that speech is one long word from beginning to end, so we do not break it into invented quotations. Because you listened to your wife is not a license to blame a wife, or to make a harsh joke. The disobedience is Adam’s, and the command was God’s. The curse falls on the ground: painful toil, thorns and thistles, sweat, and a return to dust. Work itself was already in the garden. What enters here is frustration, weariness, and death in the field where we earn our bread.

Ecclesiastes 2:22–24 tells that same weariness from inside a life of toil. What do people get for all the toil and anxious striving with which they labor under the sun? All their days their work is grief and pain; even at night their minds do not rest. This too is meaningless. And then grace is not withheld: A person can do nothing better than to eat and drink and find satisfaction in their own toil. This too, I see, is from the hand of God. The thorns are real. So is the gift of being able to eat, drink, and find some satisfaction in the work, from God’s hand, even in a cursed ground. You do not have to pretend the work is easy. You also do not have to call every frustration meaningless as if God had left the field.

I did not find a Piper /messages/ sermon whose main text is Genesis 3:17–19 or Ecclesiastes 2:22–24, so thorns and grace in frustrating work are taught from the texts themselves and from the BibleProject guides to Genesis and Ecclesiastes. The ground is cursed with painful toil, thorns, sweat, and dust. Even then, to eat and drink and find satisfaction in toil can be from the hand of God.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Genesis 3:17 has, Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree about which I commanded you, saying, You shall not eat from it; Cursed is the ground because of you; In pain you will eat of it All the days of your life. Genesis 3:19 has, By the sweat of your face You will eat bread, Till you return to the ground, Because from it you were taken; For you are dust, And to dust you shall return. Ecclesiastes 2:23 has, Because all his days his endeavor is painful and vexing; even at night his heart does not lie down. This too is vanity. Ecclesiastes 2:24 has, There is nothing better for a man than to eat and drink and have his soul see good in his labor. This also I have seen that it is from the hand of God.

The ground is cursed with painful toil, thorns and thistles, and the sweat of your brow, until you return to the dust. That is why work can be so hard, even when the work itself is good. Even at night the mind may not rest. And still, from the hand of God, a person may eat and drink and find satisfaction in their own toil. Receive the thorns honestly, and receive the grace.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has this week’s work felt like thorns, sweat, or a mind that will not rest at night? What would it look like to tell God the truth about that frustration, and still receive some satisfaction in the toil as a gift from his hand?

**Genesis 3:17–19 (NIV)**
17 To Adam he said, “Because you listened to your wife and ate fruit from the tree about which I commanded you, ‘You must not eat from it,’ “Cursed is the ground because of you; through painful toil you will eat food from it all the days of your life. 18 It will produce thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. 19 By the sweat of your brow you will eat your food until you return to the ground, since from it you were taken; for dust you are and to dust you will return.”

**Ecclesiastes 2:22–24 (NIV)**
22 What do people get for all the toil and anxious striving with which they labor under the sun? 23 All their days their work is grief and pain; even at night their minds do not rest. This too is meaningless. 24 A person can do nothing better than to eat and drink and find satisfaction in their own toil. This too, I see, is from the hand of God,

lessons.title: Vocational faithfulness over a lifetime

sources.label: John Piper, The Second Coming: Not Before the ‘Man of Lawlessness’ (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that when work is frustrating, there are thorns and there is grace, and that even then satisfaction in toil can be from the hand of God. Today the word turns to vocational faithfulness over a lifetime. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, we command you, brothers and sisters, to keep away from every believer who is idle and disruptive and does not live according to the teaching you received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to follow our example. We were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone’s food without paying for it. On the contrary, we worked night and day, laboring and toiling so that we would not be a burden to any of you. We did this, not because we do not have the right to such help, but in order to offer ourselves as a model for you to imitate. For even when we were with you, we gave you this rule: “The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat.” We hear that some among you are idle and disruptive. They are not busy; they are busybodies. Such people we command and urge in the Lord Jesus Christ to settle down and earn the food they eat. And as for you, brothers and sisters, never tire of doing what is good. Commit to the LORD whatever you do, and he will establish your plans.

Today’s official reading in 2 Thessalonians is 3:6–13, not the earlier sentences of the letter and not 3:14–15. We hear the command with care. “The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat.” is a word about willingness, not about people who cannot work, people who are looking for work, or people who are sick, injured, or caring for someone else. It is not a weapon to use against the poor. Paul had been a model among them: he worked night and day, laboring and toiling so that he would not be a burden, even though he had the right to such help. The trouble he names is a believer who is idle and disruptive, not busy but a busybody. Such people he commands and urges in the Lord Jesus Christ to settle down and earn the food they eat. And then he turns to the rest: never tire of doing what is good. Vocational faithfulness is not a hard stare at someone else’s table. It is a long obedience of honest work and of not growing weary in good.

In *The Second Coming: Not Before the Man of Lawlessness*, John Piper’s listed scripture runs from 2 Thessalonians 2:1 through 3:15. We stay inside today’s official 3:6–13, and we do not official-teach the man of lawlessness or the sentences after verse 13. In that message Piper treats Paul’s work among them as a model, the rule that the unwilling should not eat, the charge to settle down and earn the food they eat, and the word not to tire of doing what is good. Proverbs 16:3 then sets the same work before the Lord: Commit to the LORD whatever you do, and he will establish your plans. The plans are not a bargain we force on him. They are work we place in his hands, over a lifetime, and keep doing what is good.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 2 Thessalonians 3:10 has, if anyone is not willing to work, neither let him eat. 3:11 has, some among you are walking in an unruly manner, doing no work at all, but acting like busybodies. 3:12 has, working with quietness, they eat their own bread. 3:13 has, do not lose heart in doing good. lessons.title: The fruit of the Spirit

sources.label: John Piper, The War Within: Flesh Versus Spirit (Desiring God)
John Piper, Walk by the Spirit! (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that vocational faithfulness is a long obedience, and that we are not to tire of doing what is good. Today the word turns to the fruit of the Spirit. So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are in conflict with each other, so that you are not to do whatever you want. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity and debauchery; idolatry and witchcraft; hatred, discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissensions, factions and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit.

Today’s official reading is Galatians 5:16–25, not the earlier sentences of the chapter and not verse 26. We hear the acts of the flesh with care. Paul names them once, and he says they are obvious. We do not linger on them as a graphic catalog, and we do not turn them into a joke. Sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery are named as the text names them, without being described. Idolatry and witchcraft are real turning from God. Hatred, discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissensions, factions, and envy are the ordinary wars of the heart. Drunkenness, orgies, and the like are a serious warning, not a scene to replay. Those who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God. The hope in the same paragraph is not that we can list the flesh more carefully. It is that we walk by the Spirit, and so we will not gratify the desires of the flesh.

In *The War Within: Flesh Versus Spirit*, John Piper’s main text is Galatians 5:16–18. In that message he treats the conflict between flesh and Spirit as real, so that you are not simply free to do whatever you want, and he treats being led by the Spirit as the way you are not under the law. In *Walk by the Spirit!*, his listed scripture is Galatians 5:19–26. We stay inside today’s official 16–25, and we do not official-teach verse 26. In that message he treats the acts of the flesh as obvious, warns that those who live like this will not inherit the kingdom, and then holds out the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit. The fruit is one harvest, not a private talent show. We do not produce it by straining at a list. We keep in step with the Spirit who gives it.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: Galatians 5:19 has, sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality. 5:20 has, idolatry, sorcery. 5:21 has, envying, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these, and that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. 5:22 has patience where the NIV has forbearance. 5:25 has, If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk in step with the Spirit.

The war within is real, and the fruit is real. Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. Keep in step with him, and ask him for love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where has the conflict between flesh and Spirit been obvious this week—in anger, selfish ambition, or another desire the text names? What would it look like to keep in step with the Spirit, and to ask him for the fruit he actually gives, rather than to manage the flesh alone?

**Galatians 5:16–25 (NIV)**
16 So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. 17 For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are in conflict with each other, so that you are not to do whatever you want. 18 But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. 19 The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity and debauchery; 20 idolatry and witchcraft; hatred, discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissensions, factions 21 and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God. 22 But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23 gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law. 24 Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. 25 Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit.

lessons.title: Love is the greatest

sources.label: John Piper, A Call to Love — and to Death (Desiring God)

lessons.body:
Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, and that we are to keep in step with the Spirit. Today the word says that love is the greatest. If I speak in the tongues of men or of angels, but do not have love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have a faith that can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. If I give all I possess to the poor and give over my body to hardship that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing. Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres. Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be stilled; where there is knowledge, it will pass away. For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when completeness comes, what is in part disappears. When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I put the ways of childhood behind me. For now we see only a reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.

Today’s official reading is 1 Corinthians 13:1–13. Gifts without love are noise, and even costly giving without love gains nothing. We hear verse 3 with care. The NIV speaks of giving over my body to hardship that I may boast; we do not turn that sentence into a scene, and we do not treat hardship as something to display. Without love, even that gains nothing. The middle of the chapter then tells us what love is, and what it is not: patient and kind; not envious, boastful, or proud; not dishonoring, self-seeking, or easily angered; keeping no record of wrongs; not delighting in evil, but rejoicing with the truth; always protecting, trusting, hoping, persevering. Love never fails. Gifts will cease, knowledge will pass away, and we still know only in part. When completeness comes, what is in part disappears. Now we see only a reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.

In *A Call to Love — and to Death*, John Piper’s main text is 1 Corinthians 13:4–7. We teach verses 1–3 and 8–13 from the text itself. In that message Piper walks through love’s descriptions and shows that this kind of love involves a dying to self-centeredness: patience and a refusal to be easily angered, a life that does not seek its own, a love that does not keep a record of wrongs, and a love that bears, believes, hopes, and endures. The aim is not to admire the poem. It is to let this love, which is the greatest of what remains, shape a real life among real people.

Where the LSB wording differs in a way that helps the ear: 1 Corinthians 13:1 has, a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. 13:3 has, if I surrender my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing. 13:5 has, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not take into account a wrong suffered. 13:7 has, it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. 13:10 has, when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away. 13:13 has, But now abide faith, hope, love—these three; but the greatest of these is love.

Gifts will pass, and we still know only in part. Faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love. Ask him to make that love patient and kind in you, not a noise without a heart.

**For reflection.** As a man, husband, and father, where have gifts, knowledge, or even costly effort outrun love this week? What would it look like to put away a record of wrongs, to be patient and kind in one hard place, and to treat love as the greatest of what remains?

**1 Corinthians 13:1–13 (NIV)**
1 If I speak in the tongues of men or of angels, but do not have love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have a faith that can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. 3 If I give all I possess to the poor and give over my body to hardship that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing. 4 Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5 It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. 6 Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. 7 It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres. 8 Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be stilled; where there is knowledge, it will pass away. 9 For we know in part and we prophesy in part, 10 but when completeness comes, what is in part disappears. 11 When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I put the ways of childhood behind me. 12 For now we see only a reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. 13 And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.
